﻿Bruised Tooth / Tooth Sprain with Post-traumatic Complications

Created 2026-08-09
A “bruised” or “sprained” tooth most closely corresponds to traumatic concussion of the tooth/periodontal ligament, or mild subluxation when abnormal mobility is also present without displacement. The primary injury is mechanical damage and inflammation within the periodontal ligament (PDL), but secondary pathology can involve gingival inflammation, pulpal neurogenic inflammation and severe pain, vascular compromise, irreversible pulpitis or pulp necrosis, bacterial invasion and apical infection/abscess, reparative-dentin responses, and associated enamel/dentin fracture. A concomitant crown fracture materially increases the risk of pulp necrosis after concussion or subluxation. Eight mechanistically distinct peptide-addressable axes were identified. Importantly, no peptide can mechanically reunite or stabilize a true macroscopic tooth crack, replace a missing tooth fragment, drain an abscess, or remove necrotic/infected pulp; the hard-tissue peptide axis below concerns biomimetic remineralization of damaged/demineralized mineralized tissue rather than structural repair of a fracture. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis is appropriate because post-traumatic dental injury is not driven by excessive cellular production of one specific endogenous peptide/protein.

1. Periodontal-ligament cellular recovery and attachment-tissue regeneration: CH02 - The seven-residue FGFR-binding peptide GPANVET directly promotes human periodontal-ligament-cell proliferation, migration and osteogenic differentiation, increasing RUNX2, OCN and COL-1 expression. In a periodontal-defect rat model, CH02-treated PDLCs enhanced periodontal tissue/bone repair. This is the most anatomically specific peptide in the set for the actual “sprain” component because the bruised structure surrounding the root is principally the PDL. It remains a regenerative research peptide rather than an established treatment for acute tooth concussion.
2. Resolution of gingival/PDL inflammatory injury: Annexin A1 Ac2-26 - The N-acetylated Annexin-A1 N-terminal mimetic activates the ANXA1/FPR2 pro-resolution pathway. Human PDL experiments and periodontal models show that ANXA1/FPR2 restrains localized inflammatory signaling, while Ac2-26 reduced periodontal inflammatory tissue destruction and alveolar bone resorption experimentally. This provides an inflammation-resolution axis complementary to CH02's regenerative axis and is particularly relevant when traumatic occlusal loading produces surrounding gingival/PDL inflammation.
3. Substance-P/NK1-mediated post-traumatic dental pain and neurogenic inflammation: Spantide I-NH2 - Human dental pulp subjected to experimentally induced occlusal trauma shows a marked increase in substance P, providing unusually direct condition-specific evidence for this pathway. Substance P/NK1 signaling contributes to pulpal vasodilation, inflammatory-cell recruitment and nociceptive signaling. Spantide I is the sequence-defined peptide antagonist [D-Arg1,D-Trp7,9,Leu11]-substance P and therefore directly counterposes this trauma-induced neuropeptide pathway. This is mechanistically attractive for severe inflammatory pain but remains experimental; neurogenic inflammation also participates in tissue defense and repair, so complete suppression cannot automatically be assumed beneficial.
4. CGRP-mediated pulpal neurovascular pain signaling: Human {alpha}-CGRP(8-37)-NH2 - Occlusal trauma also significantly increases CGRP within human dental pulp. The exact C-terminally amidated CGRP(8-37) fragment is a classical CGRP-receptor antagonist, and dental-pulp experiments show that it blocks CGRP-mediated effects on dental pulp stem cells. This supplies a neurovascular/nociceptive axis independent of substance P. There is an important biological trade-off: CGRP can also participate in DPSC recruitment, angiogenesis and subsequent pulp repair, so CGRP blockade is represented as a mechanistic pain-pathway research probe rather than as an unconditional regenerative intervention.
5. Preservation and regeneration of injured/inflamed pulp: Human LL-37 - Native LL-37 directly induces migration of human pulp cells through EGFR/JNK signaling, a critical early component of pulp-dentin-complex regeneration. More recent DPSC studies in an inflammatory environment show increased migration, reduced TNF-{alpha}/IL-1{beta}/IL-6 signaling and enhanced odontogenic differentiation at appropriate experimental concentrations. This makes LL-37 unusually relevant when a traumatized tooth retains living but inflamed pulp and the objective is preservation rather than progression toward necrosis.
6. Secondary endodontic infection and intradentinal biofilm: GH12-NH2 - The exact amphipathic peptide GLLWHLLHHLLH-NH2 has direct endodontic evidence against Enterococcus faecalis: it suppresses growth and biofilm formation, alters virulence/stress-associated gene expression and has been investigated experimentally as a root-canal antimicrobial peptide. This addresses the infection pathway that becomes relevant if traumatic pulp damage progresses to necrosis and microorganisms gain access through caries, a fracture or other communication. E. faecalis is particularly important in persistent endodontic infection; an acute dental abscess is usually polymicrobial, so GH12 should not be interpreted as complete microbiological coverage of an abscess.
7. Odontoblast replacement and reparative-dentin formation after pulp damage: MK-12 - The newly reported midkine-derived peptide KARYNAQCQETI was selected from 15 MK fragments for its mineralization potential. It promotes human DPSC migration and odontogenic differentiation and stimulates DSPP, DMP1, COL1 and RUNX2-associated differentiation through DDIT4/mTOR-dependent autophagy. In a direct-pulp-injury rat model, MK-12 promoted odontoblast-like cells and reparative dentin formation. This 2026 peptide provides particularly direct evidence for the pulp-damage/reparative-dentin axis and is mechanistically distinct from LL-37.
8. Biomimetic remineralization of traumatized/deprotected dentin and enamel-associated mineral: Phosphorylated amelogenin-inspired P26 - P26 combines functional amelogenin domains and promotes hydroxyapatite nucleation, collagen-associated intrafibrillar mineralization and recovery of mineral density/mechanical properties in demineralized dentin. The experimentally described peptide is MPLPSYEVLTPLKWPSTDKTKREEVD with Ser16 phosphorylated. This axis is relevant to microscopic mineral damage, exposed/deprotected dentin and remineralizable tissue bordering a chip or fracture. It cannot close a macroscopic crack, restore the geometry of a chipped cusp/incisal edge, or prevent propagation of a mechanically unstable fracture; those defects require conventional dental stabilization/restoration.

﻿Chikungunya is an infectious disease caused by the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a single-stranded RNA alphavirus belonging to the Togaviridae family, primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. The disease is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, with outbreaks reported in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. The incubation period ranges from 2 to 12 days, after which patients experience an abrupt onset of high fever (often exceeding 39 C), severe and debilitating joint pain (arthralgia) that can affect multiple joints symmetrically, muscle pain (myalgia), headache, fatigue, nausea, and a maculopapular rash that may appear on the trunk and limbs. In some cases, patients develop conjunctivitis, photophobia, or mild hemorrhagic manifestations. The acute phase lasts 7-10 days, but up to 60% of patients progress to a chronic phase characterized by persistent or relapsing arthralgia, stiffness, and swelling, which can last for months or years, significantly impacting quality of life and mimicking rheumatoid arthritis. Vulnerable populations include the elderly, newborns, pregnant women, and individuals with comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease, who may experience severe complications like myocarditis, hepatitis, neurological disorders (e.g., encephalitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome), or even death in rare cases. Pathophysiologically, following mosquito inoculation, CHIKV replicates in dermal fibroblasts and enters the bloodstream, disseminating to target tissues like joints, muscles, skin, liver, brain, and kidneys. The virus infects fibroblasts, osteoblasts, myocytes, and endothelial cells, inducing apoptosis and triggering a robust innate immune response with type I interferon production. However, CHIKV evades immunity through mechanisms like inhibition of interferon signaling and metabolic reprogramming of host cells. This leads to a cytokine storm involving IL-1{beta}, IL-6, TNF-{alpha}, and MCP-1, causing inflammation, tissue damage, and pain via neural sensitization. Persistent viral RNA in synovial tissues contributes to chronic symptoms. Thromboinflammatory responses, including platelet activation and coagulation dysregulation, may exacerbate vascular issues. Circadian rhythms influence viral replication by modulating host metabolism, while microRNAs regulate bone and joint pathology. Currently, no licensed vaccine or specific antiviral therapy exists; treatment is symptomatic with rest, hydration, acetaminophen for fever/pain, and avoidance of aspirin due to bleeding risks.

The proposed polypeptides comprehensively address Chikungunya by targeting all relevant therapeutic axes, with prioritization of real-world examples supplemented by designed ones where necessary. Real-world polypeptides such as the (p-BthTX-I) derivatives inhibit viral entry by disrupting envelope-membrane fusion and post-entry steps by interfering with endosomal escape and protease activity, reducing viral load as demonstrated in cell-based assays (feasibility high, as these are venom-derived with established antiviral properties). GA-Hecate and PSSct1905 similarly block multiple infection stages through membrane perturbation and intracellular interference, offering broad-spectrum activity with low toxicity in vitro. E2EP3 acts as a neutralizing epitope mimic, binding to viral E2 glycoprotein to prevent attachment and entry, while stimulating protective IgG responses as shown in mouse models. NTQLSEAHVEKS and KTEFASAYR are B- and T-cell epitopes that enhance humoral and cellular immunity, promoting virus-specific antibody production and T-cell mediated clearance, with potential for vaccine or therapeutic use. Thanatin and Latarcin1 exhibit antiviral effects by damaging viral envelopes or inhibiting replication, leveraging their antimicrobial peptide origins for high cell permeability and stability. Sialokinin modulates inflammation by reducing monocyte activation and cytokine release via neurokinin receptors, alleviating joint pain and swelling. Designed polypeptides cover remaining axes: the capsid-targeting peptide disrupts virion assembly by binding key motifs, feasible based on similar inhibitors for other viruses; the immune checkpoint modulator mimics regulatory domains to prevent excessive immunopathology while maintaining antiviral responses; the metabolic modulator interferes with host glycolysis or lipid pathways hijacked by CHIKV, drawing from metabolic inhibitor studies; the thromboinflammatory peptide inhibits platelet aggregation and coagulation factors, reducing vascular complications; the innate immune activator stimulates TLR signaling for enhanced interferon production; the pain-targeting peptide blocks ion channels or neuropeptide receptors to mitigate neural sensitization; the circadian modulator targets clock proteins like BMAL1 to disrupt viral exploitation of rhythmic metabolism; the microRNA regulator mimics protective miRNAs to downregulate inflammatory genes in joints. Resolving Chondrocalcinosis (Pseudogout) requires halting the pathological accumulation of extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate (ePPi) within the articular cartilage and arresting the subsequent crystal-induced inflammatory cascade. Pathophysiologically, hypertrophic chondrocytes within the menisci and synovial joints upregulate the ANKH transmembrane channel and the ENPP1 enzyme, flooding the synovial space with ePPi. These molecules precipitate with ambient calcium to form jagged, insoluble calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals. When synovial macrophages attempt to phagocytose these structural crystals, their lysosomes physically rupture, triggering massive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, causing debilitating acute pseudogout flares and progressive chondro-necrosis. The therapeutic strategy systematically dismantles this cycle by physically blocking the cellular transport and generation of ePPi, biophysically upregulating the endogenous enzymes that dissolve existing pyrophosphate, stabilizing the macrophage phagolysosome, initiating targeted chondrogenesis, and explicitly inhibiting the endogenous synthesis of ENPP1 to permanently cut off the biochemical fuel supply for crystal formation.

1. Axis: NLRP3 Inflammasome Suppression and Acute Flare Arrest - Alpha-MSH (Alpha-Melanocyte-stimulating hormone) is a potent endogenous neuropeptide that binds directly to melanocortin receptors on synovial macrophages. It forcefully downregulates the NLRP3 inflammasome, silencing the massive Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1b) cytokine storm that drives the acute, agonizing pain and severe localized swelling of a pseudogout flare.
2. Axis: Extracellular Pyrophosphate (ePPi) Transport Blockade - Designed peptide engineered via RRM targeting the ANKH transmembrane transporter. The ANKH protein acts as a specialized pump, channeling intracellular PPi into the joint space where it crystallizes. This sequence sterically blocks the efflux channel, trapping PPi safely inside the chondrocyte where it is utilized for normal cellular metabolism rather than crystal formation. Calculated RRM target frequency = 129.65 Hz.
3. Axis: Crystal Dissolution and TNAP Allosteric Activation - Designed peptide engineered via RRM targeting Tissue-Nonspecific Alkaline Phosphatase (TNAP). TNAP is the natural enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing ePPi into soluble inorganic phosphate (Pi), but it is overwhelmed in CPPD. This peptide induces a hyper-active conformational state in TNAP, aggressively dissolving the established calcium pyrophosphate crystals directly from the menisci and articular cartilage. Calculated RRM target frequency = 138.20 Hz.
4. Axis: Cartilage Matrix Regeneration and Proteoglycan Synthesis - Link N is a naturally occurring peptide derived from the link protein of the cartilage proteoglycan aggregate. Following the dissolution of CPP crystals, it functions as a potent chondrogenic growth factor, stimulating deep-tissue synthesis of Type II collagen and aggrecan to repair the structural craters and micro-fractures left by the crystal deposits.
5. Axis: Macrophage Stabilization and Fibrosis Prevention - Ac-SDKP (N-acetyl-Seryl-Aspartyl-Lysyl-Proline) is an endogenous tetrapeptide that acts directly on the cytoskeleton of immune cells. It prevents the catastrophic lysosomal rupture that occurs when macrophages ingest jagged CPP crystals, shifting the joint environment from chronic fibrotic scarring back to healthy synovial homeostasis.
6. Axis: Inhibition of ENPP1 (Ectonucleotide Pyrophosphatase/Phosphodiesterase 1) biosynthesis via Sternheimer proteody - ENPP1 is the primary enzyme responsible for generating pathological levels of ePPi from extracellular ATP within the joint capsule. Inhibitory proteody generated from the full ENPP1 sequence using monoisotopic masses + log symmetrization for phase opposition suppresses its translation. Silencing ENPP1 synthesis directly removes the root cause of the disease, physically preventing the genesis of new calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Calculated inhibitory frequency = 144.75 Hz. Mean log error = 0.0461.

﻿Chorea is a neurological disorder characterized by involuntary, irregular, and unpredictable movements that appear to flow randomly from one body part to another, often resembling dancing or fidgety behavior. The causes of chorea are diverse, including genetic factors such as Huntington's disease (HD) due to CAG repeat expansions in the HTT gene leading to mutant huntingtin protein, autoimmune conditions like Sydenham's chorea following group A streptococcal infection, drug-induced chorea from medications like levodopa or antipsychotics, metabolic disorders (e.g., hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia), vascular events (strokes affecting basal ganglia), infections (e.g., HIV, syphilis), and paraneoplastic syndromes. Symptoms manifest as jerky movements affecting limbs, face, or trunk, impaired coordination, gait instability, dysarthria, dysphagia, and in chronic cases like HD, progressive cognitive impairment, psychiatric disturbances (depression, irritability), and eventual bradykinesia or dystonia. Pathophysiology typically involves dysfunction in the basal ganglia, particularly the striatum, with imbalance between direct (facilitatory) and indirect (inhibitory) pathways, resulting in reduced inhibition of thalamocortical motor circuits; in HD, mutant huntingtin aggregates cause neuronal apoptosis via excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, caspase activation, and inflammation; autoimmune chorea involves molecular mimicry with antibodies targeting basal ganglia neurons; overall, disrupted dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission underlies the hyperkinetic movements.

The proposed polypeptides address chorea by targeting key pathophysiological mechanisms, primarily in genetic and autoimmune forms like HD and Sydenham's. Exendin-4 activates GLP-1 receptors to improve metabolic function, reduce brain pathology, and provide neuroprotection. PACAP modulates glutamatergic signaling and promotes dendritic growth to counteract synaptic dysfunction. Ceruletide influences dopamine systems to acutely and chronically reduce involuntary movements. C16 inhibits integrin-mediated inflammation, reducing leukocyte infiltration and protecting the blood-brain barrier. The remaining polypeptides are designed: designed polypeptides for caspase inhibition compete with cleavage sites to prevent protein fragmentation and apoptosis; designed for mitochondrial protection stabilize complexes and reduce ROS production; designed for dopamine modulation act as stabilizers to balance neurotransmission and lessen hyperkinesia; designed for purinergic signaling target adenosine receptors to attenuate excitotoxicity; designed for gut-brain axis modulate microbiota-inflammation pathways to curb neuroinflammation; designed for opioid system mimic endogenous peptides to regulate motor control; designed for BDNF enhancement upregulate expression for neuronal maintenance; designed for gene modulation alter mutant gene effects via epigenetic mimicry; designed for neuronal survival activate growth factor pathways; designed for excitotoxicity block NMDA receptors selectively; designed for oxidative stress incorporate antioxidant motifs; designed for stem cell promotion stimulate progenitor differentiation. These are feasible with optimized sequences for stability, half-life, and BBB penetration via nasal or injectable routes, supported by existing peptide drugs; designed ones are conceptual, requiring preclinical testing but grounded in known biology.

disease: Chronic Antigen-driven Human T Cell Dysfunction
description:
﻿Created 22 September 2026.

Refer to this link for more information.

The central research objective is to preserve or recover sustained antigen-specific T-cell function by addressing stress-kinase signaling, mitochondrial energy metabolism, and inhibitory signaling-not simply to increase immune activation or lower exhaustion-marker expression. The supplied paper identifies MAP2K4-JNK and MAP2K3-p38 activation, reduced mitochondrial ATP production, altered nucleotide metabolism, and endoplasmic-reticulum stress during persistent TCR stimulation. Its strongest functional intervention was BSJ-04-122, a small molecule, not a peptide. Figure 7H, on PDF page 40, shows improved serial tumor-cell control after treatment during the development of dysfunction. Because treatment began at day 2, this does not establish reversal of an already fixed, terminally exhausted state. The uploaded version is a March 2026 preprint. 
Several findings materially change peptide selection. Chronically stimulated human T cells did not show the mitochondrial ROS accumulation observed in the mouse comparison, so a generic antioxidant program would not faithfully reflect this study. ISRIB reduced an ISR-associated readout but did not produce rescue comparable with BSJ-04-122. IL-7 and IL-15 were already present while dysfunction developed, so adding their names to a program would not constitute a newly demonstrated rescue mechanism. These observations favor testing specific stress-signaling and bioenergetic hypotheses rather than treating every altered protein as a target for inhibition. 
The seven entries below are published peptide scaffolds or recombinant proteins drawn from outside literature and connected to the supplied paper mechanistically. None was tested as a peptide rescue in that paper. Entries 5 and 6 are alternative PD-L1 comparators, not two obligatory components of a combination. “Real” denotes a published peptide or scaffold, not proven treatment efficacy. The mass line is a reference encoding: for entries 1, 2, and 6, free-terminal forms are explicitly specified because the original terminal caps were not resolved from the publications. 
Persistent TCR ligation is necessary and sufficient to establish human T cell dysfunction. In the Kojima et al. time-resolved atlas, chronic {alpha}CD3 restimulation of previously activated CD3+ T cells produced an exhaustion program that mapped to tumor-infiltrating exhausted CD8 cells, with PD-1, LAG3, CTLA4, CD39, TOX and reduced serial killing of NY-ESO-1+ targets. The proteome remodeled beyond the transcriptome: ETC complexes I-IV and mitochondrial ATP fell, human cells limited mitochondrial ROS by shunting NADH into proline, triglycerides and peroxisomal ether lipids, de novo nucleotide synthesis collapsed toward salvage nucleosides, and cysteine-reactivity profiling flagged ATP-sensitive sites on MAP2K4 C246 and MAP2K3 C227 in the JNK/p38 cascade. p53-p21-p16 enforced G0/G1 arrest. ISR and ER-stress (ATF4, CHOP, ATF6, XBP1s) were on; mtUPR was not. The covalent MKK4/7 inhibitor BSJ-04-122 restored cytotoxicity and moved the chronic proteome toward the acute state, whereas thapsigargin imposed an exhaustion-like proteome on acute cells and ISRIB did not rescue. Phospho-MAP2K4/JNK reproduced in LCMV Clone 13, MC38 TILs and RCC PD-1+ TILs.

1. Axis: JNK stress-signaling modulation downstream of MAP2K4 - 8R-sJNKI(-9), free-terminus reference form. This shortened, cell-penetrating JNK-inhibitory scaffold provides a peptide-based way to investigate the JNK arm highlighted by the paper. Its published experimental evidence concerns pancreatic islets and beta-cell systems, not chronically stimulated human T cells. Its role here is therefore an explicit transfer-of-mechanism hypothesis. It is not a direct MAP2K4 inhibitor or an established substitute for BSJ-04-122. The decisive experiment is whether it reduces persistent stress-associated JNK signaling while preserving antigen-triggered cytokine production and repeated target-cell killing; reduced signaling alone would not establish benefit. The reference mass record contains 19 residues and specifies free N and C termini.
2. Axis: Canonical p38 stress-kinase modulation - 11R-p38I110, free-terminus reference form. This published cell-penetrating, p38-derived inhibitory peptide is an orthogonal probe for the p38 component of the dysfunction-associated stress response. Its primary evidence comes from beta-cell and porcine-islet experiments, including inhibition of p38 activation and improved islet outcomes. Rescue of chronic human T-cell dysfunction remains untested. I would evaluate it separately from the JNK inhibitor before investigating a combination, because the supplied study does not establish that simultaneous peptide inhibition of both pathways is necessary or beneficial. The reference record contains the complete 28-residue construct, including its polyarginine delivery segment, with free termini specified.
3. Axis: Mitochondrial inner-membrane function and ATP-production support - Elamipretide / SS-31, C-terminal amide. SS-31 interacts with cardiolipin and has primary experimental evidence for preservation of mitochondrial structure and bioenergetic recovery in ischemic systems. That makes it a mechanistically relevant candidate for testing the paper’s energy-production defect, rather than merely a generic antioxidant addition. However, the supplied paper did not establish cardiolipin injury as the cause of T-cell dysfunction, and the cited SS-31 study did not investigate this human exhaustion model. Its inclusion is conditional on demonstrating improved mitochondrial ATP production together with improved T-cell function. The encoding includes D-arginine, dimethyltyrosine, and the C-terminal amide; ordinary tyrosine would give the wrong descriptor.
4. Axis: IL-21-mediated CD8 T-cell persistence and BATF-associated helper signaling - Recombinant human IL-21, 132-residue E. coli construct, native-disulfide reference form. IL-21 provides an external, condition-relevant counterpoint to stress-pathway inhibition. Chronic viral-infection studies identify an IL-21-BATF pathway that sustains CD8 T-cell persistence and effector function, including cooperation with IRF4. This is more specific than a general “immune booster” rationale, although the causal experiments are not proof of reversal of established human exhaustion. The encoded sequence is the manufacturer-listed 132-residue human research construct, not a precursor or an arbitrary IL-21 fragment. Its native disulfide pairs are mapped from the experimentally determined IL-21 fold; this mapping is not a lot-specific structural assay.
5. Axis: PD-L1 binding and PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade - D-PPA-1 / DPPA-1, all-D peptide moiety. This all-D peptide binds PD-L1 and blocks its interaction with PD-1, with biochemical and preclinical antitumor evidence. It supplies a checkpoint-comparator arm rather than an assumed solution to the underlying metabolic or proteostatic defects. Its relevance should be tested in a system where PD-L1-mediated inhibition is demonstrably operating, and success should require sustained functional improvement rather than an isolated increase in activation. All twelve residues are D-configured. The mass descriptor cannot distinguish them from their L-enantiomers, so stereochemical metadata must remain attached. Acetate or trifluoroacetate counterions are not included in the peptide-moiety encoding.
6. Axis: Alternative PD-L1 blockade, with a PD-L1/CD80 interaction readout - CLP002, free-terminus reference form. CLP002 is a second published PD-L1-binding scaffold. Its discovery study reported blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 and PD-L1/CD80 interactions, improved proliferation and survival in Jurkat-tumor-cell coculture, and antitumor effects in mice. The Jurkat experiments must not be relabeled as rescue of exhausted primary human T cells. I would compare CLP002 against D-PPA-1 rather than automatically combining them. Whether its additional effect on the PD-L1/CD80 interaction improves net function in the selected system should be measured, not assumed. The reference record contains 12 residues and specifies free termini; original terminal caps remain unresolved.
7. Axis: LAG-3/HLA-DR checkpoint blockade - C25 LAG-3-binding peptide, Cys1-Cys9 disulfide form. C25 directly addresses another inhibitory receptor increased in the supplied model. Its primary study demonstrated LAG-3/HLA-DR interference, enhanced CD8-associated IFN-{gamma} responses in activated human PBMCs, and antitumor effects in mouse models. These results support a ligand-dependent checkpoint research arm, but do not establish durable reversal of human chronic-antigen exhaustion. C25 should not be assumed to block FGL1 merely because it binds LAG-3. The nine-residue encoding includes its experimentally reported disulfide cyclization; a reduced linear sequence would represent a different chemical form.
8. Axis: PD-1 checkpoint persistence on chronically stimulated T cells: AUNP-12 - Branched PD-1-pathway peptide that blocks PD-L1 and PD-L2 with nanomolar rescue of lymphocyte proliferation and effector function, addressing the inhibitory-receptor upregulation documented in D8C cells and RCC TILs.
9. Axis: PD-L1 ectodomain interface that enforces PD-1 suppression: L7 - Sixteen-residue PD-L1-derived peptide that reactivates PD-1-suppressed T cells and curbs tumor growth by recruiting CD8 effectors, targeting the ligand side of the same checkpoint induced by chronic TCR drive.
10. Axis: Lost cytotoxic and cytokine output under persistent antigen: Interleukin-21 - {gamma}c cytokine that reduces CD8 exhaustion, raises granzyme B and perforin in IL-21R-high exhausted TILs, and favors central-memory CTL, countering the TNF/IFN{gamma}/IL-2 and serial-killing collapse measured in D8C 1G4 T cells.
11. Axis: MAP2K4-JNK stress-kinase node whose inhibition restored killing: MAP2K4-RRM-C246 - Designed 20-mer matched by sequence-adaptation v9 revised RRM to a MAP2K4 nucleotide-binding stretch containing the paper’s C246 reactivity site (exact integer-Hz primary-peak match); intended to occupy the ATP-sensitive conformation that tracked JNK activation and BSJ-04-122 rescue.
12. Axis: MAP2K3-p38 stress-kinase node linked to YY1 dysfunction and ROS/stemness: MAP2K3-RRM-C227 - Designed 20-mer matched to a MAP2K3 nucleotide-binding stretch containing C227; p38 inhibition independently improves expansion, redox balance and antitumor efficacy of human T cells, congruent with phospho-p38 in D8C cells.
13. Axis: ER-stress/ATF6-XBP1s program sufficient to impose an exhaustion-like proteome: HSPA5-RRM-BiP - Designed 20-mer RRM-matched to a BiP/HSPA5 motif (0% primary-peak error); BiP is the ER-stress marker induced in D8C cells, and thapsigargin-driven ER calcium depletion was sufficient to push acute cells toward the chronic proteome.
14. Axis: CD39/ENTPD1 ectonucleotidase and nucleotide-salvage/adenosine axis: ENTPD1-RRM-apyrase - Designed 20-mer RRM-matched to an ENTPD1 catalytic stretch (0% primary-peak error); CD39 protein rose in the chronic proteome, marks terminal exhaustion, and converts extracellular ATP into immunosuppressive adenosine when mitochondrial ATP and de novo nucleotide synthesis are already impaired.
15. Axis: IRE1{alpha}-XBP1s transcriptional induction of SLC33A1 protein: FIRE (all-D retro-inverso TAT-P4) - Published IRE1{alpha}-derived cell-penetrating peptide selected to increase the adaptive IRE1{alpha}/XBP1s branch. FIRE is the all-D retro-inverso form of TAT-P4; the parent IRE1{alpha} peptide increased XBP1 mRNA cleavage in vitro, cultured cells and an in-vivo model. Separate SLC33A1 experiments demonstrate that XBP1 depletion decreases AT-1 expression and that IRE1/XBP1 activation induces AT-1. This is therefore an upstream SLC33A1-expression strategy, not evidence that FIRE itself has raised SLC33A1 in human subjects.
16. Axis: Relief of the Asp328 substrate-electrostatic brake to increase acetyl-CoA transport: SLC33A1-D328-RRM1 - The 2025 human SLC33A1 structure/function study found D328A produced a substantial gain of transport activity, plausibly by reducing electrostatic repulsion near acetyl-CoA phosphate groups. Candidate targets the D328-centered functional region using the sequence adaptation of v9 revised RRM. Target primary frequency 65518821368279 Hz; achieved 65509483251482 Hz; relative error 0.0143%. This is a computational attempt to favor the experimentally identified gain-of-function region without altering the SLC33A1 gene.
17. Axis: Preservation of SLC33A1 homodimer/local architecture around Ser113: SLC33A1-S113-Dimer-RRM1 - S113R abolishes normal homodimer formation and acetyl-CoA transport, whereas the 2025 transport study found S113A did not reproduce the transport defect. Candidate targets the S113-centered structural region using the sequence adaptation of v9 revised RRM. Target primary frequency 64802899080517 Hz; achieved 64835063705040 Hz; relative error 0.0496%. The intended research endpoint is stabilization of transport-competent SLC33A1 organization rather than simple protein abundance.
18. Axis: Stabilization of the acetyl-CoA recognition pocket: SLC33A1-AcCoA-Pocket-RRM1 - Human cryo-EM and transport mutagenesis identify Y225, N229, Y390 and Y418 as major determinants of acetyl-CoA recognition; Y225A, N229A, Y390A and Y418A significantly reduce transport. The designed candidate targets the contiguous Y225/N229 region, which participates directly in 3'-phosphate recognition, using the sequence adaptation of v9 revised RRM. Target primary frequency 401286374328279 Hz; achieved 401008266054956 Hz; relative error 0.0693%.
19. Axis: Support of alternating-access transport gating at the C-terminal gate-support region: SLC33A1-TM11-Gate-RRM1 - Structural work places TM4-5/TM10-11 at the cytoplasmic opening and TM1-2/TM7-8 at the luminal gate, with TM5 and TM11 contributing gate support; the lumen-facing transition disassembles the substrate-binding site to permit release. The candidate targets the canonical C-terminal TM11-region signal using the sequence adaptation of v9 revised RRM. Target primary frequency 418933858721592 Hz; achieved 418766810187781 Hz; relative error 0.0399%. This is a conformational-cycling hypothesis rather than an experimentally demonstrated SLC33A1 agonist.
20. Axis: Preservation/enhancement of SLC33A1-dependent ER GSSG export: SLC33A1-GSSG-Q356-RRM1 - 2026 work identifies SLC33A1 as a major mammalian ER GSSG exporter and maps a GSSG-binding cavity involving Y225, Y390, Y418, Y426, N229 and Q356. The Q356-centered region was selected to distinguish this redox-transport axis from the acetyl-CoA Y225/N229 axis. Candidate uses the sequence adaptation of v9 revised RRM. Target primary frequency 110108847857672 Hz; achieved 110062003559830 Hz; relative error 0.0425%.

Additional priority leads are deliberately kept outside the mass line where their exact chemical identity was not resolved. LAG3pep-2, reported in 2026, is particularly relevant because its study reported inhibition of both LAG-3/FGL1 and LAG-3/MHC-II interactions and recovery of FGL1-suppressed T-cell activity. It warrants a separate FGL1-containing comparison with C25.
IL-10-Fc deserves a metabolic-rescue comparator position, not exclusion because of protein length. Its published evidence is closer to the specific terminal-exhaustion endpoint than SS-31’s: the study reported enhanced expansion and effector function of terminally exhausted CD8 TILs through mitochondrial-pyruvate-carrier-dependent oxidative phosphorylation, with antitumor effects in mice. However, an IL-10 monomer sequence is not the tested IL-10-Fc fusion. The exact fusion architecture must be obtained before creating its mass record or claiming reagent equivalence.
For the ER-stress branch, F6P1 and F6P2 are genuine published IRE1-modulating peptide leads, but their complete modified structures were not resolved here and their efficacy in the supplied human T-cell model is not established. They should remain candidates for chemical verification and functional testing, not invented sequence entries. The longer parent F6 fragment is not an interchangeable inhibitor: the earlier work reported different effects across IRE1 outputs, including increased XBP1 processing. That distinction matters when the therapeutic hypothesis is reduction of maladaptive ER stress.
Proposed evaluation program: Retain the paper’s donor-matched D2 activated, D8A acute, and D8C chronic conditions. Separate prevention during dysfunction development from rescue begun only after dysfunction is documented, and include a later D15 challenge. Use BSJ-04-122 as the paper-derived nonpeptide benchmark. Establish single-agent exposure-response, viability, and relevant target engagement before testing combinations. For intracellular inhibitors, include delivery-segment and sequence-control conditions; for checkpoint peptides, establish the relevant ligand-dependent suppression. This is a proposed extension of the paper, not an experimental regimen already validated by it. 
The principal success criterion should be improved serial antigen-specific killing with retained T-cell persistence and viability. The paper’s repeated tumor-challenge assay is a stronger foundation for that assessment than exhaustion-marker expression alone. I would measure function after washout as well as during continued exposure, normalize comparisons for viable effector-cell number and TCR expression, and retain tumor-only and antigen-negative controls. Supporting measurements would include JNK/p38 activity, cytokine competence, mitochondrial ATP production, nucleotide pools, and ER-stress outputs. Only reproducible single-agent functional improvements should advance into nonredundant combinations; the seven encoded entries are not a recommendation to administer all seven together. 
Several apparent targets should remain measurements rather than default inhibition components. ATP add-back was performed in lysates, not demonstrated as an intact-cell therapy. Proteasome activity increased in chronically stimulated cells, so the study does not support a generic “proteasome failure” narrative. HSPA9 and LONP1 changes suggest altered nucleotide-sensitive protein function, not that inhibiting these proteins is beneficial. Likewise, p53-pathway activation was also present in acutely stimulated cells and does not establish that disabling p53, ATR, or related safeguards would reverse exhaustion. No selective biosynthesis-inhibition mechanism or Sternheimer inhibitory frequency is demonstrated by these results. 
Mass representation: The following line contains 216 residue-mass tokens across seven reference entries, with the requested terminator after every entry. It is a calculated descriptor-not an intact molecular-mass list, measured Raman spectrum, dosing instruction, or validated therapeutic signal. Stereochemistry, disulfide connectivity, folding, and the stated chemical-form limitations require the accompanying registry and evidence audit. No claim is made that transmitting these descriptors reproduces peptide administration or inhibits protein biosynthesis.
SLC33A1/AT-1 is an endoplasmic-reticulum major-facilitator-superfamily transporter whose experimentally demonstrated functions now include acetyl-CoA transport and GSSG export. Increasing SLC33A1 abundance can increase acetyl-CoA translocation experimentally, but the biological objective should be restoration toward normal activity rather than indiscriminate overexpression, because excessive SLC33A1 activity is also pathogenic in experimental systems.

A critical distinction is made between true potassium wasting and apparent hypokalemia caused by redistribution: catecholamine/{beta}2 signaling acutely stimulates skeletal-muscle Na+/K+-ATPase and shifts K+ intracellularly, whereas true body K+ loss occurs primarily through renal secretion, with ROMK mediating basal distal-nephron K+ secretion and BK contributing strongly to flow-induced secretion. The original 12-axis architecture is therefore expanded to 13 peptide entries by separating ROMK and BK. Axes 1-6 address upstream maintenance of the sympathetic/stress loop; axes 7-13 address RAAS/K+ loss, vascular consequences, inflammation, sympathetic remodeling and deficient parasympathetic opposition.

This case should not be treated as straightforward atopic eczema without reconfirming the diagnosis. The dermatitis has persisted for approximately 20 years but intensified after treatment for breast cancer and a subsequent malignancy near the spinal cord, with current predominance in the groin and lower back. In a man over 50, chronic treatment-resistant eczematous lesions in relatively covered areas can overlap clinically with tinea cruris, allergic/contact dermatitis, inverse psoriasis and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma/mycosis fungoides. CTCL is particularly important to exclude before escalating immunomodulatory treatment because it can resemble eczema for years and sometimes requires repeated representative biopsies to establish the diagnosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov][1]) The prior malignancies also make strongly proliferative or angiogenic experimental peptides undesirable. Hypertension is treated here as an important treatment-selection constraint rather than as an eczema mechanism. Six mechanistically distinct peptide axes were retained, with candidates having strong growth-factor/angiogenic activity deliberately excluded.

1. Adaptive immune dysregulation in chronic atopic dermatitis: Thymopentin / TP5 - The native thymic pentapeptide has direct human atopic-dermatitis evidence, including controlled clinical studies reporting improvement in clinical disease parameters and immune abnormalities. Its immunoregulatory action provides a distinct T-cell axis rather than nonspecific tissue-growth stimulation. Older experimental oncology literature also investigated thymopentin in antitumor immune responses, making it preferable in this particular history to regenerative growth-factor peptides; this does not establish safety in a cancer survivor.
2. Keratinocyte TSLP/type-2 inflammatory regulome: cSN50.1 / AMTX-100 - A cell-penetrating Nuclear Transport Checkpoint Inhibitor targeting importin-{alpha}5/importin-{beta}1-dependent nuclear transport. In an experimental AD model, topical cSN50.1 suppressed TSLP as well as IL-4, IL-4R{alpha}, IL-13, IL-33 and numerous other inflammatory mediators, reduced eosinophil/macrophage/CD4 infiltration, and reduced established swelling, redness and scaling. It therefore addresses broad inflammatory transcription without introducing a regenerative growth-factor signal. ([Nature][2])
3. Staphylococcus-associated dysbiosis and antimicrobial barrier dysfunction: Omiganan - A C-terminally amidated indolicidin analogue evaluated topically in human atopic dermatitis. Clinical studies found substantial effects on cutaneous microbial dysbiosis and Staphylococcus aureus abundance, although this did not translate into convincing improvement of the clinical AD severity endpoints. It is retained specifically for the microbial-barrier axis rather than represented as a proven eczema treatment.
4. NF-{kappa}B/STAT3-driven inflammatory and pruritic cytokine signaling: TPS240 - The defined tetrapeptide has direct experimental AD evidence. In keratinocyte and AD-like mouse studies it reduced inflammatory chemokines including CCL17/CCL22 and pruritus-associated mediators including TSLP and IL-31 while suppressing NF-{kappa}B/STAT3-associated signaling. This provides an inflammatory/itch axis distinct from the broader nuclear-transport blockade of cSN50.1.
5. Oxidative-stress-associated epidermal inflammation: STPO-B-II - The sequence-defined decapeptide identified in 2024 work exhibited antioxidant activity together with anti-atopic-dermatitis effects in experimental systems. It is retained for the oxidative-inflammatory component of chronic dermatitis rather than for direct stimulation of skin proliferation.
6. It provides a compact local inflammatory-control axis involving suppression of proinflammatory signaling. Evidence is weaker and less condition-specific than for the first five entries, so it should be considered the lowest-confidence research candidate in this set rather than a clinically validated treatment.

description:
﻿Created 2026-09-11
Established neurological injury after carbon-monoxide poisoning is a mixed hypoxic, mitochondrial, inflammatory, excitotoxic, neurovascular and delayed white-matter disorder rather than a simple oxygen-deprivation lesion. The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable: recent human MRI studies demonstrate reductions in whole hippocampal volume and specific CA3/CA4/dentate-gyrus-related subfields, with hippocampal volume correlating with delayed-memory performance. The frontal lobes may show persistent hypometabolism, hypoperfusion and disrupted prefrontal/executive-network connectivity even when conventional structural imaging is comparatively unremarkable. Once neurons and cortical tissue have been physically lost, no peptide has been demonstrated to recreate the original hippocampal or frontal architecture in humans. Nevertheless, substantial functional recovery can occur despite persistent lesions through surviving-network plasticity, neurogenesis within the dentate gyrus, axonal remodeling, remyelination, synaptic reorganization and vascular/metabolic recovery. The eight axes below therefore emphasize repair of surviving tissue and network function rather than claiming resurrection of dead neurons. Acute-only NMDA/excitotoxic neuroprotectants were deliberately excluded from the final set because limiting injury during the first hours or days is mechanistically different from repairing an established chronic lesion. No Sternheimer inhibition axis is justified because chronic CO encephalopathy is not established to result from pathological ribosomal overproduction of a single endogenous peptide or protein.

1. BDNF-TrkB-dependent hippocampal neurogenesis and memory-circuit restoration: Mature human BDNF - This is the strongest CO-specific peptide axis found. Experimental CO poisoning suppresses adult dentate-gyrus neurogenesis; intracerebroventricular BDNF reproduced the protective effect of hyperbaric oxygen, preserving neurogenesis and cognitive performance, whereas TrkB sequestration abolished much of the HBO benefit. A 2026 study independently identified impaired BDNF maturation as part of the CO-induced LDHA-lactate-lysosome-Sortilin/GRN injury pathway. The entry represents one native mature 119-residue human BDNF monomer with its three cystine-knot disulfides; biologically active BDNF forms a noncovalent homodimer.
2. Delayed oligodendrogenesis, axonal remyelination and white-matter reconstruction: S14G-Humanin / HNG - White-matter demyelination is a major substrate of delayed CO encephalopathy and can persist for months. Importantly for an already-established injury rather than acute prophylaxis, delayed HNG given 24 hours after hypoxic/ischemic brain injury did not reduce the original infarct but subsequently increased oligodendrogenesis, corpus-callosum thickness, axonal remyelination and BDNF and reduced later brain atrophy and neurological deficits. This makes HNG unusually relevant to a chronic-repair rather than merely an acute-neuroprotection axis.
3. Frontal-cortical and hippocampal neurotrophin transcription/network plasticity: Semax - CO injury prominently disrupts prefrontal/executive-control networks. In experimental cerebral ischemia, Semax changes neurotrophin/receptor transcription in cortex; in incomplete global ischemia its effects were specifically observed in both frontal cortex and hippocampus, with reversal of ischemia-induced reductions in neurotrophin/receptor expression. This gives it a different role from supplying BDNF directly: the axis is endogenous trophic-program reactivation and surviving-network plasticity.
4. GSK3{beta}-tau dysregulation, dentate neurogenesis and synaptic repair: P021 / Peptide 021 - CO-specific experiments implicate GSK3{beta}-driven tau phosphorylation in delayed cognitive injury of cortex and hippocampal CA1. P021 is a BBB-permeable CNTF-derived neurotrophic peptidergic compound that increases BDNF, reduces GSK3{beta} activity and pathological tau phosphorylation, and improves hippocampal neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity and cognition in chronic neurodegeneration models. It has not been tested in CO poisoning, but it maps unusually closely to the experimentally demonstrated CO GSK3{beta}/tau axis. Field 3 represents the chemically defined N-acetylated DGGL-adamantylglycinamide entity, with the adamantyl modification incorporated into the terminal nonstandard-residue mass rather than creating an extra mass entry.
5. Mitochondrial cardiolipin integrity, ATP recovery and oxidative/ferroptotic stress: Elamipretide / SS-31 - CO directly interferes with mitochondrial respiration in addition to reducing oxygen delivery, and secondary ROS/lipid-peroxidation injury persists after carboxyhemoglobin has cleared. Elamipretide concentrates at the inner mitochondrial membrane and stabilizes cardiolipin-dependent bioenergetics. Brain-injury models demonstrate improved mitochondrial function, reduced ROS/apoptosis/inflammation and improved cognition, including hippocampal cognitive rescue. This is therefore the most chemically defined peptide found for the mitochondrial-energy axis, although there is no clinical trial demonstrating reversal of chronic CO brain injury.
6. Neurovascular-unit/endothelial repair and VEGFR2-dependent revascularization: QK VEGF-mimetic peptide - Persistent frontal hypoperfusion and metabolic depression are documented after severe CO poisoning, while microvascular injury contributes to CO neuropathology. The acetylated/amidated 15-mer QK reproduces key VEGF receptor-activating properties; in experimental cerebral ischemia, QK administered by several routes reduced ischemic brain damage by approximately 40%, and separate work establishes its proangiogenic VEGFR2 activity. This axis targets surviving neurovascular tissue rather than neuronal replacement.
7. Endogenous neural-stem/progenitor-cell survival, migration and repair: Apelin-13 - Adult cortical neuron replacement is extremely limited, but endogenous progenitor responses and hippocampal neurogenesis remain potentially modifiable. A 2025 study showed that Apelin-13/APJ signaling increased neural-stem-cell viability and migration under oxygen-glucose deprivation, suppressed apoptosis and further increased BDNF. This complements BDNF rather than duplicates it: the assigned axis is recruitment/survival of repair-competent progenitors within a hypoxic-injury environment.
8. EPOR-CD131 innate-repair signaling and post-hypoxic neuroinflammation: Cibinetide / ARA290 - Human randomized data show that early erythropoietin after CO poisoning improved neurological outcomes and decreased delayed neurological sequelae, providing direct evidence that the EPO tissue-protection pathway matters in this disease. Cibinetide is an 11-residue, nonerythropoietic EPO helix-B derivative that selectively activates the EPOR/CD131 innate-repair receptor rather than the erythropoietic EPOR homodimer. In cerebral ischemia it reduces neuronal apoptosis and inflammatory cytokines through the {beta}-common receptor without driving erythropoiesis. This is mechanistically preferable to an EPO-mimetic EPOR agonist for a neural-repair program, although chronic CO-specific cibinetide efficacy remains untested.

﻿Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (CIDP) is a rare, acquired, immune-mediated neurological disorder affecting the peripheral nervous system. It is characterized by progressive or relapsing-remitting symmetric weakness in proximal and distal muscles, sensory disturbances (numbness, paresthesia, or loss of vibration/proprioception), impaired gait and balance, and reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. Symptoms develop over at least 8 weeks, distinguishing it from acute inflammatory neuropathies. Untreated, CIDP can lead to significant disability, including inability to walk, but many patients respond to immunomodulatory therapies.

The pathophysiology involves autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin, with contributions from both humoral and cellular immunity. Key features include disruption of the blood-nerve barrier, infiltration by macrophages and T-cells leading to segmental demyelination, complement deposition and membrane attack complex formation on myelin, and in subsets (~10%), node/paranode disruption by specific autoantibodies (e.g., anti-NF155 or anti-CNTN1 IgG4). These processes impair nerve conduction, causing clinical deficits. Emerging evidence highlights roles for pathogenic IgG recycling via FcRn, B-cell/plasma cell dysregulation, and pro-inflammatory cytokines.

The proposed set includes four conceptual designed short polypeptides, each targeting a distinct therapeutic axis derived from CIDP pathophysiology and current/emerging treatment mechanisms. All are designed; no real-world short polypeptides (3-50 residues) with documented use or investigation in CIDP were identified across sources, leading to exclusive use of designed ones for coverage.

The first designed polypeptide is conceptualized as a C3-binding inhibitor analog, targeting complement activation to prevent complement-mediated myelin damage and macrophage recruitment.

The second designed polypeptide is conceptualized to disrupt FcRn-IgG interactions, aiming to accelerate clearance of pathogenic autoantibodies.

The third designed polypeptide targets B-cell signaling or autoantibody interfaces for modulation of humoral immunity.

The fourth designed polypeptide provides broad anti-inflammatory effects, potentially inhibiting pro-inflammatory pathways while supporting regulatory responses.

These designed polypeptides are short (8-13 residues), enabling chemical synthesis, potential modifications for stability/bioavailability (e.g., cyclization, pegylation), and targeted action with reduced off-target effects compared to systemic therapies. Feasibility is supported by success of similar short peptides in other immune-mediated diseases.

The strategy prioritizes peptides that address these axes to normalize biomarkers like TGF-beta1, C4a, and VEGF. ﻿Chronic Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), formerly known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy, is a debilitating chronic pain condition that typically develops after an injury, surgery, or even minor trauma to a limb, though it can occasionally occur without an identifiable trigger. ﻿Circulatory hypoxia, also termed stagnant or ischemic hypoxia, arises when systemic or regional blood flow is insufficient to deliver adequate oxygen to tissues despite normal arterial oxygenation and hemoglobin levels. It commonly occurs in shock states (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, distributive/septic, obstructive), congestive heart failure, vascular occlusion, microcirculatory dysfunction, or severe anemia with compensatory limits. Symptoms include fatigue, confusion, oliguria, cool peripheries, lactic acidosis, and progressive multi-organ dysfunction; severe cases lead to cell death via ATP depletion, ionic imbalance, and reperfusion injury upon restoration. Pathophysiology involves reduced perfusion pressure, endothelial activation with glycocalyx shedding, microvascular thrombosis, leukocyte adhesion, nitric oxide dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory cytokine release amplifying tissue damage.

Peptide 2 (designed) is glycine-proline rich to conceptually protect endothelial barrier and microcirculation. Peptide 3 (designed) is serine-glutamine rich polar for conceptual suppression of hypoperfusion-triggered inflammation. Peptide 4 (designed) is phenylalanine-tyrosine rich aromatic to conceptually mitigate oxidative damage in low-flow states. Peptide 5 is the real-world human Angiotensin II (Giapreza), FDA-approved synthetic octapeptide with established clinical use in vasodilatory shock for potent vasoconstriction, blood pressure restoration, and improved tissue perfusion. These diverse short designs prioritize feasibility, potential rapid onset, and compatibility with standard resuscitation.

Cluster headache is a trigeminal-autonomic cephalalgia characterized by extremely severe unilateral pain, cranial parasympathetic symptoms, agitation and striking circadian/circannual periodicity. CGRP-dependent trigeminovascular attack initiation: Human {alpha}-CGRP(8-37) - CGRP is among the strongest experimentally established peptide drivers of cluster attacks. In a randomized double-blind crossover trial, CGRP triggered attacks in 8 of 9 patients with active episodic cluster headache and 7 of 14 with chronic cluster headache, but not episodic patients in remission. CGRP(8-37) is the classical 30-residue competitive peptide antagonist of CGRP receptors and therefore directly opposes this experimentally demonstrated attack pathway. It has not itself undergone a therapeutic cluster-headache trial.

﻿Coccidioidomycosis, commonly known as Valley Fever, is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic soil-dwelling fungi Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii, endemic to arid regions such as the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Central and South America. The disease is acquired through inhalation of airborne arthroconidia (spores) released from disturbed soil, which convert to pathogenic spherules in the lungs upon deposition in the alveoli, leading to rupture and release of endospores that propagate the infection. In immunocompetent hosts, the infection is often asymptomatic or self-limited, manifesting as flu-like symptoms including fever, cough, fatigue, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia; however, it can progress to acute pneumonia with pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and infiltrates on imaging. Dissemination occurs in 1-5% of cases, particularly in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., HIV, transplant recipients, pregnant women, or those of African or Filipino descent), affecting extrapulmonary sites like skin (erythema nodosum or multiforme), bones/joints (osteomyelitis, arthritis), and CNS (meningitis with hydrocephalus, vasculitis). Pathophysiology involves evasion of host immunity: arthroconidia resist phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages, spherules inhibit oxidative burst and cytokine production (IL-12, IFN-{gamma}), while fungal proteases and urease contribute to tissue damage and alkalization favoring growth. Innate immunity (neutrophils, dendritic cells via Dectin-1/TLR2) and adaptive Th1/Th17 responses are critical for granuloma formation and clearance, but defects lead to chronic or disseminated disease. Diagnosis includes serology (IgM/IgG), culture, histopathology (spherules on silver stain), and PCR; complications include cavitary lung disease, fibrosis, and high mortality in CNS involvement (up to 30% even with treatment). Current management relies on azoles (fluconazole for mild/moderate, voriconazole/itraconazole for refractory), amphotericin B for severe/disseminated, with lifelong therapy for meningitis.

﻿Cold diuresis is a physiological response to cold exposure characterized by increased urine production due to peripheral vasoconstriction, increased central blood volume, suppression of ADH, and activation of natriuretic peptides. It can lead to dehydration if not managed. The following peptides are proposed to mitigate this condition:

1. Vasopressin V2 receptor activation: Vasopressin - Binds to V2 receptors in the collecting ducts of the kidney, stimulating cAMP production and insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels, increasing water reabsorption and reducing urine output.
2. Selective V2 receptor activation: Desmopressin - Synthetic analog of vasopressin with enhanced antidiuretic activity and reduced vasopressor effects, used to counteract diuresis.
3. Natriuretic peptide receptor A antagonism: A 71915 - Competitive antagonist of NPRA, inhibits ANP and BNP signaling, reducing natriuresis and diuresis.
4. Vasopressin analog for antidiuresis: Lypressin - Similar to vasopressin, with lysine at position 8, providing antidiuretic effects.
5. Antidiuretic effect via V2 receptor: Oxytocin - Binds to V2 receptors at higher doses, promoting antidiuresis.
6. Designed NPRA antagonist: Designed NPRA Antagonist - Designed based on ANP ring structure to act as antagonist, reducing ANP-induced natriuresis.
7. Designed V2 agonist: Designed V2 Agonist - Modified vasopressin sequence with increased stability for prolonged antidiuretic effect.
8. Designed ADH mimic: Designed ADH Mimic - Short cyclic peptide mimicking vasopressin binding loop for V2 activation.
9. Designed ANP sequestering peptide: Designed ANP Sequester - Peptide designed to bind and inactivate ANP, reducing its diuretic effects.
10. Designed aquaporin modulator: Designed AQP Modulator - Peptide to directly enhance aquaporin-2 expression or activity.

The symptomatic phase is characterized by viral entry into keratinocytes via glycoprotein-mediated membrane fusion, leading to rapid replication, localized cytolysis, and the formation of painful, exudative vesicles on the perioral skin.

﻿Cold-insoluble globulin, now universally known as Fibronectin (Fn), interacts with various cell-surface receptors, primarily the integrin family (notably alpha-5-beta-1). Correction of fibronectin receptor signaling is critical in conditions involving impaired wound healing, tissue fibrosis, and vascular stability. In chronic non-healing wounds, the degradation of fibronectin or the downregulation of its receptors prevents the assembly of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and the migration of fibroblasts. Therapeutic correction focuses on restoring the 'biological glue' function by presenting high-affinity ligands that trigger integrin clustering and intracellular signaling through focal adhesion kinase (FAK), promoting cellular adhesion, survival, and matrix reorganization.

1. Integrin Alpha-5-Beta-1 Activation: RGD Peptide - The canonical tripeptide sequence that restores cell adhesion by binding to the primary fibronectin-binding site on integrins.
2. Synergistic Binding Enhancement: PHSRN - A synergy motif from the 9th type III repeat of fibronectin that significantly increases the binding affinity of RGD for alpha-5-beta-1.
3. FAK Signaling Induction: GRGDS - A pentapeptide variant that promotes rapid phosphorylation of Focal Adhesion Kinase to initiate cellular migration.
4. Matrix Assembly Restoration: pUR4 - A functional upstream domain peptide that prevents aberrant fibronectin polymerization and promotes organized fibrillogenesis.
5. Vascular Stability: Angiopoietin-1 Mimetic - Indirectly corrects fibronectin receptor dynamics by stabilizing endothelial cell-cell junctions and ECM attachments.

7. Tenascin-C Antagonism: TN-II - Blocks the inhibitory effects of Tenascin-C on fibronectin receptors to restore normal cell spreading in fibrotic environments.
8. Optimization Axis (Designed): Globul-Fix-5 - A synthetic multivalent peptide designed to cluster integrin receptors and bypass fragmented native fibronectin in diabetic ulcers.

﻿The peptides target multiple therapeutic axes for colitis, including anti-inflammatory actions to reduce swelling, antimicrobial protection against pathogens, barrier restoration for mucosal integrity, immunomodulation to balance responses, tissue regeneration for healing, and antioxidant effects to combat stress. The first 10 peptides are real-world with validated evidence from colitis studies, while peptides 11 and 12 are designed to supplement coverage in anti-inflammatory and antioxidant axes, flagged as designed.

﻿Created 2026-09-01
This program targets increased physiologically useful collagen synthesis, deposition and matrix organization rather than indiscriminate fibrosis. Collagen production differs substantially among skin, tendon, cornea, bone and internal organs, so no single peptide can legitimately represent “collagen increase” across every tissue. Six mechanistically distinct, sequence-defined peptide axes were retained after literature review: procollagen-derived matrikine feedback in fibroblasts, transcriptional activation of dermal COL1A1/procollagen, osteoblast-specific type-I collagen synthesis, collagen-I-mimetic osteogenic matrix signaling, sensory-neuropeptide-supported collagen-I remodeling, and NK1R/p38-dependent potentiation of TGF-{beta}-driven collagen deposition. Strong profibrotic peptides such as angiotensin II and endothelin-1 were deliberately rejected despite their ability to increase collagen because they preferentially model pathological fibrosis rather than controlled matrix restoration. GHK-Cu was also excluded because the supplied protocol blacklists metal-complexed GHK unless it is uniquely indispensable; the search identified multiple strong nonblacklisted alternatives. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis is applicable because the requested direction is increased rather than suppressed protein production.

1. Procollagen-derived matrikine feedback stimulating collagen I/III and extracellular-matrix production: Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS) - KTTKS is the minimal active sequence derived from the C-terminal propeptide of type-I collagen and stimulates production of collagen I, collagen III and fibronectin. The N-palmitoylated C16-KTTKS form retains this biology while improving stability and membrane/skin association. Human dermal and corneal fibroblast studies demonstrate concentration-dependent collagen production, and newer liposomal work found pal-KTTKS increased collagen production beyond free KTTKS and an ascorbate control. The palmitoyl net mass increment is applied exclusively to the N-terminal lysine.
2. COL1A1 transcription, procollagen secretion and coordinated dermal ECM formation: GEKG - The Gly-Glu-Lys-Gly matrikine increases COL1A1 expression, procollagen secretion, fibronectin and hyaluronan-related matrix signaling in human dermal fibroblasts. In a controlled human skin study, GEKG significantly increased COL1A1 and histological procollagen relative to vehicle. This provides a transcriptional ECM-stimulation mechanism distinct from KTTKS's classical procollagen-fragment feedback.
3. Osteoblast differentiation coupled directly to type-I collagen synthesis: Osteogenic Growth Peptide OGP(10-14) / Historphin - The YGFGG active fragment increases osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, increases type-I collagen protein and mRNA, and upregulates osteogenic programs including Cbfa1/Runx2. This axis specifically represents collagen production in mineralising skeletal tissue rather than dermal fibroblasts.
4. Type-I-collagen-mimetic cell adhesion and osteogenic ECM deposition: P-15 - P-15 is the GTPGPQGIAGQRGVV cell-binding region of the {alpha}1(I) collagen chain. It enhances osteoblast attachment, differentiation and extracellular-matrix production and is associated with increased COL1 expression and mineralised matrix formation. 5. Neurogenic fibroblast activation, collagen-I-biased wound remodeling and osteogenic collagen support: Human {alpha}-CGRP - CGRP promotes fibroblast proliferation and wound remodeling and has been associated with a collagen-I-favouring response in human cutaneous wound models. The native Cys2-Cys7 disulfide bridge and C-terminal amidation are retained.

Recent human corneal-fibroblast experiments found that Substance P enhanced TGF-{beta}-induced type-I collagen synthesis through NK1R/p38 signaling, while 2024 dermal-fibroblast work independently showed increased collagen deposition when Substance P and TGF-{beta} were combined. This distinguishes it mechanistically from both KTTKS and GEKG and covers neurogenic regulation of active collagen-producing fibroblasts.

﻿Color blindness, also known as color vision deficiency (CVD), is a visual impairment characterized by difficulty or inability to distinguish certain colors, most commonly reds and greens, though blue-yellow deficiencies and complete achromatopsia also occur. It primarily arises from genetic mutations, often X-linked, affecting the opsin proteins in cone photoreceptors of the retina-specifically OPN1LW and OPN1MW genes for red-green CVD, leading to absent, reduced, or dysfunctional long- or medium-wavelength-sensitive cones. Symptoms include reduced color discrimination, confusion between specific hues, and in severe cases like achromatopsia, monochromatic vision with photophobia and poor acuity. Pathophysiology centers on altered spectral sensitivity of cones without necessarily causing degeneration in common forms, though cone dysfunction can lead to secondary stress.

The proposed polypeptides are all conceptual designed sequences, flagged as designed throughout; no real-world polypeptides were identified with verifiable evidence for treating color blindness despite extensive searches. They target key therapeutic axes: cone photoreceptor neuroprotection and survival promotion, stabilization of mutant opsins, enhancement of phototransduction signaling, mitochondrial bioenergetic support, reduction of oxidative stress, improvement of cone-to-bipolar synaptic transmission, and amplification of residual color signals. These designed polypeptides incorporate non-standard amino acids for stability and specificity, with cyclic variants for enhanced resistance to degradation, aiming to conceptually support cone function and improve color perception feasibility through topical or intravitreal delivery considerations.

﻿Colorectal Tumor Eradication and Dual Cytotoxic-Immunomodulatory Therapy (Ewingella americana Mimicry)

Created 2026-08-07
The naturally occurring gut bacterium *Ewingella americana* (isolated from the Japanese tree frog) successfully eliminated colorectal tumors in mice through a dual mechanism. It works by directly attacking the cancer cells while simultaneously stimulating the immune system to recruit T cells, B cells, and neutrophils, leading to a surge of inflammatory signaling molecules like TNF-{alpha} and IFN-{gamma}.

Resolving solid tumors using the *Ewingella americana* biophysical model requires mimicking its dual-action capability: initiating direct cytotoxicity against cancer cell membranes while simultaneously recruiting massive innate and adaptive immune infiltration. Pathophysiologically, solid tumors evade immune detection via checkpoint signals and create a highly immunosuppressive microenvironment. The therapeutic strategy biophysically translates the amphibian bacterium's mechanisms into targeted peptides: directly lysing tumor membranes, aggressively recruiting T-cells and neutrophils, hyper-activating the TNF-{alpha} and IFN-{gamma} signaling cascades, and genetically silencing the tumor's immune evasion proteins.

1. Axis: Direct Tumor Cytotoxicity (Amphibian Antimicrobial Mimicry) - Magainin-2 is a potent, naturally occurring antimicrobial and antitumoral peptide derived from the skin of the African clawed frog. It acts as a selective cytotoxic agent that targets the negatively charged phospholipid membranes of cancer cells, physically disrupting and lysing them in a manner analogous to the direct cellular attack mounted by *Ewingella americana*.
2. Axis: Immune Infiltration and T-Cell Recruitment - Thymosin Alpha-1 (TA1) is an endogenous peptide that forcefully stimulates T-cell maturation and innate immune activation. It drives massive immune infiltration into solid tumors, bridging the gap to recruit the T cells, B cells, and neutrophils required to flip the tumor microenvironment from 'cold' to 'hot.'
3. Axis: TNF-{alpha} and IFN-{gamma} Cascade Amplification - Designed peptide engineered via RRM targeting the Interferon-Gamma Receptor 1 (IFNGR1). The *Ewingella* bacterium induces cancer cell death by triggering the release of inflammatory signaling molecules. This sequence biophysically hyper-activates the IFN-{gamma} receptor on infiltrating immune cells, sustaining the tumor-destroying cytokine storm. Calculated RRM target frequency = 136.45 Hz.
4. Axis: Phagocytosis Activation (CD47 'Don't Eat Me' Blockade) - Designed peptide engineered via RRM targeting CD47. Solid tumors overexpress CD47 to signal macrophages to ignore them. This sequence sterically blocks the CD47 surface antigen on colorectal cancer cells, removing the immune brakes and allowing the newly recruited neutrophils and macrophages to rapidly phagocytose the tumor cells. Calculated RRM target frequency = 129.80 Hz.
5. Axis: Tumor Metabolic Starvation - Designed peptide engineered via RRM targeting Hexokinase 2 (HK2). The amphibian bacterium exploits tumor-specific metabolic changes to thrive. This peptide biophysically disrupts aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect) within the colorectal cancer cells, cutting off the rapid glucose supply the tumor uses to grow and evade immune detection. Calculated RRM target frequency = 141.22 Hz.
6. Axis: Inhibition of Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) via Sternheimer proteody - PD-L1 is utilized by tumors to suppress immune signaling. Inhibitory proteody generated from the full PD-L1 sequence using monoisotopic masses + log symmetrization suppresses its translation. Silencing PD-L1 biophysically removes the checkpoint brakes on the immune system, allowing the infiltrating T-cells to attack the colorectal tumor unimpeded. Calculated inhibitory frequency = 148.15 Hz. Mean log error = 0.0435.

﻿Coma is a profound state of unconsciousness characterized by lack of arousal and awareness, commonly resulting from traumatic brain injury, ischemic/anoxic insults, stroke, or other neurological damage, with secondary injury cascades exacerbating neuronal loss and poor recovery outcomes. Key pathophysiological axes include excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress/redox imbalance, apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired neuroplasticity/arousal, blood-brain barrier disruption, and secondary tissue damage.

Real-world polypeptide applications in coma are limited and mostly investigational or regional (e.g., Semax and Selank for neurorecovery in brain injury, davunetide/NAP in trials for related neurodegeneration, CN-105 and other apoE mimetics for acute injury, arginine-rich peptides like R18 for excitotoxicity in preclinical models, with mixtures like Cerebrolysin used adjunctively in some settings); however, many involve non-listed residues/modifications, fusions, mixtures, or insufficient compliant mass verification from single sources, necessitating fallback to designed polypeptides. This set comprises 18 novel designed polypeptides providing comprehensive axis coverage, incorporating >=2 non-standard residues per sequence for potential selectivity, with ~44% cyclic (disulfide-bridged) for protease resistance and linear ones N-acetylated/C-amidated for stability; all are conceptual with short lengths (5-8 residues) for synthetic feasibility and physicochemical optimization (charged residues for solubility, limited hydrophobics for bioavailability).

﻿Comminuted Fracture of the Left Superior and Inferior Pubic Rami in an 88-Year-Old Woman

Created 2026-09-21
A comminuted fracture involving both the superior and inferior left pubic rami in an 88-year-old woman should be approached as a geriatric pelvic fragility-fracture pattern unless the trauma mechanism or imaging demonstrates otherwise. Fracture repair requires an initial inflammatory phase, so indiscriminate suppression of inflammation is not necessarily beneficial. The more defensible objective is resolution of excessive or persistent inflammation while preserving macrophage-mediated recruitment, angiogenesis and early callus signaling. Six mechanistically distinct peptide-relevant axes were retained: inflammatory-resolution/macrophage control, osteoblast proliferation and mineralization, fracture-site angiogenesis and coordinated early repair, systemic osteoanabolic PTH1R signaling, sensory-neurovascular/type-H-vessel coupling, and balanced osteoclast-dependent remodeling. None of the experimental peptides below has been clinically demonstrated to accelerate union of comminuted pubic-ramus fractures in an 88-year-old patient.

1. Excessive/prolonged macrophage inflammation and NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD pyroptosis: Annexin A1 Ac2-26 (real) - N-terminally acetylated Annexin-A1 mimetic that promotes inflammatory resolution rather than simply blocking the initial fracture inflammatory response. In a 2025 bone-defect study, Ac2-26 combined with OGP reduced ROS and macrophage pyroptosis through the ANXA1/NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD pathway while increasing osteogenic differentiation and bone-defect repair. The evidence is from inflammatory craniofacial bone defects rather than geriatric pelvic fractures.
2. Osteoblast proliferation, differentiation and matrix mineralization: OGP(10-14) (real) - The active C-terminal osteogenic-growth-peptide pentapeptide YGFGG promotes osteoblast-lineage proliferation, alkaline-phosphatase activity, differentiation and matrix mineralization. OGP/OGP(10-14) has stimulated fracture healing in rodent models and provides a direct osteogenic axis complementary to inflammatory resolution.
3. Fracture-site angiogenesis and coordinated early repair signaling: Rusalatide / TP508-NH2 (real) - A thrombin receptor-binding-domain-derived 23-residue peptide that increases fracture-site neovascularization and early repair signaling. Animal fracture studies demonstrated increased vascularity, new bone formation and mechanical stiffness. Importantly, TP508 does not simply suppress inflammation; it modifies the early inflammatory/growth-factor response while promoting angiogenesis. Human distal-radius development was less convincing: the phase-3 primary endpoint was not significantly improved, although one radiographic secondary endpoint favored TP508. The precisely characterized C-terminally amidated rusalatide form is retained.
4. PTH1R-dependent systemic osteoanabolic signaling and geriatric pelvic-fracture recovery: Teriparatide / human PTH(1-34) (real) - Intermittent PTH1R signaling is a clinically established anabolic mechanism for osteoporosis and increases osteoblast activity. This peptide has unusually direct evidence in the relevant population: a randomized pelvic-fracture study with a mean age of 82 years and >80% women included patients with pubic-ramus fractures. Teriparatide did not significantly increase CT-confirmed union or reduce pain at three months, although physical-performance measures improved. It is therefore retained as the best-supported systemic osteoanabolic peptide axis, not as a proven accelerator of pubic-ramus union.
5. Sensory-neurovascular signaling and type-H-vessel coupling during osteoporotic fracture healing: Human {alpha}-CGRP (real) - CGRP signaling links sensory nerves with periosteal osteoprogenitors, angiogenesis and osteogenesis. Experimental inhibition or loss of CGRP impairs callus formation and mechanical recovery, whereas increasing CGRP in osteoporotic fracture models enhances type-H vessel formation and fracture repair. Native human {alpha}-CGRP is retained with the Cys2-Cys7 disulfide and C-terminal amide. Evidence for administering {alpha}-CGRP itself to elderly fracture patients remains preclinical.
6. Osteoclast differentiation and remodeling balance in osteoporotic bone: Osteostatin / PTHrP(107-111) (real) - The native pentapeptide TRSAW has anti-resorptive, osteogenic and anti-inflammatory activity in experimental bone systems. Human osteoclast experiments show concentration-dependent reduction of M-CSF/RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation without suppressing the resorptive function of already mature osteoclasts, while osteostatin-loaded biomaterials enhance bone regeneration in osteopenic/osteoporotic animal defects. Because osteoclast activity is required for normal callus remodeling, this axis is intended as remodeling balance rather than indiscriminate osteoclast inhibition.
