﻿Enteric Nervous System (Calm / Balance)

Created 2026-08-10
“Enteric Nervous System (Calm / Balance)” is interpreted as restoration of enteric homeostasis rather than generalized suppression of gastrointestinal activity. A balanced ENS requires coordinated excitatory and inhibitory motor output, appropriate visceral sensory gain, preservation of myenteric and submucosal neurons, controlled secretomotor activity, effective interdigestive propulsion, and neuroimmune signaling that resolves inflammation without disabling normal mucosal defense. Seven mechanistically distinct peptide-addressable axes with experimentally defined peptides and resolvable chemistry were identified. The resulting set deliberately contains both inhibitory/braking signals and a coordinated prokinetic signal: continuously suppressing the ENS would promote dysmotility rather than physiological balance. The particularly relevant newer finding is the 2025 discovery that enteric neurons themselves produce adrenomedullin-2, establishing a direct ENS-to-immune tissue-protection circuit. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis is appropriate because ENS imbalance is not generally caused by excessive synthesis of one specific endogenous peptide or protein.

1. Enteric neuron-ILC2 neuroimmune homeostasis and mucosal repair: Human ADM2 / Intermedin(8-47)-NH2 - ADM2 is produced by enteric neurons and signals through CALCRL/RAMP-family receptors on intestinal ILC2s. Experimental loss of this signaling impaired amphiregulin-associated tissue protection and increased susceptibility to intestinal damage, whereas therapeutic recombinant ADM2 increased tissue-protective AREG-positive ILC2 activity and limited intestinal inflammation. This is the most directly demonstrated modern peptide axis connecting the ENS itself to restoration of intestinal immune/tissue equilibrium.
2. Myenteric-neuron survival and resistance to inflammatory neurotoxicity: Human GLP-2(1-33) - GLP-2 receptors are expressed in enteric neurons. GLP-2 directly increased cultured myenteric-neuron survival and counteracted mast-cell-induced neuronal loss. Separate inflammatory models demonstrated enteric-neural mediation of GLP-2's anti-inflammatory action, preservation/increase of VIP-positive neurons and protection against inflammation-induced neuronal and glial alterations. This therefore addresses preservation of the ENS network itself rather than simply changing intestinal contraction.
3. Excessive visceral mechanosensory gain and pain/hypersensitivity: Human galanin(1-30) - Galanin is an endogenous sensory/enteric neuropeptide with particularly relevant experimental evidence for excessive visceral signaling. Exogenous galanin dose-dependently suppressed colonic afferent responses to noxious distension and prevented development of acute inflammatory hypersensitivity, with GalR1 contributing importantly to the effect. This supplies the principal sensory “calming” axis without globally inhibiting the ENS.
4. Excessive gastrointestinal propulsion, smooth-muscle activity and inflammatory activation: Cortistatin-14 (CST-14; experimental rodent form) - Cortistatin combines somatostatin-receptor signaling with additional immunomodulatory activity. In experimental colitis it suppresses inflammatory responses, while direct gastrointestinal experiments demonstrated inhibition of GI transit, bead expulsion and fecal output and relaxation of longitudinal and circular intestinal smooth-muscle rhythmic contractions. It therefore represents the hypermotility/inflammatory-braking axis and is most relevant when “overactivity” rather than impaired propulsion dominates.
5. Coordinated interdigestive propulsion and prevention of excessive stasis: Human motilin - Physiological balance also requires periods of strong, organized motility. Motilin acts through receptors on enteric neurons and smooth muscle and is a major regulator of the fasting migrating motor complex. This cyclic housekeeping motor program is mechanistically different from pathological spasm or continuous hypermotility. Motilin is therefore included specifically as the coordinated-propulsion axis so that “calming” does not incorrectly become generalized intestinal paralysis.
6. Inhibitory enteric motor-neuron signaling and physiological smooth-muscle relaxation: Human vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-NH2 - VIP is a major inhibitory enteric neurotransmitter and participates with nitrergic signaling in gastrointestinal smooth-muscle relaxation. Enteric-neuron experiments additionally demonstrate direct VIP-dependent protection of myenteric neurons, including protection against mast-cell-induced neuronal loss. This supplies a physiologic inhibitory-motor axis distinct from cortistatin's broader suppression of transit: VIP participates in the spatially coordinated relaxation required for normal peristaltic reflexes.
7. Postprandial braking, secretomotor moderation and endogenous visceral antinociception: Human peptide YY(1-36)-NH2 - PYY provides a physiological meal-responsive “brake” complementary to motilin's fasting motor program. Peripheral PYY inhibits propulsive colonic motility and intestinal secretion through Y-receptor signaling. PYY deletion experimentally exaggerates visceral pain behavior, while Y2-receptor antagonism similarly produces hyperalgesic effects, supporting an endogenous PYY contribution to restraining visceral sensory gain. This makes PYY a combined postprandial motility/secretory and sensory-balancing axis rather than simply another antidiarrheal peptide.

﻿Enteritis is an inflammation of the small intestine, often caused by infections (bacterial, viral, or parasitic), radiation therapy, medications like NSAIDs, autoimmune conditions such as Crohn's disease, or food intolerances. It can be acute or chronic, with subtypes including infectious gastroenteritis, radiation enteritis, and enteritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fever, dehydration, and in severe cases, blood in stool or weight loss. Pathophysiology involves disruption of the intestinal mucosal barrier, leading to increased permeability ('leaky gut'), invasion by pathogens or toxins, activation of inflammatory cascades (e.g., NF-{kappa}B pathway), immune dysregulation, oxidative stress, microbial dysbiosis, and impaired epithelial regeneration. Complications may include malnutrition, electrolyte imbalances, sepsis, or chronic conditions like short bowel syndrome.

The proposed polypeptides address enteritis through various therapeutic axes, emphasizing real-world examples where possible but supplementing with designed polypeptides due to limited verifiable real-world sequences under length limits (only GLP-2 retrieved with sequence <=150 aa from tool outputs; shortfall documented, using 1 real and 17 designed to meet mins). GLP-2 (real) promotes intestinal barrier repair and epithelial growth via cAMP-mediated signaling, reducing inflammation and improving nutrient absorption in radiation or chemotherapy-induced enteritis. Designed polypeptides target anti-inflammatory axis (D1, D8, D15) by inhibiting NF-{kappa}B and cytokine release, with short hydrophilic sequences for solubility and feasibility in oral delivery. For gut microbiota modulation (D2, D9, D16), peptides mimic antimicrobial motifs to restore balance, considering pI for stability in GI environment. For immune regulation (D3, D10, D17), designs modulate TLR signaling to reduce overactivation. For antioxidant effects (D4, D11), sequences include cysteine-rich motifs to scavenge ROS. For stem cell regeneration (D5, D12), peptides enhance WNT/Notch pathways for ISC proliferation. For metabolic regulation (D6, D13), they target bile acid homeostasis. For quorum-sensing (D7, D14), designs disrupt bacterial communication. Overall, feasibility involves preclinical testing for efficacy, low toxicity due to natural motifs, and physicochemical properties like MW <3 kDa for absorption.

Enterocele is a form of pelvic organ prolapse in which small bowel descends into a weakened upper/posterior vaginal support compartment. The peptide-selection rationale therefore focuses on the experimentally documented biology of pelvic-support failure: impaired vaginal fibroblast viability, reduced or disordered collagen I/III production, defective extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial repair, and insufficient vascular support during tissue repair. Evidence for peptide or growth-factor treatment of established enterocele itself is not clinical; most evidence is from pelvic-organ-prolapse fibroblasts, vaginal wound-healing models, or broader tissue-repair studies.

Vaginal fibroblast survival and collagen I/III homeostasis: Human IGF-1 - IGF-1 is reduced in POP vaginal tissue; POP-derived vaginal fibroblast studies link IGF-1 signaling to fibroblast viability and collagen I/III production through MAPK/NF-{kappa}B and, more recently, PI3K/AKT/LARP6 signaling, making it the strongest condition-specific peptide axis identified.
2. FGFR1-mediated fibroblast proliferation and matrix regeneration: FGF2-derived FGFR1 agonist peptide DPHIKLQLQAE - Basic FGF is the best-supported growth factor in the 2023 systematic review of vaginal wound healing relevant to POP, promoting fibroblast proliferation, differentiation and collagen I/III production; DPHIKLQLQAE is a characterized FGF2-derived FGFR1 agonist motif that provides a much smaller defined peptide representation of this signaling axis.
3. Vaginal epithelial proliferation and re-epithelialization: Human EGF - EGF stimulated proliferation in experimental vaginal wound-healing studies reviewed specifically in the context of improving POP surgical repair, addressing restoration of the epithelial component over mechanically compromised pelvic connective tissue.
4. Vaginal epithelial trophic support and mucosal repair: Recombinant human FGF7/KGF residues 32-194 - FGF7 is a paracrine epithelial growth factor with direct vaginal epithelial proliferative activity. The defined nonglycosylated recombinant chain is used here to avoid the heterogeneous glycoforms of native mammalian FGF7; its two established disulfide bridges are represented in the residue masses.
5. Repair-associated fibroblast recruitment and neovascularization: Substance P - Substance P promotes fibroblast migration/proliferation, extracellular-matrix deposition and vascular repair in experimental wound models. This axis is secondary to the POP-specific growth-factor axes but addresses neurogenic recruitment of reparative cells and angiogenesis needed for durable connective-tissue remodeling.
6. Angiogenesis, fibroblast migration and collagen-I remodeling: Human {alpha}-CGRP - CGRP promotes wound-associated angiogenesis and has experimental evidence for fibroblast migration and collagen-I regulation. It complements the structural collagen axes by targeting vascular supply and neurovascular control of tissue repair rather than duplicating IGF-1/FGF signaling.

Enthesitis is inflammation of the tendon-, ligament-, or joint-capsule attachment to bone. Persistent or multifocal disease is characteristic of psoriatic arthritis and other spondyloarthritides, where mechanical stress interacts with IL-23/IL-17, TNF, IL-1, immune-cell recruitment, and abnormal bone remodeling. The following is a research model comprising six experimental peptide entities; no Sternheimer-proteody axis is included because enthesitis is not driven by excessive ribosomal production of one specific host protein.

1. IL-17A effector blockade: HAP - Binds the IL-17A homodimer and sterically prevents IL-17RA engagement, targeting a principal entheseal inflammatory cytokine.
2. IL-23 receptor signaling: Peptide 2305 - All-D noncompetitive IL-23R antagonist intended to reduce IL-23-dependent STAT3 signaling upstream of entheseal IL-17/IL-22 responses.
3. Leukocyte trafficking restraint: PEPITEM - Endogenous immunoregulatory peptide that restricts trans-endothelial migration of inflammatory leukocytes; inflammatory-arthritis models report reduced infiltration, swelling, and tissue damage.

5. TNF/RANKL-linked bone remodeling: WP9QY - TNFR1-loop mimic that antagonizes TNF signaling and directly interferes with RANKL-dependent osteoclastogenesis and inflammatory bone resorption.
6. IL-1 inflammatory amplification: AF12198 - Selective human IL-1R1 antagonist that blocks IL-1-driven adhesion-molecule expression and downstream IL-6 and IL-8 production.

﻿Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, immune-mediated clinicopathologic disorder of the esophagus characterized by symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and prominent eosinophil-predominant inflammation. Pathophysiologically, EoE is driven by a Th2-type immune response typically triggered by food antigens, leading to the excessive secretion of cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. This inflammatory cascade results in the recruitment of eosinophils to the esophageal mucosa and the localized production of eotaxin-3 (CCL26), which further amplifies eosinophil infiltration. Chronic inflammation leads to tissue remodeling, including subepithelial fibrosis and esophageal narrowing (strictures), which clinically manifests as dysphagia and food impaction. Management focuses on dietary elimination, topical corticosteroids, and increasingly, targeted biologic therapies that disrupt the underlying cytokine signaling pathways to prevent irreversible fibrostenotic changes.

Created 2026-05-04

1. Esophageal Mucosal Repair: BPC-157 - A 15-residue pentadecapeptide that promotes the healing of the gastrointestinal epithelium and stabilizes the mucosal barrier, counteracting the erosive damage caused by chronic eosinophilic inflammation
2. Systemic Anti-inflammatory Signaling: KPV - A tripeptide derived from alpha-MSH that reduces the production of proinflammatory cytokines and inhibits NF-kappaB activation, providing a potent localized and systemic anti-inflammatory effect
3. Tight Junction Regulation: Larazotide - An 8-residue peptide that regulates epithelial tight junctions to reduce intestinal and esophageal permeability, preventing the translocation of food allergens across the mucosal barrier
4. Mucus Layer Stabilization: TFF3 fragment - A bioactive fragment of Trefoil Factor 3 that enhances the protective mucus layer and facilitates rapid epithelial restitution in the esophagus following inflammatory injury

﻿Erdheim-Chester Disease (ECD) is a rare multisystem non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterized by the abnormal proliferation and infiltration of lipid-laden macrophages or histiocytes into various tissues and organs, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and organ dysfunction. ﻿Fabry's Disease, also known as Fabry disease, is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, which encodes the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A ({alpha}-Gal A). Early symptoms often appear in childhood or adolescence and include acroparesthesia (intense burning pain in the hands and feet triggered by stress, temperature changes, or exercise), angiokeratomas (small, dark red spots on the skin due to vascular dilation), hypohidrosis or anhidrosis (reduced or absent sweating leading to heat intolerance), gastrointestinal disturbances such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and nausea, and corneal opacities known as cornea verticillata. ﻿Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is an inherited genetic disorder characterized by significantly elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in the blood, leading to premature cardiovascular disease. ﻿Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH) is a predominantly autosomal dominant genetic disorder characterized by lifelong, non-progressive elevation of serum calcium (hypercalcemia), low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria), and normal to slightly elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH). The condition typically results from inactivating mutations in the CASR gene (FHH Type 1), which encodes the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) responsible for monitoring extracellular calcium levels. In FHH, the receptor's 'set point' is shifted, meaning the body requires higher-than-normal calcium levels to signal the parathyroid glands to suppress PTH and the kidneys to excrete calcium. While usually benign and asymptomatic, FHH must be carefully distinguished from primary hyperparathyroidism to avoid unnecessary surgical interventions like parathyroidectomy, which are ineffective for FHH.

1. Positive Allosteric Modulation (PAM): The primary pharmacological strategy involves increasing the sensitivity of the mutated CaSR. Calcimimetic compounds bind to the transmembrane domain, inducing a conformational change that lowers the threshold for receptor activation.
2. G-Protein Signal Potentiation (G{alpha}11 Enhancement): FHH Type 2 involves mutations in GNA11. Peptides or small molecules that stabilize the G{alpha}11 hydrophobic cleft can rectify signaling defects downstream of the receptor, specifically restoring Phospholipase C (PLC) activation.
3. Endocytic Trafficking Regulation (AP2{sigma} Support): FHH Type 3 is caused by mutations in AP2S1, affecting receptor internalization. Targeting the adaptor protein complex 2 (AP2) facilitates proper CaSR trafficking and recycling to the cell surface, ensuring a sufficient receptor population is available for sensing.
4. PTH-Receptor Antagonism: In cases where mild PTH elevation contributes to symptomatic bone resorption, modulating the PTH1 receptor can mitigate systemic calcium release from the skeletal reservoir.

Forkhead Box M1 (FOXM1) is a master regulator transcription factor that is aberrantly overexpressed in a wide spectrum of human cancers, where it drives the 'hallmarks of cancer,' including uncontrolled proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and chemotherapy resistance. FOXM1 exerts its oncogenic effects by transactivating genes essential for the G1/S and G2/M cell cycle transitions and by interacting with key signaling proteins such as $\beta$-catenin, SMAD3, and the MuvB complex. Targeting FOXM1 is considered a high-priority strategy in oncology to disrupt these core survival pathways and sensitize multidrug-resistant tumors to conventional treatments. Advanced peptide-based interventions utilize recombinant domains and rationally designed interfering peptides to block FOXM1's DNA-binding capacity and its critical protein-protein interactions (PPIs).

1. The 'Decoy' Strategy (Competitive Inhibition)
FOXM1 has a specific 'hand' (the DNA-Binding Domain) that it uses to grab onto cancer-promoting genes. If we flood the cell with synthetic versions of just that 'hand,' those decoys will grab onto the DNA first.Since the decoys aren't attached to the rest of the FOXM1 'body,' they can't actually turn the gene on. They just sit there, blocking the real FOXM1 from doing its job.

2. Mimicking the 'Off Switch' (Autoinhibition)
In a healthy cell, FOXM1 has a built-in safety lock: its N-terminal domain (the front) naturally folds over and hugs its C-terminal domain (the back), keeping it 'off.' In cancer, this lock breaks, leaving the protein permanently 'on.'By introducing peptides like M1-138 (which is just the N-terminal 'lock'), we provide a 'replacement part' that swims over to the overactive FOXM1, latches onto its C-terminus, and forces it back into the 'off' position.

3. Breaking Up the 'Crew' (PPI Disruption)
FOXM1 doesn't work alone; it needs to recruit a 'crew' of other proteins (like $\beta$-catenin or the MuvB complex) to start the cancer machinery.Specific peptides, like M1-21, are designed to look exactly like the 'docking port' where these crew members attach.The crew protein sees the peptide and thinks, 'Ah, there's my docking port!'It binds to the peptide instead of the real FOXM1.The real FOXM1 is left standing alone, unable to perform its function.

Therapeutic FOXM1 Peptides

1. Global Transcriptional Repression: M1-138
A recombinant version of the full FOXM1 N-terminal domain (residues 1-138) fused to a 9×Arg cell-penetrating peptide. It acts as an autorepressor, binding to the FOXM1 C-terminal activation domain and competing with SMAD3 to inhibit cell migration, proliferation, and transcriptional activity.

2. PPI Disruption and $\beta$-catenin Inhibition: M1-21 (TAT-106-126)
A 21-mer peptide derived from the N-terminal repressor domain (residues 106-126), optimized as a stable D-retro-inverso (DRI) form and fused with a TAT sequence. It disrupts the recruitment of the MuvB complex and blocks $\beta$-catenin nuclear importation, significantly suppressing cancer cell growth.

3. CBP/Co-activator Blockade: M1-20
An optimized interfering peptide derived from the FOXM1 sequence library (targeting C- and N-terminal regions). It potently binds FOXM1 to disrupt its interaction with the transcriptional co-activator CBP and the N-terminal/MuvB complex, showing strong anti-cancer activity across multiple models.

4. DNA-Binding Inhibition: FOXM1-DBD
A representative segment from the highly conserved Forkhead DNA-binding domain (residues 232-332). This region is responsible for recognizing the consensus promoter motifs (RYAAAYA). Competitive peptides targeting this site prevent FOXM1 from initiating the expression of oncogenic target genes.

5. Transactivation Domain Modulation: FOXM1-TAD
A specific portion of the C-terminal transactivation domain (TAD, residues 641-748). This domain is essential for the recruitment of transcriptional machinery. Peptides derived from the TAD can interfere with co-activator binding or mimic the natural autoinhibitory state.

6. Designed Oncogenic Blocker: FOX-Interfere-1
A synthetic peptide motif designed for high-affinity interference with FOXM1's ability to drive mitotic genes like *Plk1* and *Cyclin B1*. It is engineered to stabilize the protein in an inactive conformation or block specific regulatory phosphorylation sites.

Standard management relies on early diagnosis via endomyocardial biopsy, hemodynamic support (including mechanical circulatory devices as bridge), and aggressive combination immunosuppression-typically high-dose corticosteroids plus calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine or tacrolimus), often with adjunctive agents like anti-thymocyte globulin or muromonab-CD3 for T-cell depletion-yielding improved transplant-free survival in registry data. No short polypeptide therapeutics are established or in advanced clinical use; full-length biologics (e.g., polyclonal antibodies) dominate experimental immunomodulation. The first designed peptide, enriched in aromatic and basic residues, conceptually inhibits aberrant T-cell activation and myocardial infiltration to halt primary autoimmune attack. The second designed peptide targets cytokine-driven amplification, potentially interfering with proinflammatory signaling to dampen secondary inflammation. The third designed peptide aims to disrupt giant cell formation and necrotic processes through hydrophobic interactions with damaged myocardium. The fourth designed peptide supports myocyte viability and anti-remodeling effects to preserve cardiac function. Physicochemically, these peptides feature balanced hydrophobicity/cationic profiles for axis-specific targeting, no excessive residue repeats to limit aggregation, high sequence diversity (>50% pairwise differences) for multifaceted action, and short length enabling scalable production and potential cardiac delivery.

﻿Gigantism is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by excessive linear growth and tall stature resulting from chronic overproduction of growth hormone (GH) during childhood or adolescence, before the closure of epiphyseal growth plates. Glial-cell health is not a single disease state but a set of homeostatic functions distributed among astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and peripheral Schwann cells. Astrocytes regulate extracellular glutamate, neuronal metabolic support and trophic signaling; oligodendrocytes generate and maintain CNS myelin; Schwann cells perform analogous myelinating and regenerative functions in the peripheral nervous system; and microglia provide immune surveillance, debris clearance and trophic signals required for repair. Seven mechanistically distinct peptide-support axes were identified from direct glial-cell literature: astrocytic glutamate clearance, astrocytic trophic-factor secretion, oligodendrocyte myelin-membrane formation, glial sulfatide/myelin-lipid metabolism, reparative microglia-to-oligodendrocyte signaling, microglial inflammatory-state/debris-clearance regulation, and protection of oligodendrocytes from activated-microglial oxidative/proNGF toxicity. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis is included because normal glial support is not driven by pathological overproduction of a specific endogenous protein.

1. Astrocytic glutamate clearance and glutamate-glutamine metabolism: PACAP-38 - PACAP acts directly on astroglia involved in glutamate turnover. Experimental cortical-glia work showed increased glutamate-uptake capacity together with increased GLT-1, GLAST and glutamine-synthetase expression. PAC1-dependent PKA/PKC signaling therefore provides a highly specific astrocytic homeostasis axis relevant to prevention of extracellular-glutamate accumulation and excitotoxic stress.
2. Astrocytic survival and neurotrophic secretome support: Human VIP - VIP participates in neuron-astrocyte communication rather than acting only as a neuronal peptide. Astrocyte-containing cultures require VIP for much of their protective effect against glutamate toxicity; VIP enhances astrocytic glutamate uptake and promotes release of trophic/protective mediators. Additional experimental work shows that VIP-supported astrocytes release factors capable of promoting secondary neuronal and axonal repair. This is assigned separately from PACAP because its principal role here is the astrocytic trophic secretome rather than direct GLT-1/GLAST regulation.
3. Oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelin-membrane formation: Laminin-411-derived A4G47 - This 2025 peptide is one of the most glia-specific recent findings. Laminin-411 strongly supported oligodendrocyte differentiation and survival, and screening of short laminin-{alpha}4-derived peptides identified A4G47 as the sequence specifically capable of promoting sheet-like myelin-membrane formation. Scrambled versions lacked the activity. This provides a direct extracellular-matrix-to-oligodendrocyte myelination axis without relying on a generic neurotrophic peptide.
4. Sulfatide synthesis, myelin-lipid support and survival of oligodendrocytes/Schwann cells: Prosaptide TX14(A) - Prosaposin-derived TX14(A) directly increases sulfatide production in glia. Experiments found substantial increases in sulfatide in both primary Schwann cells and differentiated oligodendrocytes, together with protection against glial cell death and activation of ERK/PI3K-related trophic signaling. Because sulfatides are major myelin lipids, this axis complements A4G47: A4G47 targets morphological myelin-membrane formation, whereas TX14(A) targets the lipid/trophic machinery supporting myelin-forming glia. Its D-Ala residue has the same monoisotopic mass as L-Ala and is represented accordingly.
5. Reparative microglia-to-oligodendrocyte trophic signaling and remyelination: GV1001 - A 2025 EAE study identified microglia as the principal glial target of GV1001. The peptide increased the NF-{kappa}B antagonist PRMT1 and microglial IGF-1, reduced neuroinflammatory gene expression, protected oligodendrocyte progenitors, promoted their maturation and facilitated remyelination in glial co-cultures and diseased CNS tissue. This is assigned specifically to the beneficial microglia-to-OPC trophic-support axis rather than simply to general inflammation suppression.
6. Microglial homeostatic inflammatory-state regulation and debris clearance: Tuftsin - Tuftsin acts through neuropilin-1/TGF-{beta}-associated signaling in microglia. Experimental studies found increased IL-10, reduced TNF-{alpha} and a strong shift toward an anti-inflammatory/reparative microglial phenotype under excitotoxic conditions. Separate work connected tuftsin-enhanced microglial phagocytosis and debris clearance with improved remyelination. Modern microglial biology is more complex than the older binary M1/M2 terminology, so this entry is best interpreted as promotion of a reparative/homeostatic microglial state rather than conversion into a single fixed subtype.
7. Protection of oligodendrocytes from activated-microglial ROS/proNGF toxicity: Acylated human ghrelin - Activated microglia can damage oligodendrocytes through ROS, proNGF and stress-kinase signaling. Ghrelin directly reduced microglial p38/JNK/c-Jun activation, proNGF production and ROS and significantly decreased oligodendrocyte death in microglia-oligodendrocyte co-culture. This provides a distinct glial survival axis for inflammatory oxidative stress. The biologically active native peptide contains the essential Ser3 O-n-octanoyl modification, which is represented by modifying that residue's mass rather than adding a separate entry.

Fascia is a mechanically active connective-tissue network whose functional properties depend on regulated collagen and extracellular-matrix turnover, fibroblast behavior, myofibroblast contractility, tissue perfusion, sensory-neurovascular signaling and appropriate remodeling after mechanical loading or injury. Healthy fascia is therefore not simply a matter of increasing collagen synthesis: excessive collagen deposition, persistent TGF-{beta} signaling, myofibroblast activation and matrix stiffening can impair normal tissue compliance and gliding. Seven mechanistically distinct peptide-addressable support axes were identified. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was included because normal fascial physiology is not driven by pathological overproduction of one specific endogenous peptide or protein.

1. RXFP1-mediated fascial extracellular-matrix remodeling: B7-33 - A single-chain C-terminally amidated relaxin-2 B-chain analogue and selective RXFP1 agonist. Human fascial fibroblasts respond directly to relaxin signaling, which reduces collagen-I, collagen-III and other extracellular-matrix synthesis. B7-33 provides a chemically simpler relaxin-pathway agonist with documented antifibrotic signaling and collagen-remodeling activity.
2. TGF-{beta}1-driven fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition: P144 / Disitertide - A 14-residue peptide derived from the extracellular region of TGF-{beta} receptor III/betaglycan that inhibits TGF-{beta}1 activity. TGF-{beta} signaling is a central regulator of pathological fascial fibrosis, matrix accumulation and myofibroblast differentiation; P144 has demonstrated antifibrotic activity in experimental soft-tissue fibrosis.
3. {alpha}-SMA-dependent myofibroblast contractility: Ac-EEED - The N-terminal acetylated tetrapeptide corresponding to the specific amino-terminal sequence of {alpha}-smooth-muscle actin. Ac-EEED disrupts incorporation of {alpha}-SMA into myofibroblast stress fibers and decreases contractile force, directly addressing excessive fascial contraction and mechanically sustained tissue stiffness without broadly stimulating collagen synthesis.

Nutrient and calorie absorption depends on adequate gastric acid, pancreatic enzymes, bicarbonate, bile delivery, intestinal surface area, epithelial integrity, appropriate transit time, mucosal blood flow, and functioning nutrient transporters. Impairment may result from pancreatic insufficiency, bile-acid deficiency, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel syndrome, atrophic gastritis, intestinal infection, small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, medication effects, or excessive gastrointestinal transit. Eight peptide-responsive axes were identified. These candidates address defined absorptive mechanisms rather than appetite alone. No universal excessively synthesized endogenous peptide or protein drives malabsorption, so a Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was not justified.

1. Intestinal villus growth and direct macronutrient absorption: Teduglutide - This degradation-resistant GLP-2 receptor agonist promotes crypt and villus growth, mucosal blood flow, epithelial repair, reduced gastrointestinal secretion, slower transit, and increased absorptive surface. Human metabolic-balance studies in short-bowel syndrome demonstrated greater water, sodium, monosaccharide, and energy absorption together with reduced fecal energy loss and reduced dependence on parenteral support.
2. Ileal and colonic brake with increased nutrient-contact time: Human peptide YY(1-36), C-terminally amidated - Peptide YY slows gastric emptying and mouth-to-cecum transit, suppresses intestinal chloride secretion, and can reduce rapid postprandial intestinal losses. Short-bowel patients retaining a colon have higher peptide YY concentrations and slower gastric emptying than patients without a colon, supporting a compensatory “colonic brake” that prolongs exposure of nutrients to the remaining absorptive mucosa.
3. Pancreatic enzyme secretion and coordinated bile delivery: Sulfated cholecystokinin-8, C-terminally amidated - Physiological cholecystokinin signaling stimulates pancreatic trypsin and lipase secretion, contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi through neural pathways, and slows gastric emptying. These coordinated effects improve digestion of protein and fat before enterocyte uptake. Excessive stimulation could instead cause nausea, abdominal pain, biliary colic, or pancreatitis.
4. Duodenal acid neutralization and digestive-enzyme activation: Human secretin, C-terminally amidated - Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal bicarbonate and fluid secretion, helping neutralize acidic gastric contents. An appropriate duodenal pH is required for pancreatic lipase, proteases, amylase, brush-border enzymes, bile-salt micelles, and mucosal integrity. Secretin supports the chemical environment for absorption but cannot overcome severe loss of pancreatic tissue or obstructed ducts.
5. Gastric protein digestion and liberation of food-bound micronutrients: Sulfated human gastrin-17, N-terminal pyroglutamate and C-terminally amidated - Gastrin stimulates enterochromaffin-like-cell histamine release, parietal-cell acid production, gastric motility, and mucosal trophic signaling. Gastric acid activates pepsin and facilitates release or solubilization of food-bound vitamin B12, iron, calcium, and dietary protein. Gastrin would be inappropriate in acid-peptic disease, gastrinoma, severe reflux, or uncontrolled hypergastrinemia.
6. Intestinal epithelial restitution and tight-junction recovery: Monomeric human trefoil factor 3 with three intramolecular disulfides and reduced Cys57 - Trefoil factor 3 is secreted by intestinal goblet cells and stabilizes the mucus-epithelial interface. It promotes epithelial migration and restitution and increases tightening junctional proteins while reducing inflammation-associated permeability. This axis preserves functional absorptive epithelium after injury rather than directly stimulating nutrient transporters.
7. Prevention of zonulin-associated barrier disruption and inflammatory absorptive loss: Larazotide free-acid octapeptide - Larazotide antagonizes zonulin-associated tight-junction opening and has been investigated orally in celiac disease. Human trials reported some symptom improvement during gluten exposure, but permeability measurements and major efficacy outcomes were inconsistent. Its potential contribution is reduction of ongoing antigen entry and secondary mucosal injury, not generalized enhancement of calorie uptake.
8. GRP-receptor-mediated intestinal adaptation after major mucosal loss: Bombesin, N-terminal pyroglutamate and C-terminally amidated - Bombesin-family signaling stimulates gastrointestinal trophic responses, secretion, mucosal cellularity, and intestinal adaptation. In a rat short-bowel model, bombesin improved D-xylose absorption, reduced fecal fat, limited weight loss, and increased serum protein and albumin. Evidence remains preclinical, and bombesin-receptor stimulation can also promote gastrointestinal smooth-muscle activity and growth of some receptor-positive tumors.

The lacrimal glands produce the aqueous, electrolyte, antimicrobial, and protein-rich component of the tear film. Reduced function may result from autoimmune inflammation, aging, autonomic or sensory denervation, diabetes, medication effects, radiation, surgery, ductal dysfunction, or chronic ocular-surface inflammation. Eight mechanistically distinct peptide-responsive axes were identified. Lacripep is the only selected peptide tested topically in a controlled human study involving lacrimal-associated disease; the remaining entries are supported principally by animal or isolated-gland experiments. No peptide is established as a general treatment for restoring damaged human lacrimal glands. No single excessively synthesized endogenous protein is a universal driver of lacrimal dysfunction, so a Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was not justified.

1. Lacritin-deficient ocular-surface and lacrimal homeostasis: Lacripep / lacritin N-94/C-6, N-terminally acetylated and C-terminally amidated - Lacripep is the biologically active carboxyl-terminal fragment of human lacritin, a tear protein reduced in several forms of dry eye and particularly in Sjögren-associated disease. It supports epithelial homeostasis, stress resistance, tear-film stability, and lacritin-dependent secretory signaling. Topical treatment was safe and well tolerated in a 204-subject Sjögren trial, although the prespecified corneal-staining and eye-dryness efficacy endpoints were not met; secondary and post hoc subgroup signals were reported.
2. Acinar water permeability and aqueous tear secretion: Human PACAP-38, C-terminally amidated - PACAP activates the PAC1 receptor on lacrimal acinar cells, increasing adenylate cyclase activity, cyclic AMP, protein kinase A signaling, aquaporin-5 phosphorylation, and movement of aquaporin-5 to the apical membrane. Lacrimal-gland aquaporin-5 suppression reduced PACAP-induced tearing, directly linking this pathway to acinar water output.
3. Lacrimal duct electrolyte transport and fluid secretion: Human vasoactive intestinal peptide, C-terminally amidated - Vasoactive intestinal peptide activates VPAC receptors and cyclic-AMP-dependent epithelial transport. Lacrimal duct studies support stimulation of chloride and fluid secretion involving the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. It also stimulated both tear-fluid volume and protein secretion in cannulated rabbit lacrimal glands.
4. Acinar protein and aqueous secretion through an alternate VIP-family secretagogue: Porcine peptide histidine-isoleucine-27, C-terminally amidated - This endogenous VIP-family peptide dose-dependently stimulated both fluid and protein output from rabbit lacrimal glands. It provides an experimentally distinct secretagogue input that may recruit overlapping VPAC signaling while differing in receptor potency and tissue distribution from vasoactive intestinal peptide.
5. Fluid-selective lacrimal secretion: Sulfated cholecystokinin-8, C-terminally amidated - Sulfated cholecystokinin-8 stimulated lacrimal fluid output without significantly increasing protein secretion in the rabbit preparation. This makes it a condition-specific candidate for selectively recruiting the aqueous secretory component rather than broadly increasing exocytosis of glandular proteins.
6. Sensory-neuroimmune stimulation of glandular secretion: Human substance P, C-terminally amidated - Substance P released serotonin from resident lacrimal mast cells and increased lacrimal protein and peroxidase secretion in isolated rat glands. This provides a mechanistic link between sensory innervation, mast-cell signaling, and glandular output. Because substance P also promotes pain, vasodilation, and inflammation, excessive activation could worsen ocular discomfort rather than improve gland health.
7. CGRP-dependent neurovascular and periductal secretory regulation: Human alpha-CGRP disulfide peptide, C-terminally amidated - CGRP-containing nerves occur around lacrimal ducts and blood vessels. CGRP directly increased protein and peroxidase output in isolated rat lacrimal tissue and modulated substance-P-driven mast-cell responses. This axis addresses neural regulation, local vascular supply, and neuroimmune coordination, but CGRP can provoke migraine, flushing, nociception, and hypotension.
8. EGFR-mediated glandular protein secretion and epithelial trophic signaling: Human epidermal growth factor disulfide peptide - Epidermal growth factor activates lacrimal acinar EGFR, raises intracellular calcium, recruits protein kinase C, and stimulates concentration-dependent protein secretion. The evidence establishes a secretory signaling role in lacrimal acini, but does not demonstrate regeneration of chronically fibrotic, irradiated, or autoimmune-destroyed human lacrimal tissue.

Thyroid homeostasis depends on coordinated hypothalamic-pituitary signaling, intrathyroidal neural and paracrine regulation, iodide uptake and hormone biosynthetic machinery, adequate thyroid perfusion, controlled thyroid-hormone release, and protection against inappropriate thyroid-directed immunity. Because this is a general thyroid-support program rather than a program for specifically diagnosed hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, the selected peptides deliberately include both stimulatory and restraining physiological regulators rather than driving thyroid output in only one direction. Eight mechanistically distinct axes are represented.

1. Hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis initiation: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH/protirelin) - The endogenous pyroGlu-His-Pro-NH2 tripeptide is the principal hypothalamic signal stimulating pituitary TSH synthesis and release. TRH signaling is fundamental to the physiological HPT feedback loop, and TRH receptors are also expressed by thyroid follicular cells, supporting an additional local paracrine regulatory role.
2. Thyrocyte cAMP activation, iodide uptake and thyroid-hormone secretion: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) - Human VIP directly activates cultured human thyroid cells through cAMP signaling. Experimental thyroid preparations show stimulation of T4/T3 secretion, while iodine-deficiency studies demonstrate enhancement of thyroidal iodide uptake, giving VIP a direct intrathyroidal functional axis separate from pituitary TSH signaling.
3. Central T3 feedback and HPT set-point regulation: PACAP-38 - PACAP regulates hypothalamic type-2 deiodinase activity in tanycytes, modifying local T4-to-T3 conversion and thereby TRH/TSH feedback. PACAP-containing nerves and PAC1/VPAC receptors are also present around thyroid follicles and thyroid vasculature, supporting both central and local thyroid regulatory functions.
4. Thyroid microvascular perfusion: PHI-27 - Peptide histidine isoleucine produced a roughly fourfold increase in experimental thyroid blood flow without requiring a corresponding rise in circulating thyroid hormones. PHI-containing nerves occur around thyroid follicles and blood vessels, making this a distinct gland-perfusion axis rather than another direct hormone-stimulation axis.
5. Intrathyroidal neural modulation of stimulated hormone release: Neuropeptide Y - NPY is present in sympathetic thyroid nerve fibers and modulates thyroid blood flow and stimulated iodothyronine release. Experimental studies show that NPY can modify TSH-, adrenergic-, and VIP-dependent thyroid responses, consistent with a fine-tuning rather than constitutively stimulatory role.
6. Thyroglobulin/TPO/NIS and metabolic-thyroid coupling: Octanoylated human ghrelin - Ghrelin and its receptor are present within thyroid regulatory systems. Experimental thyrocyte studies demonstrate modulation of the TSH response, including thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase and sodium-iodide-symporter expression. The biologically active human peptide contains the essential Ser3 O-octanoyl modification, represented as a +126.104 Da residue-localized mass change.
7. Thyroid-directed autoimmune antigen-presentation restraint: RT-15 - This 15-residue all-D retro-inverso peptide was specifically engineered against HLA-DR{beta}1-Arg74, an HLA configuration implicated in autoimmune thyroid disease. RT-15 blocked thyroglobulin-peptide binding, suppressed thyroid-autoreactive T-cell activation ex vivo, and showed activity in an experimental autoimmune-thyroiditis model. This is a highly specific preclinical thyroid-autoimmunity axis rather than a generic anti-inflammatory peptide.
8. Protection against excessive TSH-driven thyroid activity: Somatostatin-14 - Endogenous somatostatin is present in thyroid parafollicular cells and directly suppresses TSH-stimulated thyroid hormone secretion in humans. It also reduces TSH-stimulated cAMP signaling and proliferation of human thyroid follicular cells, providing the counter-regulatory brake required for balanced rather than exclusively stimulatory thyroid support.

High intraocular pressure with impaired aqueous humor drainage is treated here as glaucoma-relevant ocular hypertension: aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body, flows through the posterior chamber and pupil into the anterior chamber, and exits mainly through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm’s canal, with a smaller uveoscleral route. The core pathologic map is increased trabecular/juxtacanalicular resistance, Schlemm-canal endothelial dysfunction, excess trabecular extracellular-matrix stiffness, ROCK/actomyosin contractility, TGF-{beta}2/SMAD/CTGF fibrosis pressure, ciliary-body aqueous overproduction, MYOC/ER-stress risk, endothelin/vascular dysregulation, retinal ganglion-cell mitochondrial stress, and optic-nerve neuroinflammation. Acute angle-closure symptoms such as severe eye pain, red eye, halos, nausea/vomiting, headache, or sudden visual change are urgent/emergency signs. This is research-format only and does not replace tonometry, gonioscopy, optic-nerve/OCT monitoring, visual-field testing, prescription drops, laser trabeculoplasty, iridotomy, minimally invasive glaucoma surgery, trabeculectomy, or shunt procedures.

Hypertriglyceridemia reflects excessive circulating triglyceride-rich lipoproteins arising from increased hepatic VLDL production, impaired lipoprotein-lipase-mediated clearance, excessive apoC-III activity, excessive postprandial chylomicron production, insulin resistance/visceral adiposity, and disturbances of whole-body fatty-acid oxidation. Six mechanistically distinct peptide axes with exact, non-ambiguous chemistry were retained. Generic hypertriglyceridemia was not assigned a Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition entry because it is etiologically heterogeneous and cannot be assumed to result from excessive synthesis of one endogenous protein such as APOC3 without phenotype-specific evidence. Pegozafermin has unusually strong clinical evidence in severe hypertriglyceridemia, but its proprietary 20-kDa glycoPEG conjugate cannot be represented with an exact residue-localized mass delta from the publicly available chemistry; it was therefore rejected from the mass-string set rather than approximated.

1. Impaired LPL-mediated triglyceride-rich-lipoprotein clearance plus apoC-III inhibition: D6PV (real) - A 40-residue apoC-II mimetic derived largely from human apoC-II that directly activates LPL while displacing/antagonizing apoC-III. It increased LPL-dependent lipolysis in human hypertriglyceridemic plasma, produced approximately 80-85% acute triglyceride reductions in several hypertriglyceridemic mouse models, reduced apoC-III and apoB, and retained substantial triglyceride-lowering activity even in inducible LPL-knockout mice, indicating an additional apoC-III/hepatic-remnant-clearance mechanism.
2. Excess postprandial chylomicron and apoB-48 production: Exenatide / exendin-4-NH2 (real) - In a randomized double-blind crossover human study, a single premeal dose markedly suppressed postprandial triglycerides, apoB-48, apoC-III, remnant-lipoprotein triglyceride and remnant cholesterol. This represents a GLP-1-receptor-dependent intestinal/postprandial axis distinct from direct LPL activation. The chemically defined 39-residue C-terminally amidated peptide is retained.
3. Visceral-adiposity/GH-axis contribution to triglyceride overproduction: Tesamorelin (real) - A stabilized GHRH(1-44) analogue with an N-terminal trans-3-hexenoyl group. In randomized human studies involving visceral adiposity/relative GH deficiency, tesamorelin reduced visceral adipose tissue and produced significant triglyceride reductions, including an approximately 20% placebo-adjusted reduction in one 12-month obesity study. This axis is phenotype-dependent and is not evidence that tesamorelin should be used for every form of hypertriglyceridemia. The trans-3-hexenoyl modification contributes a calculated net residue-localized delta of +96.058 Da to Tyr1.
4. APJ-dependent adiposity, adiponectin and thermogenic energy-expenditure dysregulation: Human apelin-13 (real) - Administration of apelin-13 to lean and high-fat-fed obese mice reduced serum triglycerides and insulin without reduced food intake, while increasing adiponectin, BAT UCP1, skeletal-muscle UCP3, oxygen consumption and energy expenditure. The exact linear human apelin-13 sequence QRPRLSHKGPMPF with free termini is retained.
5. Mitochondrial AMPK/{beta}-oxidation and metabolic inflexibility: MOTS-c (real) - The 16-residue mitochondrial-derived peptide MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR regulates AMPK-linked metabolic pathways, insulin sensitivity and fatty-acid oxidation. A 2026 diet-induced-obesity study reported significant lowering of serum triglycerides, cholesterol and free fatty acids by native MOTS-c; earlier mechanistic studies independently demonstrated effects on lipid handling and {beta}-oxidation. Evidence remains preclinical.
6. Hepatic lipogenesis, insulin resistance and triglyceride accumulation: Human adropin(34-76) (real) - The biologically active 43-residue adropin peptide alters hepatic and systemic substrate metabolism. Adropin treatment in diet-induced obese mice reduced hepatic triglyceride accumulation and expression of lipogenic programs including SREBP1c, SCD1 and DGAT2 while improving insulin resistance. Native adropin(34-76) contains the experimentally specified Cys1-Cys23 disulfide, represented by applying -2.016 Da to the higher-index Cys23.

This program treats “hip imbalance” as functional pelvic/hip asymmetry involving unequal hip-abductor or external-rotator strength, impaired gluteal recruitment, asymmetric muscular endurance, altered proprioceptive control, compensatory soft-tissue stiffness and unequal load tolerance. Hip-abductor weakness can contribute to contralateral pelvic drop and compensatory trunk motion, while reduced external-rotator control can permit excessive femoral internal rotation; these mechanisms can propagate abnormal loading through the pelvis, knee and lower limb. The program therefore targets the biological systems that support symmetrical muscle force production, muscle regeneration, mitochondrial endurance, proprioceptive afferent integrity and freedom from fibrotic soft-tissue restriction. It does not assume that peptides can correct fixed structural causes such as true leg-length discrepancy, hip dysplasia, scoliosis, advanced osteoarthritis, femoroacetabular deformity or a mechanically rotated pelvis. Six mechanistically distinct axes were identified.

1. Hip-abductor and external-rotator muscle regeneration with restoration of force-generating capacity: Apelin-13 - Apelin-13 stimulates the vascular skeletal-muscle stem-cell niche through endothelial APJ signaling. ﻿Hirschsprung’s disease (HSCR), also known as congenital aganglionic megacolon, is a rare developmental disorder occurring in approximately 1 in 5000 live births, characterized by the absence of enteric nervous system ganglia in variable lengths of the distal bowel due to failed migration, proliferation, differentiation, or survival of neural crest-derived enteric neural crest cells (ENCCs) during embryogenesis. This aganglionosis results in tonic contraction of the affected segment, causing functional intestinal obstruction, severe constipation, abdominal distension, failure to pass meconium in neonates, and a high risk of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC), a potentially life-threatening inflammatory complication. The primary pathophysiological mechanisms involve disruptions in key signaling pathways, predominantly RET/GDNF and EDNRB/endothelin-3, with contributions from genetic mutations (e.g., in RET, EDNRB, GDNF, EDN3) and microenvironmental factors affecting ENCC dynamics.

Current treatment is predominantly surgical (pull-through procedures to resect aganglionic bowel), with supportive care for complications, but many patients experience persistent bowel dysfunction, incontinence, or HAEC postoperatively. No established polypeptide therapies exist, and searches across PubMed, clinical trials, patents, and databases yielded no real-world polypeptides with documented therapeutic application in HSCR meeting validation criteria.

The proposed polypeptides are all conceptual designed sequences addressing core axes: the first designed polypeptide hypothetically mimics neurotrophic effects to activate RET signaling, promoting ENCC migration, proliferation, and survival; the second designed polypeptide conceptually emulates endothelin-like signaling via EDNRB to support ENCC proliferation and differentiation; the third designed polypeptide provides potential anti-inflammatory modulation to mitigate HAEC risk by dampening neuroimmune dysregulation. These short peptides use standard residues for synthetic feasibility, stability, and low immunogenicity potential, with modes of action inspired by pathway deficiencies, though requiring preclinical testing for efficacy and delivery (e.g., targeted enteric administration).

﻿Histamine Intolerance (HIT) arises from an imbalance between histamine accumulation and degradation, primarily driven by Diamine Oxidase (DAO) deficiency or mast cell over-activation. Anti-inflammatory modulation (VIP, Thymosin Alpha-1) and neuro-immune regulation (Selank, Semax) provide systemic control over histamine-mediated symptoms. Designed peptides [11-12] target DAO catalytic mimicry and specific IgE-receptor signaling inhibition to prevent degranulation.

﻿Histotoxic hypoxia is a form of tissue hypoxia in which cells are unable to utilize delivered oxygen due to toxic inhibition of cellular respiration, primarily at the mitochondrial level. The prototypical cause is cyanide poisoning (acute from inhalation, ingestion, or smoke; chronic rare), but similar effects occur with hydrogen sulfide, azide, formate, or certain drugs/metabolites. Acute symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, tachypnea, seizures, cardiovascular collapse, and profound lactic acidosis; untreated severe cases rapidly progress to coma and death. Pathophysiology involves toxin binding to cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the electron transport chain, preventing oxygen acceptance, abolishing oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production, forcing anaerobic metabolism with lactate accumulation, calcium dysregulation, reactive oxygen species generation despite blocked chain, membrane damage, and apoptotic/necrotic cell death-especially devastating in CNS and cardiac tissues due to high energy demands.

The proposed polypeptides target core mechanistic axes in histotoxic hypoxia with short synthetic sequences for rapid action and feasibility. Peptides 1-4 are designed conceptual sequences flagged accordingly; Peptide 5 is the real investigational octapeptide NAP (davunetide), derived from activity-dependent neuroprotective protein, with established preclinical evidence directly protecting neurons against cyanide-induced cytotoxicity through microtubule stabilization, prevention of tubulin pool disruption, and broader anti-apoptotic effects. Peptide 1 (designed) is arginine-lysine rich cationic for conceptual enhanced cell penetration and potential competitive interference at toxin binding sites. Peptide 2 (designed) glycine-proline rich to conceptually maintain cytoskeletal and membrane stability during ATP crisis. Peptide 3 (designed) serine-glutamine rich polar for conceptual support of intracellular osmotic and enzymatic integrity. Peptide 4 (designed) phenylalanine-tyrosine rich aromatic to conceptually scavenge secondary ROS from dysfunctional mitochondria. These diverse designs complement the real polypeptide for multimodal potential in acute toxin-mediated cellular poisoning.

﻿Holoprosencephaly (HPE) is a severe congenital malformation of the forebrain characterized by incomplete cleavage of the prosencephalon into distinct cerebral hemispheres, occurring between the 18th and 28th days of gestation. It presents on a spectrum from alobar (complete failure of division, single ventricle, absent interhemispheric fissure) to semilobar (partial division) and lobar (near-complete division with fused frontal lobes), with middle interhemispheric variant as a milder form. Causes include genetic mutations in key developmental genes (e.g., SHH, ZIC2, SIX3, TGIF) leading to disrupted signaling pathways like Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Nodal/TGF{beta}, and FGF, as well as environmental factors such as maternal diabetes, alcohol exposure, or teratogens like cyclopamine. Symptoms vary by severity but often include cyclopia or closely spaced eyes in severe cases, midline facial defects (cleft lip/palate), developmental delays, seizures, endocrine dysfunction (e.g., diabetes insipidus), hydrocephalus, and motor impairments. Pathophysiology stems from impaired ventral midline patterning, resulting in fused basal ganglia, absent corpus callosum, hypothalamic-pituitary axis anomalies, and neuronal migration defects, leading to high mortality in severe forms (up to 50% in first year) and significant neurodevelopmental challenges in survivors.

The proposed designed polypeptides target core therapeutic axes in HPE to potentially mitigate developmental disruptions. For SHH signaling enhancement, the designed polypeptide conceptually acts as a cyclic enhancer to boost SHH pathway activity, promoting midline cleavage and reducing forebrain fusion. In the Nodal/TGF{beta} pathway, a designed modulator aims to stabilize signaling for proper prosencephalon division and neural axis determination. For FGF signaling, a mimic design supports fibroblast growth factor cascades to aid in forebrain patterning and reduce associated craniofacial anomalies. These flagged designed polypeptides consider physicochemical stability for potential prenatal delivery, with feasibility grounded in pathway modulation, though requiring further preclinical validation to assess safety and efficacy in addressing genomic instability and teratogenic effects.

A “hooked coccyx” generally corresponds to a markedly anteriorly curved or acutely angulated coccygeal morphology, particularly Postacchini type II or type III; anterior subluxation is classified as type IV. These morphologies are over-represented in people with coccydynia, but the shape itself is an anatomical configuration and cannot realistically be straightened by peptide signaling. Pain can instead arise from abnormal pressure while sitting, sacrococcygeal/intercoccygeal joint degeneration and inflammation, traction on coccygeal ligaments and pelvic-floor attachments, coccygeal or anococcygeal nerve irritation, sympathetic nociceptive transmission through the ganglion impar, secondary pelvic-floor guarding/spasm, and chronic remodeling or fibrosis around mechanically stressed tissues. Six complementary peptide axes were therefore selected: restoration of coccygeal disc/cartilage matrix, resolution of mechanically maintained joint inflammation, suppression of peripheral nociceptive afferent hyperexcitability, ASIC-dependent mechanical/inflammatory pain, spinal nociceptive amplification, and reduction of maladaptive periarticular/connective-tissue fibrosis. The program is intended to address biological consequences of a hooked coccyx rather than claiming to remodel a fixed adult coccyx into a different geometric shape. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was identified because coccydynia is not driven by excessive synthesis of one specific endogenous protein.

1. Sacrococcygeal/intercoccygeal disc and fibrocartilage matrix degeneration: Short Link N [Link N(1-8)] - Short Link N, DHLSDNYT, retains the biologically active region of the link-protein-derived peptide. Link N stimulates proteoglycan and collagen synthesis in intervertebral-disc cells, increases aggrecan expression, decreases matrix-metalloproteinase expression and partially restores disc height in experimental degeneration models. Because intercoccygeal and sacrococcygeal articulations can contain disc-like fibrocartilaginous tissue, this provides the closest sequence-defined regenerative peptide model for degeneration associated with abnormal coccygeal loading.
2. Chronic mechanically maintained joint/periarticular inflammation and nociception: Annexin A1-derived Ac2-26 - Ac2-26 is a pro-resolving Annexin-A1 mimetic rather than a generic anti-inflammatory suppressor. Recent experimental joint data show reduced mechanical nociception, inflammatory synovial-cell activation, MMP-3 expression and tissue damage. This is relevant to hooked-coccyx configurations because abnormal mobility or repeated loading can produce chronic inflammatory change at sacrococcygeal or intercoccygeal articulations.
3. Coccygeal/perineal sensory-afferent hyperexcitability and neuropathic pain: {alpha}-Conotoxin Vc1.1 - Vc1.1 reduces dorsal-root-ganglion excitability through GABAB-dependent inhibition of N-type Cav2.2 calcium channels and has experimental neuropathic-pain activity. Coccygeal pain can involve the coccygeal plexus, anococcygeal nerves and sympathetic/nociceptive pathways around the ganglion impar, while pelvic-floor afferents include substantial small-fiber nociceptive populations. Vc1.1 therefore represents suppression of mechanically sensitized peripheral afferent input rather than alteration of the coccyx anatomy. Its two disulfide bridges and C-terminal amidation are retained.
4. Pressure-, inflammation- and tissue-acidosis-dependent nociception: Mambalgin-1 - Mambalgin-1 is a 57-residue disulfide-rich ASIC inhibitor with potent opioid-independent analgesic effects in experimental mechanical inflammatory and neuropathic pain. ASIC1-containing channels detect extracellular acidification associated with inflamed or mechanically stressed tissues and contribute to sensitization of nociceptive afferents. A hooked coccyx concentrates mechanical pressure at the anteriorly angulated distal segments during sitting, making an ASIC-mediated mechanonociceptive/inflammatory axis biologically plausible. The native four-disulfide topology is retained.
5. Spinal amplification of coccygeal nociceptive input and persistent pain signaling: Nociceptin/Orphanin FQ - Nociceptin is the endogenous 17-residue ligand of the NOP receptor. Spinal administration produces dose-dependent analgesia experimentally and suppresses nociceptive transmission through mechanisms distinct from classical {mu}-opioid signaling. This axis represents the central amplification component that can maintain chronic coccygeal pain after repeated mechanically evoked peripheral input. Nociceptin biology is strongly site-dependent-supraspinal exposure can produce different or even opposing effects-so this peptide is used specifically as a mechanistic representation of spinal NOP-mediated antinociception.
6. Periarticular/ligamentous fibrosis, restricted soft-tissue mobility and chronic pelvic-floor connective-tissue stiffness: B7-33 - B7-33 is a 27-residue single-chain human relaxin-2 mimetic and selective RXFP1-signaling agonist. It reproduces major antifibrotic effects of relaxin through fibroblast RXFP1 signaling, increasing MMP-2 and opposing excessive TGF-{beta}/ECM accumulation. Relaxin-family signaling has increasingly been investigated in musculoskeletal fibrosis involving ligaments, tendons, joint capsules, connective tissues and muscles. This axis does not claim to straighten the coccyx; it targets maladaptive fibrosis/stiffness around chronically stressed ligamentous and pelvic-floor attachments that can perpetuate pain and restricted movement. The validated C-terminally amidated B7-33 chemical form is retained.

﻿Hookworm infection, also known as hookworm disease, is a widespread parasitic infestation primarily caused by the soil-transmitted helminths Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, with occasional involvement of Ancylostoma ceylanicum. Transmission occurs when infective larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin, often through bare feet, leading to a condition called 'ground itch' characterized by localized pruritus and erythema. The larvae then migrate via the bloodstream to the lungs, where they cause respiratory symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and hemoptysis as they ascend the bronchial tree and are swallowed into the gastrointestinal tract. In the small intestine, they mature into adult worms that attach to the mucosal wall using hook-like teeth or cutting plates, feeding on host blood and causing chronic blood loss. This results in iron-deficiency anemia, hypoproteinemia, and malnutrition, particularly in endemic areas with poor sanitation and hygiene. Symptoms vary by infection intensity: light infections may be asymptomatic, while heavy burdens lead to fatigue, weakness, pallor, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and in children, stunted growth, cognitive impairments, and developmental delays. Pathophysiology involves mechanical trauma to the intestinal mucosa, anticoagulant secretion by worms to facilitate blood feeding, immune evasion through modulation of host responses (e.g., induction of Th2-biased immunity with eosinophilia and elevated IgE), and secondary complications like bacterial superinfections or heart failure in severe anemia. Chronic infections exacerbate poverty cycles in tropical and subtropical regions, affecting over 400 million people globally as of recent estimates.

The proposed polypeptides address hookworm infection via diverse therapeutic axes, including vaccine-induced immunity, immune modulation, enzyme inhibition, and symptomatic relief. Real-world polypeptides such as p3, A291Y, and P25 focus on the APR-1 axis by eliciting neutralizing antibodies that block the worm's hemoglobin-digesting protease, reducing nutrient acquisition and worm viability. Acan1 and Nak1 leverage ES-derived immunomodulation to dampen excessive Th2 responses and cytokine storms, mitigating tissue damage and allergic manifestations. The designed polypeptides extend coverage: one targets GST-1 to impair heme detoxification, starving the parasite; another inhibits cysteine proteases critical for tissue migration and feeding; one disrupts complement pathways to prevent amplified host inflammation; another promotes microbiota balance to bolster intestinal barrier integrity against larval penetration; one mimics hematopoietic factors to alleviate anemia; one fine-tunes Th2 cytokines for optimal antiparasitic immunity without pathology; and one hinders worm receptor binding to intestinal epithelium, preventing establishment and chronicity. These mechanisms collectively aim to prevent infection, reduce worm burden, alleviate symptoms, and enhance host resilience, with designed ones conceptualized based on known parasite biology for feasibility in therapeutic development.

Human cellular polarity encompasses the highly regulated spatial differences in shape, structure, and function within cells, relying upon the maintenance of resting membrane bioelectric potentials, apical-basal orientation, and coordinated intercellular communication. Disruption of this polarity-whether induced by inflammatory cytokines, metabolic stress, or channelopathies-results in the depolarization of the resting membrane potential, disassembly of tight junctions, loss of Planar Cell Polarity (PCP), and mitochondrial membrane depolarization. Pathophysiologically, this degradation of cellular spatial and electrical orientation drives epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), limits gap junction-mediated bioelectric field signaling, and destabilizes the cytoskeletal architecture. ﻿Hypoparathyroidism is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by insufficient production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands, leading to hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and associated clinical manifestations. The condition can be congenital, often due to genetic mutations such as in the GCM2, PTH, or AIRE genes, or acquired, most commonly from surgical damage during thyroidectomy, autoimmune destruction, or infiltration by diseases like hemochromatosis or metastasis. Symptoms arise from low serum calcium levels and include neuromuscular irritability (tetany, paresthesia, muscle cramps), cardiac arrhythmias (prolonged QT interval), seizures, basal ganglia calcification, cataracts, dental abnormalities, and skeletal changes with increased bone density but reduced remodeling. Pathophysiologically, PTH deficiency impairs renal calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion via reduced activation of PTH receptor 1 (PTHR1) in the kidney, decreases 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity leading to low calcitriol and diminished intestinal calcium absorption, and limits bone resorption by osteoclasts, resulting in disrupted mineral homeostasis. Chronic cases may lead to nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, and reduced quality of life.

The proposed polypeptides address hypoparathyroidism through targeted mechanisms across key pathophysiological axes, with real-world polypeptides prioritized for PTH replacement and supplemented by designed ones for comprehensive coverage. The real-world rhPTH(1-84) directly replaces missing PTH, activating PTHR1 to enhance renal calcium retention, phosphate excretion, and bone turnover, with proven efficacy in clinical trials for normalizing serum calcium without hypercalciuria. Similarly, teriparatide (PTH(1-34)) mimics PTH's N-terminal active domain to stimulate PTHR1, improving calcium homeostasis and used off-label or in studies for hypoparathyroidism. Palopegteriparatide, a pegylated PTH(1-34) prodrug, provides sustained PTH activity for once-daily dosing, addressing compliance and fluctuating levels. Eneboparatide, a modified PTH analog, selectively activates the R0 conformation of PTHR1 for prolonged signaling without excessive bone resorption. These designed polypeptides are engineered for stability, specificity, and bioavailability, with rationales based on pathway analyses and analogous therapeutics.

﻿Infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome or infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), is a rare but severe form of epilepsy that typically manifests in infants between 3 and 12 months of age, with peak onset around 4-7 months. It is characterized by clusters of sudden, brief muscle contractions or jerks (spasms), often involving the head, trunk, and limbs in flexion, extension, or mixed patterns. Accompanying symptoms include developmental stagnation or regression, such as loss of previously acquired skills like smiling, rolling over, or babbling, and potential cognitive impairments if untreated. ﻿Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS) is a rare multisystem mitochondrial disorder characterized by onset before age 20 with the classic triad of progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction defects, often progressing to complete heart block. The real-world polypeptide elamipretide (SS-31) is a clinically investigated mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide that binds cardiolipin, prevents its peroxidation, maintains cristae structure, optimizes electron transport chain activity, and suppresses ROS production, addressing energy failure and oxidative damage in primary mitochondrial diseases including deletion syndromes. These designs leverage established physicochemical principles of mitochondria-penetrating peptides, offering feasible complementarity to symptomatic management by ameliorating molecular defects in oxidative phosphorylation, membrane stability, and oxidative stress.

﻿Klippel-Trenaunay Syndrome (KTS) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by a classic triad of cutaneous capillary malformations (port-wine stains), venous and/or lymphatic malformations with varicose veins, and soft tissue and/or bony hypertrophy typically affecting one limb, though manifestations can be more extensive. It results primarily from post-zygotic somatic mutations in the PIK3CA gene, leading to overactivation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which promotes excessive cell proliferation, abnormal vascular development, and tissue overgrowth. Symptoms often present at birth or early childhood and include visible port-wine stains, limb discrepancy with progressive overgrowth causing gait abnormalities and scoliosis, chronic pain from venous insufficiency, recurrent infections or cellulitis due to lymphatic involvement, edema, thrombosis risk, bleeding from malformed vessels, and potential complications like pulmonary embolism or high-output heart failure in severe cases.

The condition falls within the PIK3CA-Related Overgrowth Spectrum (PROS), with variable severity and no cure; management is multidisciplinary and symptom-focused, including compression therapy, sclerotherapy or embolization for venous malformations, laser for stains, orthopedic interventions for hypertrophy, and off-label use of mTOR inhibitors like sirolimus or PI3K inhibitors like alpelisib in severe PROS cases to slow progression.

No established, investigational, or emerging polypeptide-based therapies were identified for KTS across comprehensive searches of medical literature, clinical trials, and patents. The proposed polypeptides are therefore all conceptual designed short peptides targeting key pathophysiological axes to complement existing approaches.

The first designed peptide conceptually targets dysregulated PI3K signaling, aiming to interfere with downstream proliferation and overgrowth signals; its sequence incorporates basic and hydrophobic residues for potential pathway modulation, with feasibility considerations including cell permeability challenges typical of peptides, though precedents in inhibitory peptides for kinase pathways suggest potential if optimized.

The second designed peptide addresses excessive angiogenesis underlying capillary and venous malformations, designed with motifs to potentially disrupt endothelial proliferation; amphipathic character supports vascular targeting, with moderate feasibility based on anti-angiogenic peptide analogs in other vascular conditions.

The third designed peptide focuses on lymphatic dysfunction and edema, conceptually enhancing drainage and reducing inflammation in malformed lymphatics; hydrophilic residues promote solubility, with higher feasibility drawing from lymphatic-modulating peptides in related edematous disorders.

These designed polypeptides represent hypothetical strategies for adjunctive therapy emphasizing pathway-specific mitigation and symptom relief, potentially via topical, intralesional, or systemic routes pending preclinical testing in KTS models.

﻿Recurrent Bilateral Inflammatory Knee Effusions with Synovitis, Baker’s Cysts and Meniscal Pathology

Created 2026-09-28
The defining phenotype is recurrent, very large bilateral inflammatory knee effusions with extremely rapid fluid reaccumulation after aspiration, persistent synovial inflammation, Baker’s cyst formation, high inflammatory markers, known bilateral meniscal pathology and only short-lived suppression by corticosteroids. For program design, the principal mechanistic axes are excessive bradykinin-linked synovial permeability and inflammatory mediator release; abnormal leukocyte recruitment into synovium; defective endogenous resolution; inadequate macrophage clearance/efferocytosis with IL-1{beta} persistence; adaptive/autoreactive inflammatory signaling; TNF-driven pannus and osteoclast activation; pathological synovial neovascularization; deficient lymphatic/fluid clearance; and ongoing mechanical irritation from damaged menisci. Baker’s cysts are treated as a downstream manifestation of high intra-articular fluid pressure rather than an independent disease mechanism. The reported negative bacterial and crystal testing is important but does not, without the complete synovial-fluid report, establish a specific autoimmune diagnosis or absolutely exclude infection/crystal disease. The menopause/HRT chronology is retained as a clinical observation but is not promoted to a causal therapeutic axis because the history does not establish that relationship. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was identified because no single excessively synthesized endogenous protein has been established as the primary driver.
1. Bradykinin-B2-driven synovial permeability, edema and inflammatory fluid production: Icatibant - Selective B2-receptor antagonist addressing a mechanism capable of simultaneously increasing vascular permeability and activating inflamed synoviocytes. Human synovial fibroblasts respond to bradykinin with IL-6 and IL-8 production, which B2 antagonism with icatibant suppresses. This axis is directed specifically at the rapid-fluid-production phenotype rather than pain alone.
2. Dysregulated leukocyte trafficking into inflamed synovium: Native PEPITEM - Endogenous immunoregulatory peptide of the adiponectin-PEPITEM pathway that restrains memory-T-cell transendothelial migration. A 2026 study found impaired adiponectin-PEPITEM signaling and reduced local synovial PEPITEM in newly diagnosed RA and PsA and demonstrated reduced inflammatory arthritis after PEPITEM replacement. The treatment experiments used a stabilized PEG352-amidated derivative; the chemically defined native endogenous PEPITEM is encoded here rather than assuming an incompletely specified PEG attachment mass.
3. Failure of endogenous synovial inflammation resolution: Annexin A1 Ac2-26 - N-acetylated Annexin-A1 mimetic acting predominantly through FPR2/ALX-associated pro-resolving pathways. Direct 2026 knee-OA work showed reduction of joint pathology, MMP-3-associated damage and inflammatory synovial-cell phenotypes. This addresses failure to terminate inflammation rather than indiscriminately suppressing all immune activity.
4. Persistent IL-1{beta} signaling and inadequate macrophage efferocytosis: Modimelanotide/AP214 - N-acetylated, C-terminally amidated melanocortin agonist whose anti-inflammatory and resolution-promoting actions are strongly MC3-dependent. AP214 markedly reduced macrophage IL-1{beta} release, promoted uptake of apoptotic neutrophils and significantly reduced clinical inflammatory-arthritis scores. This gives a distinct resolution axis complementary to Annexin-A1/FPR2 signaling.
5. Autoreactive/Th1-dominant synovial immune activation: Rat Cortistatin-29 - Native pGlu-containing, Cys17-Cys28-disulfide cortistatin form used in the experimental arthritis literature. Treatment of established collagen-induced arthritis markedly reduced joint swelling, inflammatory cytokines and chemokines and antigen-specific Th1 responses while increasing IL-10 and TGF-{beta}1-associated regulatory responses.
