Peptide program based on this paper.

Optic-nerve repair requires preservation of retinal ganglion cells, activation of axonal growth, passage through an inhibitory extracellular environment, and durable reconnection with appropriate visual targets. The program below encodes fourteen chemically specified research peptides/proteins. Entries 1-6 represent named trophic or cytokine signals in the supplied review; entries 7-14 are explicitly identified extensions from additional literature. These are conditional research modules, not a demonstrated combination treatment. Genetic interventions, cell transplantation and physical scaffolds are not replaced by peptide mass strings. No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition entry is included: the review does not establish that its successful gene-deletion experiments can be reproduced by a mass-derived inhibitory signature. Likewise, no numerical RRM match is presented as evidence of target binding or therapeutic activity.

1. Inflammation-associated initiation of retinal ganglion cell axon growth: Recombinant human oncomodulin, tag-free apo form - Named in the review. Oncomodulin is a growth-promoting inflammatory-cell-derived protein with direct experimental optic-nerve evidence. Its regenerative activity depends on a permissive neuronal environment, including cyclic-AMP signaling; this does not establish correct target reconnection or restored vision. The encoded entity is the complete recombinant human chain without an assigned bound metal.
2. CXCR4-dependent support of the oncomodulin regenerative response: Human CXCL12-alpha / SDF-1-alpha(1-68) - Named in the review. The mature chemokine supports oncomodulin-associated retinal ganglion cell regeneration through CXCR4-dependent signaling in the cited experimental model. This is a conditional module: other injury-site experiments show that CXCL12 gradients can trap or misdirect regenerating axons. It is not an instruction to maximize CXCL12 throughout the injured nerve.
3. CNTFR-LIFR-gp130 signaling and JAK-STAT3-associated neuronal growth: Recombinant human ciliary neurotrophic factor / CNTF - Named in the review. CNTF supplies a trophic cytokine signal associated with retinal ganglion cell survival and regenerative competence. The sustained-release CNTF-chitosan study investigated a combined protein, biomaterial and surgical intervention. Encoding CNTF does not reproduce that scaffold, its spatial delivery, or the reported functional outcomes.
4. TrkB-associated trophic support and retinal ganglion cell preservation: Mature human BDNF(129-247), native-disulfide protomer - Named in the review. Mature BDNF supports neuronal survival through TrkB. Survival and axon extension must be assessed separately: a direct study found that BDNF improved survival while impairing lens-injury-associated regeneration. This entry represents the mature chain, not proBDNF or the engineered F-iTrkB receptor construct; noncovalent receptor-active assembly is not specified by the mass line.
5. GDNF-receptor trophic support and durable survival of injured retinal ganglion cells: Mature human GDNF, nonglycosylated disulfide-linked homodimer - Named in the review. Sustained GDNF plus CNTF expression improved long-term retinal ganglion cell protection, but did not increase distal regeneration beyond CNTF alone in the cited study. The encoded entity contains two mature 134-residue chains and seven disulfide bonds. Their residue records are concatenated for this format; no peptide bond between the two chains is implied.
6. Context-dependent IL-6-receptor/gp130 regenerative cytokine signaling: Recombinant human IL-6(30-212), nonglycosylated and unphosphorylated - IL-6 is discussed in the review, and primary optic-nerve experiments demonstrate a contribution to inflammation-stimulated regeneration. It is retained as a conditional research signal, not a universal anti-inflammatory or protective treatment. Native IL-6 is not equivalent to hyper-IL-6, which has a soluble-receptor fusion and different signaling accessibility.
7. Peptide antagonism of PTEN-mediated restraint on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling: PTEN antagonist peptide 4 / PAP4, 30-residue Tat-containing form - External pathway extension. PAP4 is a chemically specified PTEN-antagonist construct with neuronal-growth and spinal-cord-injury evidence. It provides an experimental peptide approach to the review’s PTEN pathway; the appropriate intended direction is release of growth signaling, not mTOR inhibition. It does not reproduce retinal-ganglion-cell-specific PTEN or TSC1 deletion, and optic-nerve efficacy of this exact construct is not established here.
8. Biochemical antagonism of SOCS-mediated negative feedback on cytokine signaling: pJAK2(1001-1013), unlipidated Tyr1007-phosphorylated core - External pathway extension. This phosphorylated JAK2 activation-loop peptide is a characterized SOCS1/SOCS3 antagonist. It is included as a biochemical lead for the SOCS3-JAK-STAT pathway, not as a validated optic-nerve treatment. Published intracellular activity requires successful delivery; this record deliberately encodes the defined unlipidated core, not an unspecified lipid-delivery construct.
9. Nogo-66/NgR1-associated extracellular inhibition of axon extension: NEP1-40, N-acetylated and C-terminally amidated - External pathway extension. NEP1-40 is a defined Nogo-66 receptor antagonist with experimental CNS axon-growth evidence. It addresses one component of the myelin-associated inhibitory environment discussed in the review. Its Nogo antagonism must not be generalized to complete blockade of MAG, OMgp, RGM or all RhoA-ROCK signaling.
10. CSPG-PTPsigma inhibitory signaling and optic-pathway remyelination: Intracellular sigma peptide / ISP, C-terminal amide - External pathway extension, included specifically for proteoglycan-receptor modulation rather than generic regeneration. ISP is a cell-penetrating PTPsigma-wedge mimetic. A direct optic-chiasm demyelination study reported improved remyelination and functional recovery. Those results concern surviving demyelinated pathways and do not demonstrate reconstruction of a completely severed optic nerve.
11. PACAP-receptor/cyclic-AMP-CREB-Bcl-2 neuronal survival signaling: Human PACAP-38 amide - External pathway extension with direct optic-nerve-crush evidence. PACAP reduced retinal ganglion cell apoptosis through CREB-Bcl-2-associated signaling. It offers a receptor-mediated route into the cyclic-AMP and survival mechanisms relevant to the review, but has not been shown here to substitute for the particular cyclic-AMP manipulation used with oncomodulin. Exosomal delivery studies do not establish equivalence of free PACAP.
12. Melanocortin-associated control of secondary retinal inflammatory and apoptotic injury: Native alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone / alpha-MSH - External pathway extension. Native alpha-MSH has experimental retinal ischemia-reperfusion evidence for preservation of retinal structure and reduced apoptosis. It addresses damaging secondary inflammatory injury rather than replacing growth-inducing inflammation. It should not be presumed additive with every cytokine-stimulation module, because suppressing a beneficial inflammatory signal can oppose regeneration.
13. Mitochondrial membrane and bioenergetic stress in vulnerable retinal ganglion cells: Elamipretide / SS-31 - External pathway extension. This mitochondria-targeting tetrapeptide has preliminary retinal ganglion cell protection evidence, including an experimental-glaucoma conference abstract. It is a candidate for mitochondrial stress support, not an established optic-nerve regeneration treatment. It does not reproduce the mitochondrial donation, axonal transport changes or cell-replacement interventions discussed in the paper.
14. FGFR-associated progenitor support in the retinal cell-differentiation branch: Recombinant human FGF2, 155-residue low-molecular-weight isoform - Extension from the review’s cited cell-replacement literature. FGF2 was used in a differentiation strategy for embryonic-stem-cell-derived neural progenitors. It is represented as a defined growth factor, not as a substitute for a transplanted retinal ganglion cell. The cited transplantation experiment did not establish axonal extension into the optic nerve; free FGF2 cannot be assumed to reproduce cell manufacturing or integration.

The oncomodulin and CXCL12 entries are supported by experimental optic-nerve studies, with the important qualification that CXCL12 can either support the regenerative response or impede distal extension through injury-site entrapment. CNTF’s scaffold-dependent results, BDNF’s survival-regeneration trade-off, GDNF-CNTF combination findings, and IL-6’s contribution to inflammation-stimulated regeneration come from their respective primary studies.

PAP4 and pJAK2 are independently characterized research interventions, but neither is presented here as a demonstrated substitute for the review’s cell-specific genetic manipulations. The pJAK2 publication used a lipid-assisted intracellular-delivery preparation; the encoded entry explicitly identifies the unlipidated core. NEP1-40 and ISP address different extracellular inhibitory mechanisms; ISP is included specifically because of its direct optic-chiasm remyelination evidence.

PACAP and alpha-MSH have direct experimental optic-nerve or retinal-injury evidence. SS-31’s evidence here is more preliminary, while FGF2 belongs to the cited cell-differentiation branch rather than constituting cell replacement itself. GDNF’s two-chain, seven-disulfide chemistry is independently established; BDNF’s mature-chain boundaries and three intrachain disulfides are recorded in UniProt.

Orthopnea is positional dyspnea that worsens when supine. It is a symptom rather than a single disease: the most common mechanism is cardiogenic elevation of pulmonary capillary pressure, but diaphragmatic paralysis/weakness, obesity or ascites reducing functional residual capacity, pleural disease, and other pulmonary or neuromuscular disorders can produce the same symptom. Because no etiology was supplied, this peptide set specifically models the common cardiogenic/intravascular-congestion phenotype rather than assuming that every case of orthopnea is heart failure. In heart failure, recumbency increases central preload; orthopnea is particularly associated with intravascular congestion, while sympathetic splanchnic venoconstriction, RAAS activation, elevated cardiac filling pressures, impaired vascular adaptation and myocardial stiffness can amplify the response. Six mechanistically distinct axes were retained. No Sternheimer inhibition axis was added because cardiogenic orthopnea is not established as being driven by pathological overproduction of one specific endogenous peptide/protein.

1. Renal sodium/water retention and excessive cardiac filling pressure: Ularitide, native Cys11-Cys27 disulfide form - Ularitide is the 32-residue human urodilatin analogue acting through natriuretic-peptide/guanylyl-cyclase signaling. In a randomized decompensated-heart-failure trial it significantly lowered pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, reduced systemic vascular resistance and improved dyspnea, while its renal biology provides natriuretic and diuretic effects. This is the most direct peptide axis for reducing the intravascular-congestion component that produces cardiogenic orthopnea.
2. Vascular maladaptation and congestion-associated dyspnea: Human relaxin-2/serelaxin, native pGlu-A-chain/two-chain three-disulfide form - Relaxin-2 signals predominantly through RXFP1 and has systemic and renal vasodilatory effects distinct from natriuretic-peptide receptor signaling. Native human relaxin-2 contains a 24-residue A-chain and 29-residue B-chain joined by CysA11-CysB11 and CysA24-CysB23 disulfides, with CysA10-CysA15 forming the intrachain bond and the A-chain N-terminus cyclized to pyroglutamate.

This directly matches several hemodynamic abnormalities capable of worsening orthopnea.
4. Human heart-failure evidence remains limited, but HF tissue and translational studies support activation of this axis, while experimental CHF studies report reductions in aldosterone and cardiac hypertrophy with chronic Ang-(1-7).
6. Myocardial fibrosis, impaired relaxation and diastolic filling-pressure amplification: Ac-SDKP - N-acetyl-Ser-Asp-Lys-Pro is an endogenous antifibrotic tetrapeptide degraded by ACE. This addresses ventricular stiffness as a chronic substrate for excessive supine filling pressures rather than attempting acute decongestion. The evidence is preclinical and not specific to orthopnea.

Oct4 (POU5F1) and Sox2 function through a synergistic DNA-binding mechanism where their respective POU and HMG domains form a ternary complex on composite Sox-Oct elements. ﻿Osteoarthritis of the hips, also known as hip OA, is a degenerative joint disease characterized by the progressive breakdown of articular cartilage, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, synovial inflammation, and joint space narrowing. It primarily affects older adults but can occur earlier due to factors like joint injury, obesity, genetic predisposition, or biomechanical abnormalities such as hip dysplasia or femoroacetabular impingement. Symptoms include chronic pain, stiffness, reduced mobility, and functional limitations, often leading to disability and the need for hip replacement surgery. Pathophysiologically, hip OA involves an imbalance between cartilage anabolism and catabolism, driven by mechanical stress, inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, TNF-{alpha}), matrix-degrading enzymes (e.g., MMPs, ADAMTS), and altered signaling pathways like Wnt/{beta}-catenin or TGF-{beta}. Metabolic factors, including dysregulated bile acid metabolism and gut microbiota influences, contribute via the gut-joint axis, exacerbating inflammation and cartilage loss. Advanced stages feature subchondral bone sclerosis, cyst formation, and nociceptive sensitization, amplifying pain.

The proposed polypeptides address hip OA through multiple therapeutic axes: anti-inflammatory (reducing cytokine-mediated damage), cartilage regeneration (promoting matrix synthesis and repair), pain modulation (targeting nociceptive pathways), and metabolic modulation (influencing GLP-1 signaling and systemic factors). Real-world polypeptides like VIP inhibit pro-inflammatory mediators in synovial tissue, BPC-157 stimulates tissue healing and angiogenesis, calcitonin suppresses osteoclast activity and pain signaling, and GLP-1 enhances chondroprotection via anti-catabolic effects. Feasibility is supported by preclinical data showing reduced cartilage degradation, improved joint function, and biocompatibility; physicochemical properties favor intra-articular delivery with low immunogenicity and favorable pharmacokinetics.

Therapeutic strategies center on enhancing the anabolic bone environment, inhibiting excessive osteoclastic resorption, and promoting the proper assembly and stabilization of collagen fibrils within the hydroxyapatite scaffold.

﻿Osteomalacia is a metabolic bone disorder characterized by the softening of bones in adults due to defective bone mineralization, primarily resulting from vitamin D deficiency, phosphate wasting, or disruptions in calcium metabolism. ﻿Osteomyelitis is a severe inflammatory condition of the bone and bone marrow, typically triggered by pyogenic bacteria or fungi. The pathophysiology involves the introduction of pathogens via hematogenous spread, contiguous infection from adjacent soft tissues, or direct inoculation following trauma or surgery. Staphylococcus aureus is the primary causative agent, often forming resilient biofilms on necrotic bone fragments (sequestra) and orthopedic implants. These biofilms provide a physical and metabolic shield against host immune defenses and systemic antibiotics, leading to chronic, recalcitrant infections. The inflammatory response further exacerbates tissue damage through the release of proteolytic enzymes and the activation of osteoclasts, resulting in localized bone destruction and impaired vascularization.

The proposed therapeutic polypeptides address osteomyelitis through a multi-pronged mechanistic strategy. Human-derived cathelicidins like LL-37 and defensins like HBD-3 offer dual benefits by directly killing pathogens and modulating the local immune environment to favor resolution over chronic inflammation. To address the critical need for tissue repair, osteogenic fragments like Teriparatide and P15 stimulate osteoblast differentiation and mineral deposition, filling the voids left by infection. Biofilm-disrupting designed peptides (D1-Disruptor) are engineered with high cationic density to penetrate the extracellular matrix and sensitize bacteria to treatment. Finally, angiogenic mimics (D4-Vessel) promote revascularization, ensuring that the bone receives the necessary nutrients and immune support for long-term recovery.

﻿Otitis externa, commonly known as swimmer's ear, is a diffuse inflammation of the external auditory canal, often triggered by moisture exposure, trauma, or skin conditions that disrupt the protective barrier. Primary causes include bacterial infections (predominantly Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus), fungal infections (such as Malassezia pachydermatis or Candida species), or non-infectious factors like eczema. Symptoms encompass severe ear pain, itching, swelling, discharge, and hearing impairment due to canal edema. Pathophysiology involves maceration of the canal skin, loss of acidic pH and cerumen's protective lipids, and pathogen overgrowth, often with biofilm formation in persistent cases.

An 'overactive mind' is often the subjective experience of a hyper-connected Default Mode Network (DMN). This network is the brain’s 'background radio station'-the circuit responsible for self-referential thought, rumination, and day-dreaming. While it is essential for creativity, an inability to 'switch off' the DMN during focused activities like meditation or reading creates a persistent state of cognitive noise. This state is frequently driven by an imbalance in the Glutamate-GABA axis, where excitatory 'noise' overrides the inhibitory 'silence.' Peptide modulation seeks to reinforce GABAergic tone, stabilize neural membranes, and modulate NMDA receptor activity to achieve that elusive state of 'radio silence' or mental blankness. 

1. GABAergic Stabilization: Selank
This synthetic enkephalin-mimetic acts as a gentle volume knob for the internal radio. It works by increasing the half-life of endogenous enkephalins and modulating GABA receptors, which provides an anxiolytic effect without sedation, allowing the mind to remain sharp but quiet.

2. Neural Noise Reduction: DSIP
Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide is not merely for sleep; it acts as a global neural stabilizer. By modulating the response to stress and stabilizing neuronal membranes, it helps reduce the 'fuzz' of background thoughts, facilitating a deeper entry into states of presence and meditation.

3. Circadian Mental Rhythm: Pinealon
This short bioregulator targets the pineal gland and the cortex to normalize the rhythm of thought. It is particularly effective for those who find their minds racing with 'decades of accumulated stuff,' as it supports the cognitive clarity required to categorize and dismiss irrelevant background information.

4. Neuro-Epigenetic Regulation: Epitalon
By acting on the pineal gland to regulate melatonin production and cellular telomerase activity, Epitalon helps reset the 'background clock' of the brain. It fosters a more balanced neuro-endocrine environment, which can make those rare, heavenly 'mind blanks' more frequent by reducing systemic neural hyper-arousal.

5. Glutamatergic Modulation: GLYX-13
Also known as Rapastinel, this peptide acts as a partial agonist at the glycine site of the NMDA receptor. It helps 'unstick' the brain from repetitive thought loops and over-analysis, promoting synaptic plasticity that favors new, quieter mental pathways over old, noisy ones.

6. DMN Suppression: Silence-DMN-1
This designed peptide motif is engineered to target the functional connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex and the posterior cingulate cortex. Its goal is to selectively dampen the power of the Default Mode Network, allowing for a profound state of 'being' rather than constant 'thinking.'

﻿Paget's Disease of Bone is a chronic skeletal disorder characterized by excessive and disorganized bone remodeling. The condition initiates with an overabundance of osteoclasts that are larger and more active than normal, leading to rapid bone resorption. In response, osteoblasts attempt to compensate by producing new bone at an accelerated rate; however, this new bone is structurally inferior, characterized by a 'mosaic' pattern of woven bone that is weaker and more vascular than healthy lamellar bone. This process results in bone enlargement, deformities, and an increased risk of fractures. Clinically, patients often present with bone pain, secondary osteoarthritis, and neurological complications if the skull or spine is involved.

The proposed polypeptides target the pathological acceleration of bone turnover through several mechanisms. Salmon Calcitonin and its analogs act as direct inhibitors of osteoclast activity by binding to G-protein coupled receptors on the osteoclast surface, rapidly reducing bone resorption. The OPG-derived fragments and Denosumab-inspired sequences serve as decoys or blockers for RANKL, the primary cytokine driving osteoclast differentiation. To manage the structural integrity of the bone, PTHrP and Sclerostin fragments are included to modulate osteoblast behavior and favor the formation of more organized bone tissue. Designed polypeptides like D1-RANK-Bind are engineered to competitively inhibit the RANK-RANKL interaction, while D2-Vasc-Stop addresses the hyper-vascularization typical of Pagetic lesions by mimicking anti-angiogenic signaling motifs.

Mitochondrial proton leak is not intrinsically pathological. A regulated basal leak contributes to thermogenesis, limits excessive membrane potential, and can reduce reactive-oxygen-species production. Pathological leak is characterized by excessive proton entry into the matrix without ATP generation, reduced oxidative-phosphorylation coupling, ATP depletion, elevated compensatory respiration, membrane depolarization, permeability-transition events, and progressive membrane or cristae damage. Potential causes include cardiolipin phase disruption or peroxidation, abnormal adenine-nucleotide-translocator conductance, permeability-transition-pore opening, respiratory-chain injury, calcium overload, pathological mitochondrial fission, and loss of oxidative-phosphorylation complexes. Seven peptide-addressable axes were retained. No universal excess of UCP2, UCP3, ANT1, or another endogenous proton conductor can be assumed from this phenotype alone; therefore, a Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition entry was not justified.

1. Cardiolipin phase stabilization and reduction of non-bilayer membrane leak: HDAP2, biotinylated and C-terminally amidated - HDAP2 uses a dense aromatic core flanked by D-arginines to bind cardiolipin, inhibit formation of inverted cardiolipin micelles and other non-bilayer phases, and stabilize cardiolipin within the inner-membrane bilayer. This addresses a direct lipid-phase mechanism capable of increasing proton permeability, disrupting cristae curvature, and dissipating membrane potential. Evidence currently consists of membrane systems, cultured cells, and recent animal neuroprotection studies.
2. ANT1- and ATP-synthasome-associated pathological proton conductance: Elamipretide / SS-31, C-terminally amidated - SS-31 associates with cardiolipin, ANT1, and the ATP synthasome. In aged cardiomyocytes it reduced oligomycin-resistant respiration, directly slowed proton entry into the mitochondrial matrix during imposed pH-gradient stress, reduced permeability-transition activity, and improved oxidative-phosphorylation coupling. This is the most direct peptide evidence for reducing experimentally measured pathological proton leak.
3. Cytochrome-c electron-transfer integrity and prevention of secondary uncoupling: SS-20, C-terminally amidated - SS-20 binds cardiolipin and preserves the methionine-to-heme-iron coordination of cytochrome c during mitochondrial stress. Experimental treatment preserved electron transport, coupled respiration, cristae architecture, OPA1, and ATP recovery while reducing cardiolipin oxidation. It targets electron leakage and respiratory-chain failure that can amplify proton leak, rather than serving as a direct channel blocker.
4. Calcium- and oxidant-triggered mitochondrial permeability transition: Human Bcl-xL BH4-domain peptide - This peptide inhibits VDAC1 activity, limits excessive calcium transfer into mitochondria, and prevents calcium-associated loss of mitochondrial membrane potential in isolated mitochondria and cellular experiments. It addresses catastrophic permeability transition and depolarization rather than normal basal proton conductance. The molecular identity of the permeability-transition pore remains debated, and the unconjugated peptide has limited cellular delivery.
5. Bax/Bid-dependent mitochondrial outer-membrane leakage: Humanin - Humanin binds Bax and Bid, inhibits their membrane recruitment and oligomerization, suppresses Bax pore formation, and reduces cytochrome-c release. This does not directly close proton pathways in the inner membrane, but it addresses the broader “leaky mitochondria” phenotype in which outer-membrane permeabilization follows or aggravates loss of inner-membrane potential.
6. Stress-induced Drp1-Fis1 fission and membrane-potential collapse: Linear P110 heptapeptide - P110 selectively interferes with pathological Drp1-Fis1 signaling. In stressed cells and animal disease models, delivered P110 constructs reduced mitochondrial fragmentation and reactive oxygen species while preserving membrane potential, respiratory reserve, ATP production, and mitochondrial integrity. The unconjugated heptapeptide has poor cellular uptake; most functional studies used a TAT carrier, lipid conjugation, cyclic derivative, or delivery vehicle.

This axis addresses inadequate proton pumping and ATP utilization that can mimic or magnify apparent proton leak. Direct proton-conductance measurements with SHLP2 have not been reported.

﻿Pendred syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often profound and present from birth or early childhood, associated with inner ear malformations such as enlarged vestibular aqueduct (EVA) or Mondini dysplasia, and thyroid goiter that typically develops in late childhood or adolescence, with variable hypothyroidism. Additional features may include vestibular dysfunction leading to balance issues, vertigo, or delayed motor milestones. The condition accounts for up to 10-15% of syndromic hereditary deafness, with prevalence estimated at 1-9 per 100,000, and is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC26A4 gene encoding pendrin, a chloride-iodide/bicarbonate anion exchanger critical for ion homeostasis in the inner ear endolymph and thyroid iodide efflux/organification. Pendrin dysfunction disrupts endolymphatic pH and fluid balance, leading to cochlear hair cell degeneration and hearing impairment, while impairing apical iodide transport in thyrocytes causes defective thyroid hormone synthesis and compensatory goiter. Diagnosis involves audiometry, temporal bone imaging (CT/MRI for EVA), perchlorate discharge test, thyroid ultrasound/function tests, and SLC26A4 sequencing.

Current management is supportive: cochlear implants or hearing aids for deafness (with excellent outcomes if implanted early), thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine) if hypothyroid, iodine moderation, and vestibular rehabilitation; precautions against head trauma due to EVA fragility. Emerging small-molecule correctors (e.g., chaperones for misfolded pendrin) and gene therapies are investigational but not polypeptide-based.

Searches across PubMed, patents, clinical trials, and databases confirmed no documented real-world polypeptide or peptide therapies for Pendred syndrome. The proposed set thus consists entirely of designed conceptual polypeptides. These short synthetic peptides are rationally designed for potential membrane interaction, stability, and modulatory effects on anion transport or compensatory pathways:

- The first designed peptide (D1) features mixed charged and hydrophobic residues to hypothetically support endolymph ion balance and protect cochlear function.

- The second designed peptide (D2) incorporates aromatic and polar motifs aimed at facilitating iodide-handling mimicry in thyroid cells.

- The third designed peptide (D3) is intended for potential stabilization of vestibular epithelial integrity.

- The fourth designed peptide (D4) includes acidic and basic residues for broad anion exchange compensation.

Feasibility considerations encompass lengths of 10 residues for cost-effective synthesis, predicted good solubility from balanced hydrophilicity, minimal predicted immunogenicity, and opportunities for optimization (e.g., cyclization or tagging for targeted delivery to ear/thyroid). Physicochemical profiles favor stability; however, these are hypothetical designs requiring extensive preclinical testing in SLC26A4 models for specificity, efficacy in restoring pendrin-like function or mitigating symptoms, and safety without disrupting native ion gradients.

﻿Petechiae are tiny, pinpoint-sized hemorrhages under the skin or mucous membranes, appearing as red, purple, or brown spots that do not blanch under pressure, resulting from the rupture of small blood vessels or capillaries and subsequent leakage of red blood cells into surrounding tissues. This condition is typically a symptom rather than a standalone disease, often signaling underlying issues such as low platelet counts (thrombocytopenia), impaired platelet function, abnormalities in the coagulation cascade, or compromised vascular wall integrity due to inflammation, infection, or mechanical stress. Common causes include viral or bacterial infections (e.g., meningococcemia or Rocky Mountain spotted fever), autoimmune disorders like immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) where platelets are destroyed by the immune system, medication side effects (e.g., from anticoagulants or chemotherapy), nutritional deficiencies (e.g., vitamin C or K scarcity leading to scurvy or coagulopathy), physical straining (e.g., during vomiting, coughing, or childbirth), and systemic conditions such as vasculitis, sepsis, or leukemia. Symptoms are usually cosmetic and asymptomatic but may accompany more severe manifestations like easy bruising, prolonged bleeding from cuts, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, blood in urine or stool, fatigue, fever, or joint pain depending on the root cause. Pathophysiologically, petechiae arise when the hemostatic mechanisms fail: platelets normally aggregate to form plugs at sites of vascular injury, supported by coagulation factors that stabilize clots, but deficiencies in these components or vessel fragility allow extravasation of blood; for instance, in thrombocytopenia, fewer platelets mean inadequate sealing of microvascular leaks, while in vasculitis, inflammatory damage weakens endothelial barriers.

The proposed polypeptides target these pathophysiological axes to mitigate petechiae by enhancing platelet production, function, and survival; modulating coagulation pathways; strengthening vascular integrity; reducing inflammation; and combating infectious triggers. For thrombocytopenia due to reduced platelet production, polypeptides like TMP mimic thrombopoietin to stimulate megakaryocyte maturation and platelet release from bone marrow via receptor activation, increasing circulating platelet counts to better seal vascular leaks. In immune-mediated destruction, immune-modulatory effects help suppress autoantibody production or platelet clearance. For platelet dysfunction, peptides like pENW, RGDS, and GLP-1 improve aggregation and activation through signaling pathways such as Akt inhibition or nitric oxide modulation, ensuring effective hemostasis. Anti-thrombotic peptides from milk (VPP, IPP, MAIPPKKNQDK) balance coagulation by inhibiting excessive thrombin activity or platelet aggregation without promoting bleeding, feasible given their natural origin and low toxicity. For coagulation disorders, Tridegin inhibits factor XIIIa to prevent over-stabilization of clots while allowing necessary hemostasis. Vascular integrity is bolstered by Ac-SDKP, BPC157, C16, and TFPI-2 C-terminal peptides, which promote endothelial repair, reduce permeability, and protect against oxidative stress via mechanisms like angiogenesis stimulation or protease inhibition, with high solubility and stability enhancing bioavailability. LL37 addresses infection-related petechiae through antimicrobial action against bacteria and viruses, disrupting membranes and modulating immune responses. Chemerin15 attenuates inflammation in vasculitis by regulating leukocyte recruitment and cytokine release. Designed polypeptides (flagged below) conceptually extend coverage: D1 for enhanced immune tolerance in autoimmune thrombocytopenia via hypothetical receptor antagonism; D2 for additional vascular stabilization through endothelial junction reinforcement; D3 for fine-tuned coagulation modulation by targeting specific factors; D4 for broad anti-inflammatory effects on HPA axis-related stress responses. These designed ones are feasible based on peptide engineering principles, with modes of action inferred from similar structures, physicochemical properties like amphipathicity for membrane interaction, and potential for therapeutic delivery via injection or topical application.

﻿Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant hereditary disorder caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a master kinase regulating cellular energy homeostasis, polarity, and growth. The absence of functional LKB1 leads to constitutive activation of the mTORC1 signaling pathway due to impaired AMPK-mediated inhibition, resulting in uncontrolled protein synthesis, cell proliferation, and the development of characteristic hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Patients face a dramatically elevated lifetime risk of gastrointestinal, breast, pancreatic, and gynecologic malignancies, necessitating rigorous surveillance protocols. While current management relies on endoscopic and surgical polypectomy alongside cancer screening, there is no approved medical therapy to prevent polyp formation or progression. Preclinical studies highlight three key therapeutic axes: (1) restoration of LKB1 function, (2) inhibition of hyperactive mTORC1 signaling, and (3) modulation of downstream translational effectors like S6K and 4E-BP1. The proposed set includes one real-world investigational peptide-the LKB1 nuclear localization signal (NLS) peptide (YARAAARQARA)-demonstrated in peer-reviewed studies to restore LKB1 nuclear trafficking and function in STK11-deficient cells. Complementing this, two designed peptides are introduced: D1-mTORC1inhibitor, a short motif hypothesized to disrupt mTORC1 assembly, and D2-4EBP1mimetic, engineered to mimic the eIF4E-binding domain of hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1, thereby suppressing cap-dependent translation. Together, these candidates offer a multi-pronged theoretical approach to counteract the core molecular pathology of PJS.

﻿Pfeiffer syndrome is a rare genetic craniosynostosis disorder characterized by premature fusion of multiple cranial sutures, resulting in turribrachycephaly (tower-shaped skull with broad, short anteroposterior dimension), midface hypoplasia, shallow orbits with severe proptosis, hypertelorism, and airway compromise risks. Patients exhibit distinctive broad and radially deviated thumbs and great toes, partial syndactyly, and variable ankylosis of digits. Three clinical subtypes exist: Type 1 (classic, mild-moderate, good prognosis with surgical intervention), Type 2 (cloverleaf skull, severe proptosis, elbow ankylosis, higher neurodevelopmental risk), and Type 3 (similar to Type 2 but without cloverleaf skull, poor prognosis due to visceral anomalies and early lethality in severe cases). Additional features may include hydrocephalus, Chiari malformation, hearing loss, dental issues, and occasional intellectual disability in severe forms.

The condition arises from autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations primarily in FGFR2 (most cases, especially Pro252Arg or Cys342 variants) and less commonly FGFR1, leading to constitutive receptor activation, enhanced ligand-independent dimerization, and prolonged downstream signaling via RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and PLC{gamma} pathways. This disrupts balanced osteoblast proliferation/differentiation at cranial sutures and endochondral/periosteal bone formation in limbs, promoting premature osteogenic commitment and suture obliteration while causing abnormal chondrogenesis and joint fusion.

Current management is supportive and surgical (cranial vault remodeling, midface advancement, digit separation), with no approved disease-modifying pharmacotherapy. Small-molecule FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors have shown preclinical promise in models but carry toxicity concerns for pediatric use.

No real-world short polypeptides (3-50 residues) with documented therapeutic investigation or use in Pfeiffer syndrome were identified across sources; treatment remains surgical. The proposed set comprises four conceptual designed short polypeptides, each targeting a distinct mechanistic axis to hypothetically attenuate mutant FGFR-driven pathology.

The first designed polypeptide conceptually interferes with mutant FGFR dimerization or activation domains.

The second designed polypeptide mimics or competes with FGF ligand binding to reduce receptor stimulation.

The third designed polypeptide targets intracellular downstream hyperactivation of MAPK signaling.

The fourth designed polypeptide aims to restore balance in osteoblast/suture homeostasis.

These designed polypeptides are short (10 residues), supporting synthetic accessibility, potential modifications (e.g., stapling, N-methylation) for protease resistance and bioavailability, and focused action with minimized systemic effects relative to broader kinase inhibitors.

Phantosmia is the perception of an odor in the absence of an external odorant and is a mechanistically heterogeneous qualitative olfactory disorder rather than a single disease. Relevant causes include post-viral or other olfactory-epithelium injury, chronic inflammatory disease, head trauma, migraine, temporal-lobe/piriform-network seizures, neurodegenerative disease, and structural central-nervous-system pathology. The experimentally supportable peptide axes divide into peripheral olfactory-neuroepithelial repair, olfactory-bulb inflammatory control, neuronal maturation and reinnervation, plus conditional central hyperexcitability and migraine branches. Structural lesions and primary neurodegenerative etiologies are intentionally not assigned generic peptides because doing so would be mechanistically unjustified. No peptide listed here has been clinically established to eliminate phantosmia, and no Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was identified because pathological overproduction of one specific endogenous peptide or protein is not an established driver of phantosmia.

Olfactory-bulb neuroinflammation and epithelial neuronal maturation after peripheral injury: Native {alpha}-MSH - Recent experimental peripheral olfactory-dysfunction work found {alpha}-MSH improved olfactory behavior, partially restored olfactory-epithelium thickness and OMP-positive mature sensory neurons, and shifted olfactory-bulb inflammatory signaling including TNF-{alpha} and IL-10. Earlier work also demonstrated suppression of inflammatory NF-{kappa}B activation in olfactory ensheathing cells, giving this peptide unusually direct olfactory inflammatory and maturation evidence.
2. Olfactory basal-progenitor proliferation and neuronal survival: Human PACAP-38 amide - PACAP/PAC1 signaling is intrinsic to the olfactory neuroepithelium. Exogenous PACAP-38 markedly increased olfactory neurons in culture through combined progenitor proliferation and neuronal-survival effects, while blockade of endogenous PACAP signaling produced selective neuronal loss. This directly addresses restoration of the sensory-neuron population after epithelial injury.
3. Injury-responsive NPY-Y1/ERK neuroregeneration and olfactory receptor-neuron survival: Human Neuropeptide Y amide - NPY functions as an endogenous trophic regulator in the olfactory epithelium. NPY deficiency reduces mature olfactory receptor neurons and increases neuronal apoptosis, while injury-associated ATP signaling stimulates NPY release and NPY-Y1/ERK signaling drives regenerative proliferation. This provides an injury-coupled regenerative axis distinct from PACAP.
4. IGF1R-mediated maturation of immature olfactory receptor neurons after epithelial degeneration: Human IGF-1 - IGF signaling supports olfactory neuronal generation and survival. In experimentally degenerated aged olfactory epithelium, intranasal IGF-1 increased epithelial thickness and OMP-positive mature olfactory receptor neurons, with evidence that its major effect includes progression of immature neurons toward mature sensory-neuron identity rather than merely increasing progenitor proliferation.
5. FGFR-mediated globose basal-cell expansion and olfactory neuronal differentiation: Human low-molecular-weight FGF2 isoform - FGF2 acts directly on olfactory epithelial progenitors, stimulates globose basal-cell proliferation, and promotes neuronal differentiation. 6. Reserve horizontal-basal-cell activation and injury-induced sensory-neuron regeneration: Recombinant mature human HB-EGF(63-148), unglycosylated - HB-EGF provides a distinct EGFR-driven reserve-stem-cell axis. The direct regeneration study was performed in zebrafish olfactory epithelium, so translation of this mechanism to human phantosmia remains unproven.

Recent murine olfactory-epithelium experiments examining regenerative axon growth found particularly strong elongation when early FGF2 exposure was followed by FGF2 plus NGF, supporting NGF as a later-stage reinnervation signal. This is therefore a conditional axis for phantosmia associated with epileptiform olfactory-network hyperexcitability, not for peripheral post-infectious phantosmia.

﻿Portal Hypertension is a clinical syndrome defined by an increase in the portal venous pressure gradient (typically hepatic venous pressure gradient >5 mmHg, with clinically significant at >=10 mmHg and severe complications at >=12 mmHg), leading to life-threatening sequelae in advanced liver disease. ﻿Presbyopia (age-related loss of accommodation due to lens and ciliary apparatus stiffening)

Presbyopia is an age-related optical condition characterized by the gradual loss of the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects. 

This decline is primarily attributed to the progressive hardening and loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens, alongside the weakening of the ciliary muscles responsible for lens accommodation. Primary orthostatic tremor (POT) is a rare neurological oscillatory disorder characterized by a highly coherent approximately 13-18 Hz tremor of the legs and trunk that emerges during unsupported standing and improves markedly with sitting, walking or weight transfer. ﻿Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare and frequently fatal demyelinating opportunistic infection of the central nervous system caused by lytic reactivation of the JC polyomavirus (JCV) in the context of profound cellular immunodeficiency. It most commonly occurs in patients with HIV/AIDS (prior to effective antiretroviral therapy), hematologic malignancies, organ transplantation, primary immunodeficiencies, or iatrogenically from immunosuppressive monoclonal antibodies (e.g., natalizumab, rituximab, ofatumumab) and other agents. Clinical presentation is subacute and progressive, encompassing cognitive impairment, motor weakness, gait ataxia, visual deficits, aphasia, and seizures, reflecting multifocal white matter lesions predominantly in cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem. Pathophysiology centers on JCV tropism for oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, mediated by VP1 binding to {alpha}2,6-linked sialic acid and 5-HT2A receptors for entry, followed by intracellular replication driven by large T antigen, non-coding control region rearrangements, and evasion or absence of robust CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte surveillance due to impaired immunity, culminating in oligodendrocyte death, demyelination, and axonal preservation with minimal inflammation (except in immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome cases).

No approved direct antiviral therapy exists with proven efficacy against JCV, and management relies primarily on rapid immune reconstitution (e.g., cART initiation in HIV, drug discontinuation and plasma exchange in natalizumab-associated cases). Emerging immunotherapies show promise but remain investigational. The proposed polypeptides are all designed conceptual short amidated cationic amphipathic peptides leveraging established principles of antiviral and cell-penetrating peptide design to address complementary mechanisms in the absence of established polypeptide therapeutics. These designs prioritize blood-brain barrier penetration via cationic charge, enhanced plasma stability through C-terminal amidation, and multifaceted actions: the first designed polypeptide employs alternating aromatic (phenylalanine) and cationic (arginine) residues to potentially interfere with JCV capsid stability or receptor-mediated entry through electrostatic and hydrophobic disruption; the second incorporates tryptophan for superior membrane partitioning and intracellular delivery to inhibit viral replication processes; the third utilizes histidine and tyrosine for pH-sensitive interactions and potent reactive oxygen species scavenging to protect neural tissue from secondary oxidative injury; the fourth features leucine-lysine alternation for helical amphipathicity to stabilize membranes and potentially facilitate immune effector cell engagement at sites of infection. All polypeptides are designed with physicochemical properties supporting feasibility as injectable therapeutics, including short length for synthesis, resistance to proteolysis via amidation, and low predicted immunogenicity.

﻿Progressive Muscular Atrophy (Motor Neuron Type 2), also known as Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type 2 (SMA Type 2), is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by homozygous deletions or mutations in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene on chromosome 5q13, leading to insufficient production of the SMN protein essential for motor neuron survival. This results in progressive degeneration of lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem, manifesting as symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, hypotonia, and atrophy, typically onsetting between 6 and 18 months of age. Affected individuals can usually sit unassisted but cannot stand or walk independently, and the disease progresses to involve respiratory muscles, leading to frequent infections, scoliosis, joint contractures, and feeding difficulties due to bulbar involvement. ﻿Propionic Acidemia (PA) is a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficient activity of the mitochondrial enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC), encoded by the PCCA or PCCB genes, leading to impaired catabolism of propiogenic amino acids (isoleucine, valine, methionine, threonine), odd-chain fatty acids, and cholesterol. This results in the toxic accumulation of propionyl-CoA and its derivatives, including propionic acid, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, methylcitrate, and propionylglycine, which disrupt multiple metabolic pathways. The pathophysiology involves mitochondrial dysfunction from propionyl-CoA inhibiting enzymes like pyruvate dehydrogenase, succinyl-CoA synthetase, and N-acetylglutamate synthase, causing energy deficits, lactic acidosis, hyperammonemia, and oxidative stress. Acute metabolic decompensations, triggered by infections, fasting, or high-protein intake, manifest as vomiting, lethargy, seizures, encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy, and can lead to coma or death. Chronic complications include intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, cardiomyopathy, pancreatitis, optic neuropathy, renal tubular acidosis, and bone marrow suppression. Gut microbiota-derived propionate exacerbates the propionate load, while secondary effects like aberrant protein propionylation and histone modifications alter gene expression and cellular signaling, contributing to neurotoxicity and cardiac issues. Diagnosis involves elevated C3 acylcarnitine on newborn screening, urine organic acids showing characteristic metabolites, and genetic confirmation. Without intervention, prognosis is poor, with high mortality in neonatal-onset forms.

The proposed polypeptides address key mechanisms of PA through multiple therapeutic axes. For enzyme replacement, the designed polypeptide mimics PCC activity to metabolize propionyl-CoA, reducing toxic buildup; feasibility stems from peptide-based enzyme mimetics, with action via substrate binding and considerations for mitochondrial targeting to enhance stability. For redox homeostasis, the designed polypeptide acts as an antioxidant mimetic, scavenging ROS and supporting NRF2 activation to mitigate oxidative damage, feasible through thiol-containing peptides, functioning by redox buffering with emphasis on cellular penetration. For ammonia scavenging enhancement, the designed polypeptide potentiates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase via N-acetylglutamate mimicry, aiding urea cycle flux; this is supported by peptide analogs of NAG, acting as allosteric activators with solubility optimizations. For serine metabolism correction, the designed polypeptide modulates serine biosynthetic enzymes to restore levels disrupted in PA, feasible in regulatory peptides, via enzyme activation with bioavailability focus.

N{epsilon}-carboxymethyllysine (CML) is a chemically stable advanced glycation end product formed on lysine residues through glycoxidative/carbonyl chemistry. Three mechanistically different problems must be separated: preventing additional CML formation, blocking biological injury from existing CML through RAGE and related pathways, and actually converting already-modified CML residues back to lysine. The last of these was achieved for the first time in 2026 with the engineered enzyme CrGO-897/CMLase: it oxidized protein-bound CML and restored lysine, reducing detectable CML by 52-97% across experimental proteins, by >70% in elderly human arterial tissue, and by >55% in elderly human skin ex vivo. This is substantially different from ordinary “antiglycation” agents. However, CMLase is a 299-residue engineered bacterial enzyme, not an established therapeutic peptide; the published work is entirely in vitro/ex vivo, with no animal or human administration, pharmacokinetic, immunogenicity, delivery, or clinical-efficacy evidence. Because the complete final CrGO-897 sequence was not available from a primary sequence record with sufficient certainty for atomic insertion, it is deliberately not fabricated into Field 3. The six peptide axes below therefore address formation of new glycation and reversal/suppression of established AGE/CML-induced cellular damage rather than falsely claiming that they chemically remove pre-existing CML.

1. Reactive-carbonyl trapping and suppression of new CML formation: Carnosine - Beta-alanyl-L-histidine directly reduced methylglyoxal-induced CML formation in ex-vivo human skin explants, with approximately 64% suppression in epidermis and 41% in reticular dermis for aqueous carnosine. It is retained as the single exception to the default carnosine blacklist because the evidence is specifically CML-directed in human tissue rather than generic antioxidant evidence. It prevents formation; it does not convert established CML back to lysine.
2. Methylglyoxal detoxification through Nrf2/GLO1: Exendin-4 - Exendin-4 activates Nrf2 and increases glyoxalase-1, enhancing removal of methylglyoxal before it generates AGE adducts. In methylglyoxal-exposed mesangial cells this reduced AGE formation and downstream RAGE/inflammatory signaling; GLO1 manipulation supported a causal role for this pathway. Exact chemistry is the 39-residue C-terminal serinamide.
3. Direct blockade of CML-RAGE signaling: iRAGE - An 11-residue human-serum-albumin-derived peptide centered on the frequently glycated Lys378 site, with that lysine deliberately replaced by N{epsilon}-carboxymethyllysine. It functions as a competitive CML-pattern RAGE antagonist. In CML-HSA-stimulated vascular smooth-muscle cells, iRAGE blocked approximately 69.6% of the increase in NF-{kappa}B signaling and reduced executioner-caspase activation by approximately 63.5%, while reducing ER-stress/apoptotic injury. This is the most CML-specific downstream peptide in the set.
4. AGE-induced endothelial apoptosis and vascular dysfunction: Human octanoyl-ghrelin - Native active ghrelin protects human endothelial cells from AGE-BSA-induced apoptosis through GHSR1a and NO/cGMP signaling. Pharmacologic GHSR1a blockade abolished the protective effect, supporting receptor-specific action. Exact native chemistry includes Ser3 O-n-octanoylation.
5. Reversal of AGE-induced hypertrophic/myofibroblast phenotype: Angiotensin-(1-7) - In renal epithelial cells exposed to methylglyoxal-modified albumin, AGE exposure depleted endogenous Ang-(1-7), induced cellular hypertrophy and drove myofibroblast transformation. Replacement Ang-(1-7) reversed hypertrophy and {alpha}-SMA-associated myofibroblast conversion and abolished AGE-induced ERK1/2 activation through the Mas-receptor axis. This is reversal of an established AGE-induced cellular phenotype, not chemical deglycation of CML.
6. AGE/RAGE-driven vascular calcification and glucose-amplification loop: Human intermedin/adrenomedullin-2(1-47)-NH2 - Intermedin/ADM2 reduced tissue AGE content and RAGE expression and attenuated diabetic vascular calcification. Mechanistic experiments implicated cAMP/PKA-dependent inhibition of GLUT1; the IMD17-47 receptor antagonist and PKA inhibition abolished key effects. Exact mature human peptide chemistry uses the native Cys10-Cys15 disulfide and C-terminal Tyr amide.

﻿Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by end-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH levels despite normal or high PTH production. This impairs PTH's ability to promote renal phosphate excretion and calcium reabsorption, as well as bone resorption, resulting in disrupted calcium-phosphate homeostasis. Subtypes include PHP1A (with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features like short stature, obesity, and brachydactyly due to maternal GNAS mutations causing multi-hormone resistance), PHP1B (imprinting defects leading to renal PTH resistance), and PHP1C (similar to 1A but normal Gs alpha activity). Symptoms typically emerge in childhood and include tetany, seizures, muscle cramps from hypocalcemia, developmental delays, cognitive impairment, and ectopic ossifications. Pathophysiology involves defective cAMP signaling, secondary hyperparathyroidism-like effects without PTH efficacy, potential thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) resistance in PHP1A leading to hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency, and increased risk of basal ganglia calcifications. Without intervention, complications escalate to cataracts, dental anomalies, and renal issues from chronic hyperphosphatemia.

The proposed polypeptides address key therapeutic axes in PHP through conceptual designs, as no established real-world polypeptides directly target the resistance mechanisms beyond symptomatic management. For calcium-phosphate homeostasis, a calcitonin-inspired design modulates phosphate excretion and calcium balance to alleviate hyperphosphatemia. Bone metabolism and ossification are targeted by a designed modulator to prevent ectopic bone formation and improve skeletal integrity. These flagged designed polypeptides offer feasibility in restoring gene expression or pathway function, with physicochemical properties favoring stability and bioavailability, though clinical validation is needed.

﻿Rectal prolapse is a debilitating condition characterized by the protrusion of the rectal wall through the anus, often resulting from a combination of factors including chronic straining due to constipation, weakening of the pelvic floor muscles and supportive ligaments from aging, multiple childbirths, or previous surgeries, neurological impairments such as pudendal nerve damage, inflammatory bowel diseases contributing to tissue inflammation and altered motility, and connective tissue disorders like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Symptoms manifest as a visible red mass protruding from the anus, especially during bowel movements, fecal incontinence, mucus discharge, rectal bleeding, chronic constipation or obstructed defecation, pain or discomfort in the anal region, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. In severe cases, it can lead to ulceration, strangulation, or gangrene of the prolapsed tissue. Pathophysiologically, rectal prolapse involves multifactorial disruptions: pelvic floor dysfunction with sphincter atrophy and paradoxical puborectalis contraction, impaired sensorimotor function leading to reduced rectal sensation and propulsion, anatomical abnormalities such as rectocele or intussusception, chronic inflammation exacerbating tissue weakness, and potential circadian rhythm disturbances in immune responses that worsen bowel inflammation. Conservative management includes stool softeners and pelvic floor exercises, but surgical approaches like rectopexy or resection are often necessary for correction.

The proposed polypeptides target various therapeutic axes to mitigate rectal prolapse. Real-world polypeptides like BPC-157 facilitate wound healing, nerve regeneration, and fistula closure, addressing sphincter repair and post-surgical recovery. Linaclotide and Plecanatide activate guanylate cyclase-C to enhance intestinal fluid secretion and motility, alleviating constipation and reducing straining that exacerbates prolapse. Teduglutide, a GLP-2 analog, improves bowel absorption and adaptation, supporting overall gastrointestinal function. VIP regulates motility and vasodilation, aiding in rectal propulsion. Substance P enhances sensory perception, improving rectal sensation. Alpha-MSH and Cortistatin provide anti-inflammatory effects, reducing bowel inflammation associated with prolapse. Ghrelin modulates gastrocolic reflexes and motility. TGF-beta2 promotes connective tissue remodeling and repair, strengthening pelvic support. CCK-8 influences postprandial gallbladder and rectal responses, aiding sensation. GLP-1 regulates incretin effects and gut hormones, supporting defecation. CGRP induces vasodilation and modulates motility, potentially relieving obstructed defecation. Argireline relaxes facial-like muscle contractions, conceptually aiding puborectalis relaxation. The designed polypeptides are flagged as conceptual: Peptide [15] targets circadian clock modulation to normalize immune responses in bowel tissue; Peptide [16] provides additional anti-inflammatory support; Peptide [17] enhances pelvic floor muscle strengthening; Peptide [18] improves rectal propulsion to address obstructed defecation.

﻿Rectocele, also known as posterior vaginal wall prolapse, is a condition where the rectum bulges into the vagina due to weakening of the rectovaginal fascia, often resulting from childbirth trauma, chronic straining from constipation, aging, menopause-related estrogen decline, obesity, or connective tissue disorders. This leads to fascial tears, levator ani muscle atrophy, perineal body damage, and potential nerve impairment, causing symptoms such as vaginal bulging, pelvic pressure, difficulty with bowel movements requiring manual splinting, incomplete evacuation, fecal incontinence, dyspareunia, and low back pain. This is recurrent, previously fulminant myopericarditis in a young man whose initial left-ventricular ejection fraction fell to approximately 10% and subsequently recovered to approximately 50%, followed by a second troponin-positive episode in June 2025 with chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension and tachycardia. The causal attribution to COVID-vaccine “shedding” is not supported by current evidence: mRNA COVID vaccines do not contain replicating virus and vaccinated people do not shed vaccine-derived virus or spike protein to close contacts. A vaccinated person can transmit an actual SARS-CoV-2 infection if infected, which is biologically different. Negative SARS-CoV-2 tests during the myocarditis episodes also do not establish the cause; myocarditis may follow an infection that has already cleared, and other infectious, immune and genetic causes remain possible. Of particular importance in a young person with recurrent severe myocarditis, current ACC guidance recognizes pathogenic cardiomyopathy variants-especially DSP and TTN, but also FLNC, LMNA, DSG2, RBM20 and others-as established susceptibility factors and specifically prioritizes genetic evaluation in recurrent myocarditis. A result described only as genetic “spike-protein sensitivity” should therefore not substitute for a validated cardiomyopathy/arrhythmia gene-panel interpretation. Six distinct peptide-addressable experimental axes were identified: cardiac-directed autoimmune T-cell inflammation, inflammatory-cell infiltration and fibrotic remodeling, conditional cardiotropic-enterovirus replication, NPR-B/cGMP-mediated inflammatory and microvascular dysfunction, myocardial inflammatory edema, and impaired cardiac-lymphatic inflammatory clearance. No Sternheimer protein-biosynthesis inhibition axis is included because recurrent myocarditis is not established to be driven by pathological ribosomal overproduction of one defined endogenous protein.

This is highly relevant to a recurrent episode in which an autoimmune/postinfectious mechanism remains possible. The native human/rat 14-mer PCKNFFWKTFSSCK with the Cys2-Cys13 disulfide is represented.

This axis is particularly pertinent after recovery from an EF near 10%, where residual inflammatory fibrosis and scar-not only acute inflammation-affect long-term prognosis.

﻿Increasing Redox Signaling Molecules refers to the targeted enhancement of reactive species such as ROS (e.g., H2O2, superoxide), RNS (e.g., NO), and metabolites like itaconate, which act as signaling messengers in cellular processes including inflammation, metabolism, stress response, and immunity. Deficient redox signaling can contribute to aging, impaired wound healing, or weakened immune function, while controlled increase can promote adaptive responses. ﻿Regeneration of nerves, tissues, ligaments, bone, and muscle is a complex biological process that is highly efficient in certain organisms and during early development but significantly limited in adult mammals due to evolutionary trade-offs favoring scar formation over full restoration, reducing risks like cancer but impairing functional recovery after injury. Peripheral nerves regenerate slowly via axonal sprouting and Schwann cell support, but with frequent misdirection and incomplete functional recovery; central nerves barely regenerate due to inhibitory glial scars and lack of growth-permissive environment. Ligaments and tendons heal poorly due to low cellularity and vascularity, often resulting in weak scar tissue prone to re-injury. Bone regenerates well through endochondral or intramembranous ossification but fails in large defects or with comorbidities, forming non-unions. ﻿Cell membrane potential, commonly referred to as the resting membrane potential, represents the electrical voltage difference across the plasma membrane of cells, typically maintained between -40 mV and -90 mV in various cell types, with neurons around -70 mV and cardiac myocytes around -90 mV. This potential is crucial for fundamental cellular processes, including nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction, nutrient uptake, and overall cellular homeostasis. Disruptions to cell membrane potential can arise from multiple causes, such as physical trauma causing membrane pores or tears, oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species leading to lipid peroxidation and altered membrane permeability, genetic mutations affecting ion channel function (e.g., channelopathies like long QT syndrome), toxin exposure blocking channels or pumps, energy depletion impairing ATP-dependent ion pumps, inflammatory responses altering channel expression, or pathological states like ischemia, hypoxia, neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cardiac arrhythmias, or cancer where bioelectric signaling is dysregulated. Symptoms vary by cell type: in neurons, depolarization may cause hyperexcitability leading to seizures or pain, while hyperpolarization results in reduced signaling and neuropathy; in cardiac cells, it manifests as irregular heartbeats or fibrillation; in skeletal muscle, weakness, cramps, or paralysis; and systemically, it can lead to cell swelling, apoptosis, or necrosis if prolonged. The pathophysiology involves the breakdown of ion concentration gradients-high intracellular K+ and low Na+-maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump and leak channels. When disrupted, passive ion flux alters the Nernst equilibrium, shifting the potential away from rest, impairing action potential generation, and triggering downstream cascades like calcium overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory signaling, ultimately compromising cell viability.

The proposed polypeptides provide a comprehensive approach to restoring cell membrane potential by addressing key therapeutic axes through modulation of ion transport, membrane repair, and supportive mechanisms. Real-world polypeptides such as vasopressin and oxytocin act via G-protein-coupled receptors to influence calcium channels and secondary messengers, helping to normalize potential in responsive cells like those in the kidney or smooth muscle. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) bind to their receptors to elevate cGMP, which activates protein kinase G to modulate sodium and potassium channels, promoting repolarization and reducing cellular excitability in cardiac and vascular tissues. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) stimulates adenylate cyclase, increasing cAMP levels that open potassium channels and stabilize potential in gastrointestinal and neural cells. Toxin-derived peptides like apamin, charybdotoxin, and iberiotoxin selectively block specific potassium channels (e.g., SK or BK channels), fine-tuning efflux to prevent excessive depolarization in excitable cells. Mu-conotoxin targets sodium channels to inhibit influx, aiding in potential restoration during hyperexcitable states, while omega-conotoxin blocks calcium channels to prevent overload and maintain balance. Cell-penetrating peptides TAT and penetratin enable intracellular access for therapeutics, indirectly supporting pump activity or repair enzymes. pHLIP exploits acidic environments in damaged tissues to insert into membranes, stabilizing structure and aiding resealing. BPC-157 enhances wound healing and membrane integrity through angiogenic and anti-inflammatory effects, facilitating potential recovery in injured tissues. The designed polypeptides (D1-D4) are conceptualized to fill gaps: D1 modulates chloride channels to correct anion imbalances; D2 activates Na+/K+ ATPase to rebuild ion gradients; D3 integrates into lipids to seal disruptions; D4 triggers stress responses to boost chaperone activity and resilience. These interventions are feasible due to polypeptides' biocompatibility, targeted delivery, and tunable properties like net charge for membrane interaction (+ for penetration, hydrophobic for insertion), with rationales grounded in ion electrodiffusion models (Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation), repair kinetics, and clinical precedents for peptide therapeutics, ensuring physicochemical stability (e.g., disulfide bonds for structure) and minimal off-target effects.

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is an acute neurovascular disorder characterized by thunderclap headaches and multifocal, segmental constriction of intracranial arteries. It is mechanistically distinct from delayed vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, although both involve disturbed vascular tone. Proposed RCVS mechanisms include sympathetic overactivity, endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilator reserve, oxidative stress, blood-brain-barrier disruption, and abnormal responses to serotonergic, adrenergic, hormonal, and other vasoactive stimuli. The selected peptides comprise one RCVS-linked CGRP candidate and seven cerebral-vasospasm or neurovascular-unit research candidates. None is an established RCVS treatment. No single excessively synthesized endogenous peptide has been demonstrated to drive RCVS consistently enough to justify a Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition entry.

1. CGRP-dependent cerebral vasodilatory reserve: Human beta-CGRP disulfide peptide, C-terminally amidated - Both human CGRP isoforms potently relax intracranial arteries through the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, receptor-activity-modifying protein 1, cyclic AMP, and potassium-channel signaling. RCVS onset or severe exacerbation has been reported after pharmacological CGRP blockade, supporting a protective vasodilatory role. Beta-CGRP was selected instead of the previously repeated alpha isoform. Evidence supports the CGRP pathway rather than direct beta-CGRP treatment of RCVS, and infusion could provoke severe headache, tachycardia, flushing, or hypotension.
2. Endothelin-A-receptor-mediated smooth-muscle constriction: BQ-123 head-to-tail cyclic pentapeptide - BQ-123 selectively antagonizes the endothelin-A receptor and reduces endothelin-driven calcium sensitization and sustained vascular smooth-muscle contraction. Intrathecal or intracisternal BQ-123 prevented or attenuated cerebral arterial narrowing in several rat, dog, rabbit, and primate subarachnoid-hemorrhage models, although results were inconsistent between models and systemic delivery was ineffective because of poor central penetration. It has not been tested for RCVS.
3. Urotensin-II-receptor vasoconstriction and vascular inflammation: Urantide disulfide cyclic peptide - Urantide is a modified urotensin-II fragment that acts as a UT-receptor antagonist or pathway-biased ligand. UT antagonism with urantide prevented vasospasm and improved neurological performance in a mouse subarachnoid-hemorrhage model, while increased circulating urotensin II was associated with symptomatic cerebral vasospasm in human patients. Newer work implicates UT signaling in vascular smooth-muscle calcium mobilization, meningeal inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and delayed vasospasm. There is no RCVS trial.

﻿Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) is a serious complication arising from acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which is an inflammatory autoimmune disorder triggered by an untreated or inadequately treated infection with group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (GAS) bacteria, typically following pharyngitis. Predominantly affecting children and young adults in low- and middle-income countries, RHD develops when the immune system's response to GAS cross-reacts with host tissues, particularly cardiac valves, through molecular mimicry. Antibodies produced against streptococcal antigens, such as M protein, mistakenly target similar epitopes on cardiac proteins like myosin, laminin, and vimentin, leading to initial carditis. Repeated episodes of ARF exacerbate valve damage, causing chronic inflammation, fibrosis, scarring, calcification, and eventual valvular dysfunction, most commonly involving the mitral valve (stenosis or regurgitation), followed by the aortic valve. Risk factors include genetic predisposition (e.g., polymorphisms in immune response genes like HLA-DR), overcrowding, poverty, limited access to healthcare, and poor hygiene, which facilitate GAS transmission. Symptoms often manifest years after initial infection and include dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, fatigue, palpitations, chest pain, edema, and signs of heart failure or atrial fibrillation due to left atrial enlargement. In severe cases, complications such as pulmonary hypertension, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis, and sudden cardiac death can occur. Pathophysiologically, the disease involves multiple axes: streptococcal infection persistence, autoimmune activation, chronic inflammation mediated by cytokines (TNF-{alpha}, IL-6, IL-1{beta}), oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species damaging valve endothelium, fibrotic remodeling via TGF-{beta} and matrix metalloproteinases leading to collagen deposition, valve calcification resembling atherosclerosis with calcium-phosphate accumulation, heart failure from volume/pressure overload, and impaired valve repair mechanisms. ﻿Scurvy is a nutritional deficiency disease caused by prolonged lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in the diet, leading to a range of debilitating symptoms and potentially fatal complications if left untreated. The primary cause is insufficient intake of fresh fruits and vegetables, which are the main dietary sources of vitamin C, though it can also arise from malabsorption issues such as those seen in gastrointestinal disorders, alcoholism, or restrictive diets. Historically prevalent among sailors, explorers, and populations during famines, scurvy manifests initially with nonspecific symptoms like fatigue, malaise, muscle weakness, and irritability. As the deficiency progresses, more characteristic signs emerge, including swollen and bleeding gums (gingivitis), easy bruising (ecchymoses), pinpoint hemorrhages around hair follicles (perifollicular petechiae), poor wound healing, joint pain and swelling due to hemarthrosis, anemia from blood loss or impaired iron absorption, and brittle hair that coils like a corkscrew. In advanced stages, patients may experience internal bleeding, infections, convulsions, heart failure, and death. Pathophysiologically, vitamin C serves as an essential cofactor for enzymes like prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, which are critical for stabilizing the triple-helix structure of collagen through hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues. Without this, collagen becomes unstable, resulting in weakened blood vessels, skin, bones, and other connective tissues. Additionally, vitamin C plays roles in carnitine biosynthesis for energy metabolism, catecholamine and neurotransmitter synthesis (e.g., dopamine, norepinephrine), antioxidant defense against reactive oxygen species, immune cell function (enhancing neutrophil motility and phagocytosis), and hormone production via peptide amidation. Deficiency disrupts these processes, leading to metabolic imbalances like hypoglycemia, cognitive impairments, and dysregulated stress responses via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Bone health suffers from impaired osteoid formation, causing subperiosteal hemorrhages and fractures, while vascular fragility promotes hemorrhages and edema.

Immune support via D5 employs cationic lysine-phenylalanine alternations for membrane-disrupting antimicrobial activity, enhancing innate defenses compromised in scurvy. description:
﻿Secondary diastolic hypertension in person with Chronic Fight-or-Flight Loop and associated potassium wasting

Created 2026-09-26
This phenotype is treated as six separable mechanistic axes: excessive catecholamine release, central sympathetic/noradrenergic drive with impaired autonomic buffering, peripheral catecholamine/angiotensin-II vasoconstriction, renal-vascular RAAS/APJ imbalance, aldosterone-linked pressure/volume regulation, and ROMK-mediated renal potassium secretion. Hypertension accompanied by documented potassium wasting should not be presumed to arise solely from chronic sympathetic activation; primary aldosteronism is an important potentially overlapping secondary cause. No Sternheimer-proteody axis was added because the supplied phenotype does not establish pathological excess biosynthesis of a specific peptide/protein; the principal stated fight-or-flight mediators are catecholamines, while aldosterone is a steroid.

1. Catecholamine-release inhibition: Human catestatin - Endogenous chromogranin-A-derived peptide that inhibits nicotinic-cholinergic activation of adrenal/neuronal catecholamine secretion at the initial nicotinic cationic-signalling step. Human and experimental hypertension literature links impaired catestatin/catecholamine balance to hypertension, making this the most direct peptide axis for the stated chronic fight-or-flight phenotype.
2. Central sympathetic outflow and baroreflex regulation: Angiotensin-(1-7) - Counter-regulatory RAS peptide whose central actions can reduce hypothalamic norepinephrine release through bradykinin/NO-dependent signalling and improve autonomic/baroreflex regulation in hypertensive models, addressing persistent central sympathetic drive rather than only peripheral vasoconstriction.
3. Peripheral norepinephrine/angiotensin-II vasoconstriction: Human {alpha}-CGRP, native disulfide/C-terminal-amide form - Potent sensory-neuropeptide vasodilator. CGRP directly reduced blood pressure and total peripheral resistance in experimental hypertension produced by chronic norepinephrine or angiotensin-II exposure, making this axis specifically relevant to catecholamine-driven vascular resistance.
4. Renal-vascular RAAS/APJ counter-regulation: Apelin-13 - APJ-receptor peptide with rapid vasodilatory and cardiorenal actions; intravenous apelin-13 reduced both systolic and diastolic pressure in the two-kidney-one-clip hypertensive rat model. Its vascular response is endothelial-state dependent, so this remains an experimental mechanistic axis rather than an established treatment.
5. Aldosterone/GC-A/cGMP counter-regulation: MANP, native Cys7-Cys23 disulfide form - Published 40-residue ANP analogue acting at GC-A. Human hypertension studies show BP reduction, cGMP activation, natriuresis and aldosterone suppression; experimental work also demonstrates attenuation of RAAS activation. This specifically addresses the aldosterone component that can couple hypertension to renal potassium loss, although MANP itself has not been established as potassium-sparing and its natriuretic action could alter distal sodium delivery.
6. ROMK-mediated renal potassium secretion: Tertiapin-Q, native two-disulfide/C-terminal-amide form - Direct peptide blocker of ROMK/Kir1.1, a major apical pathway for distal-nephron potassium secretion. This is the most direct peptide-level match to a true renal potassium-wasting axis. Tertiapin-Q is strictly an experimental research tool: it also inhibits GIRK and BK-family potassium channels and is not an established systemic therapy.
