﻿Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign tumors of uterine smooth muscle and connective tissue, driven by hormonal factors (estrogen/progesterone), excessive extracellular matrix deposition, inflammation, and dysregulated growth signaling, leading to heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, infertility, and compressive symptoms. The selected real-world polypeptides target five evidence-based therapeutic axes derived from preclinical studies, investigational peptide research, and mechanistic applications in fibrosis, tissue repair, and gynecological disorders.

1. Gastric pentadecapeptide-mediated myometrial protection: BPC-157 supports endothelial maintenance, growth factor modulation, and healing relevant to uterine tissue integrity.

﻿Uterine polyps are benign overgrowths of the endometrial lining, frequently linked to hormonal imbalances, chronic inflammation, excessive angiogenesis, and microbiota disruptions, leading to abnormal bleeding and potential fertility issues. The proposed polypeptides target evidence-based therapeutic axes from preclinical and clinical studies on endometrial repair, hyperplasia inhibition, inflammation modulation, antimicrobial support, and matrix stabilization to promote regression, healing, and recurrence prevention.

﻿Uterine prolapse is a form of pelvic organ prolapse where weakened pelvic floor muscles, ligaments, and connective tissues cause the uterus to descend into or outside the vaginal canal, often related to childbirth trauma, menopause-associated estrogen decline, chronic strain, and extracellular matrix degradation. The proposed polypeptides target mechanistically relevant axes from regenerative medicine and tissue repair literature to enhance collagen synthesis, promote healing, stabilize structures, reduce inflammation, and support overall pelvic integrity.

﻿Uveitis encompasses a group of inflammatory disorders affecting the uveal tract of the eye (iris, ciliary body, and choroid), often extending to adjacent structures like the retina, vitreous, or sclera. It is classified anatomically as anterior, intermediate, posterior, or panuveitis, with non-infectious (autoimmune or idiopathic) forms being predominant in developed regions and infectious causes more common elsewhere. Causes include autoimmune diseases (e.g., associated with HLA-B27, sarcoidosis, Behçet's), infections (viral, bacterial, parasitic), trauma, or masquerade syndromes. Symptoms range from acute pain, redness, photophobia, and vision blur in anterior uveitis to floaters and vision loss in posterior forms. Pathophysiology involves breakdown of the blood-ocular barrier, infiltration of leukocytes (primarily T cells), release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., via JAK/STAT pathways), sustained immune activation, and tissue damage risking complications like macular edema, glaucoma, or blindness.

The proposed polypeptides target complementary anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory mechanisms to suppress uveitis while promoting resolution. Real R9-SOCS1-KIR inhibits excessive JAK/STAT signaling downstream of cytokines, reducing pro-inflammatory gene expression in preclinical EAU and EIU models. Real Annexin A1 Ac2-26 (N-terminal mimetic) activates formyl peptide receptors to promote active inflammation resolution and efferocytosis. Real VIP exerts broad immunomodulatory effects via VPAC receptors, inhibiting T cell activation and cytokine release in EAU. Real ACTH(1-39) engages melanocortin receptors (especially MC1R/MC3R) to deliver potent steroid-independent anti-inflammatory action, as explored in clinical investigations for refractory uveitis. Designed polypeptides are rationally derived for enhanced drug-likeness: the stabilized SOCS1-KIR (terminal capping) builds on the real motif for better stability; the cyclic AnxA1-mimetic (disulfide-cyclized extended Ac2-26) enhances resistance to proteolysis while retaining pro-resolving activity; the cyclic VIP analog (disulfide-cyclized core) improves pharmacokinetic properties based on VIP's active region; the alpha-MSH analog (capped core from ACTH) leverages the primary melanocortin anti-inflammatory fragment with modifications for ocular delivery. Together, these provide multi-axis coverage of cytokine suppression, resolution promotion, neuropeptide modulation, and melanocortin pathways for comprehensive control of immune-mediated uveitis.

﻿Created 2026-09-23
Every major adverse pathway covered in the 2021 Seneff-Nigh paper is treated here. The paper proposes PEG-triggered complement activation, ADE/Fc-receptor effects, pathogenic priming/autoimmunity, impaired autophagy, platelet-neutrophil NETosis, suppression of antiviral interferon signaling and ACE2/AngII dysregulation as possible adverse pathways. It separately develops hypotheses involving spike-associated protein misfolding, exosomal dissemination, immune-pressure selection of variants and LINE-1-mediated reverse transcription/integration. The paper's overlapping proposals are consolidated into twelve mechanistically distinct intervention axes: PEG/complement pseudoallergy, Fc{gamma}R-dependent antibody enhancement, pathogenic-priming autoimmunity, impaired autophagy, platelet-neutrophil NETosis, suppression of antiviral type-I-interferon activity with latent-virus reactivation, ACE2/AngII/Ang-(1-7) imbalance, mitochondrial/endothelial injury, prion-like protein aggregation/cross-seeding, exosomal cargo trafficking and shedding, antibody-resistant variant entry, and LINE-1-dependent retrotransposition/integration. The first eleven axes use peptides whose own targets have independent literature support.

PEG/complement-mediated pseudoallergy and anaphylactic amplification: Compstatin (real) - Compstatin is a cyclic C3-binding peptide that blocks central complement activation and thereby prevents downstream complement amplification. Under the paper's assumed PEG/complement mechanism, it targets the complement arm upstream of C3a/C5a generation rather than attempting to neutralize PEG-specific antibodies. The native cyclic peptide form is represented with its Cys2-Cys12 disulfide and C-terminal amide.
Fc{gamma}R-dependent antibody-dependent enhancement and immune-complex effector amplification: TG19320 / D-PAM (real) - TG19320 is a protease-resistant, branched Ig-binding peptide constructed from four all-D Arg-Thr-Tyr units on a three-Lys/Gly core. It interferes with IgG recognition by Fc{gamma} receptors and suppresses immune-complex-dependent effector processes experimentally. Within the paper's ADE assumption, it addresses Fc-mediated amplification rather than viral replication itself. D-residues retain the corresponding L-residue masses.
Molecular-mimicry/pathogenic-priming autoimmunity: Edratide / hCDR1 (real) - Edratide is a tolerogenic peptide derived from the human anti-DNA antibody 16/6 idiotype CDR1 region. Experimental autoimmune studies show induction of regulatory immune responses involving FoxP3/TGF-{beta} and suppression of pathogenic inflammatory/autoantibody responses. It therefore supplies an antigen-tolerance/immunoregulatory axis. It is not spike-specific and has not been shown to reverse vaccine-associated molecular mimicry.
Impaired autophagy and clearance of intracellular/aggregated material: Tat-Beclin 1 (real) - This cell-permeable Beclin-1-derived peptide potently induces autophagy by disrupting an endogenous inhibitory interaction involving Beclin-1/GAPR-1. Experimental work demonstrates enhanced clearance of intracellular pathogens and aggregate-prone proteins. Under the paper's autophagy-suppression assumption it addresses impaired cellular disposal.
Platelet-neutrophil NETosis and thromboinflammatory amplification: Neonatal NET-inhibitory factor / nNIF (real) - nNIF is an endogenous 29-residue peptide that potently suppresses neutrophil extracellular-trap formation, including nuclear decondensation and histone citrullination. It therefore directly maps onto the paper's platelet-neutrophil/NET inflammatory-thrombotic feedback loop. 
Type-I-interferon suppression and latent-herpesvirus reactivation: Thymosin {alpha}1 / thymalfasin (real) - Thymosin {alpha}1 promotes antiviral innate signaling through dendritic-cell TLR/MyD88/IRF pathways and can enhance IFN-{alpha}/IFN-{gamma}-associated responses. Experimental viral studies support improved antiviral immune competence. This provides a host antiviral-response axis rather than direct anti-herpesviral killing. Native human thymosin {alpha}1 is retained with its N-terminal acetylation.
ACE2 loss, AngII excess and endothelial/BBB injury: Angiotensin-(1-7) (real) - Ang-(1-7) is the principal counter-regulatory product of the ACE2 arm of the renin-angiotensin system and acts through Mas. Experimental studies show preservation of endothelial/BBB integrity, suppression of inflammatory MMP remodeling and protection from AngII-driven endothelial injury. It therefore directly replaces the signaling branch the paper proposes is reduced when ACE2 function is impaired.
Spike-associated mitochondrial oxidative and endothelial apoptotic injury: Humanin (real) - Humanin is a mitochondrial-derived cytoprotective peptide. In human vascular endothelial cells it suppresses oxidative stress and apoptosis, while related studies demonstrate preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration and cellular bioenergetics. This supplies a mitochondrial/endothelial resilience axis independent of RAAS signaling. It has not been demonstrated to selectively antagonize vaccine-derived spike.
Prion-like/cross-seeded {alpha}-synuclein aggregation: 4554W (real) - 4554W is a ten-residue {alpha}-synuclein-binding peptide that suppresses formation of {alpha}-synuclein fibrils and associated cellular toxicity. It addresses the protein-misfolding/cross-seeding consequence rather than prion replication itself. Subsequent in-vitro studies have shown that certain proteolytically generated SARS-CoV-2 spike fragments can be amyloidogenic and that selected spike-derived fibrils can accelerate {alpha}-synuclein aggregation.
Exosomal CD63-syntenin cargo trafficking and shedding: Cytopermeable CD63-blocking peptide (real) - This peptide disrupts the interaction between the tetraspanin CD63 and syntenin, experimentally rerouting extracellular-vesicle cargo organization and co-enrichment. It is therefore a direct peptide tool for an exosomal-cargo axis. It prevents person-to-person “vaccine shedding”; its inclusion follows the requested assume-true treatment of the paper's exosome hypothesis.
Antibody-resistant/new-variant spike-mediated membrane fusion: EK1 (real) - EK1 is a pan-coronavirus HR1-targeting fusion-inhibitory peptide that blocks formation of the HR1/HR2 six-helix bundle required for membrane fusion and retains activity against multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants. Under the paper's immune-pressure/new-variant mechanism, EK1 addresses the biological consequence-entry by antigenically altered coronavirus spike proteins-not the evolutionary generation of variants itself.
LINE-1/PABPC1-dependent reverse transcription, retrotransposition and germline integration: L1-PIE-RRM26 (designed) - No experimentally validated peptide inhibitor of LINE-1 ORF2p retrotransposition was identified. ﻿Von Hippel-Lindau Disease (VHL) is a rare, autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25.3, leading to a predisposition for developing multiple benign and malignant tumors across various organs. Symptoms vary by tumor location and include headaches, ataxia, visual disturbances, hypertension, abdominal pain, and potential organ failure; untreated, it can lead to severe morbidity or mortality from tumor progression or complications like hemorrhage. The pathophysiology centers on loss of VHL-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of HIF-{alpha} subunits under normoxia, mimicking hypoxic conditions and driving pseudo-hypoxic signaling that fosters vascularized tumor growth. Diagnosis typically involves genetic testing for VHL mutations and surveillance imaging (MRI, CT, ultrasound) starting in childhood for at-risk individuals.

﻿WAGR syndrome is a rare contiguous gene deletion syndrome caused by heterozygous deletions on chromosome 11p13, primarily affecting the WT1 and PAX6 genes, with variable involvement of adjacent genes such as BDNF in larger deletions. ﻿Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) is a rare, indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder classified as a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the malignant proliferation of lymphoplasmacytic cells in the bone marrow and the overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulin M (IgM) paraprotein, known as macroglobulin. The condition primarily affects older adults, with a median age at diagnosis around 70 years, and has an incidence of approximately 3-5 cases per million people annually, showing a slight male predominance. Genetic factors play a pivotal role in its etiology, with the MYD88 L265P somatic mutation present in over 90% of cases, leading to constitutive activation of the NF-{kappa}B pathway and enhanced cell survival; additionally, CXCR4 mutations occur in about 30-40% of patients, promoting cell migration, adhesion, and resistance to therapy. ﻿Mechanistic Rationale 
Warts are benign epithelial hyperproliferative lesions caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), primarily HPV types 2, 4 (common warts), 1, 2, 4, 27, 57 (plantar warts), and 6/11 (genital). Key pathophysiological axes include: (1) viral entry and intracellular persistence via E6/E7 oncoprotein-mediated p53/Rb degradation; (2) immune evasion through downregulation of MHC-I and IFN signaling; (3) dysregulated keratinocyte proliferation and impaired differentiation; (4) local immunosuppression via T-reg recruitment and IL-10 overexpression; (5) angiogenic support via VEGF upregulation; and (6) resistance to apoptosis via Bcl-2 stabilization and caspase inhibition. Our peptide design framework targets six mechanistic axes: (i) E6-p53 PPI disruption, (ii) TLR7/8 agonism to restore innate sensing, (iii) IFN-{gamma} mimetic signaling via JAK-STAT potentiation, (iv) pro-apoptotic BH3-mimicry to counteract E6-mediated survival, (v) angiostatic VEGFR2 antagonism, and (vi) epidermal barrier reinforcement via filaggrin mimicry and tight-junction stabilization. Scaffold selection draws from: (a) {alpha}-helical stapled motifs for intracellular PPI inhibition; (b) constrained cyclic {beta}-hairpins for receptor agonism/antagonism; (c) D-enantiomeric sequences for protease resistance in extracellular niches; (d) lipidated antimicrobial-like peptides for membrane perturbation of virion envelopes; and (e) N-terminally modified cell-penetrating sequences for keratinocyte delivery. All designs incorporate strategic PTMs (e.g., N-methylation for stability, farnesylation for membrane anchoring, phosphorylation for signaling mimicry) and terminal modifications (acetylation/amidation/PEGylation) tuned to subcellular localization and half-life requirements.

﻿X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is a rare peroxisomal genetic disorder caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene on the X chromosome, encoding the adrenoleukodystrophy protein (ALDP), a peroxisomal membrane transporter responsible for importing very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) into peroxisomes for {beta}-oxidation. Defective ALDP leads to toxic accumulation of VLCFA (particularly C26:0 and C24:0) in plasma and tissues, most critically affecting the central nervous system white matter, spinal cord, and adrenal cortex. Clinical phenotypes vary widely even within families: the childhood cerebral form (onset 4-10 years) involves rapid progressive inflammatory demyelination with behavioral changes, cognitive decline, vision/hearing loss, seizures, and vegetative state/death within years if untreated; adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN, adult-onset) features slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory loss, bladder dysfunction, and adrenal insufficiency; Addison-only form presents primary adrenal failure; heterozygous females may develop milder AMN-like symptoms later in life. Pathophysiology encompasses direct VLCFA-induced membrane perturbation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative damage from excess ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, microglial activation with proinflammatory cytokine release, blood-brain barrier disruption, oligodendrocyte apoptosis, and axon loss, culminating in inflammatory cerebral demyelination resembling autoimmune processes while adrenal involvement causes cortisol/aldosterone deficiency and potential life-threatening crises.

The proposed polypeptides are entirely conceptually designed short sequences, as comprehensive searches across PubMed, clinicaltrials.gov, patents, and related databases identified no real-world polypeptide, peptide, antibody, or protein therapeutics (established, investigational, or preclinical) specifically for ALD; current management includes hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or ex vivo gene therapy (e.g., elivaldogene autotemcel) for early cerebral forms to halt demyelination, Lorenzo's oil (glycerol trioleate/triercuate mixture) to normalize plasma VLCFA, and hormone replacement for adrenal insufficiency, with emerging small-molecule trials targeting alternative transporters or antioxidants. These designed polypeptides target five core mechanistic axes derived from established pathogenesis: (1) VLCFA accumulation and peroxisomal impairment, addressed by the first designed polypeptide to conceptually enhance {beta}-oxidation or reduce toxicity; (2) neuroinflammation and microglial activation, targeted by the second designed polypeptide to suppress proinflammatory cascades; (3) oxidative stress and ROS-mediated damage, countered by the third designed polypeptide with antioxidant properties; (4) demyelination and oligodendrocyte/axon loss, modulated by the fourth designed polypeptide to support myelin stability; (5) mitochondrial dysfunction and energy deficit, ameliorated by the fifth designed polypeptide to improve cellular energetics. Collectively, these provide multi-axis conceptual coverage aiming to slow progression, protect neural tissue, and complement existing therapies, with feasibility informed by pathway validation in ALD models and parallels in peroxisomal/neurodegenerative disorders.

﻿X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA) is a primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by mutations in the BTK gene on the X chromosome, leading to impaired B cell development and maturation, resulting in absent or very low levels of circulating B cells and immunoglobulins. This genetic defect disrupts B cell signaling, preventing the production of antibodies essential for humoral immunity. Symptoms typically emerge in infancy or early childhood, including recurrent bacterial infections such as otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia, and gastrointestinal infections due to encapsulated bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Chronic infections can lead to complications like bronchiectasis, enteroviral meningoencephalitis, and increased risk of malignancies or autoimmune phenomena. Pathophysiology centers on the failure of pre-B cells to progress to mature B cells in the bone marrow, with secondary effects on innate immunity including neutrophil and monocyte dysfunction, contributing to persistent inflammation and tissue damage.

The proposed polypeptides address XLA through targeted mechanisms: designed D1 mimics IgG fragments to support humoral responses; designed D2 emulates BTK motifs for signaling restoration; Thymosin alpha-1 (real) boosts T cell function to aid infection control; designed D3 provides antimicrobial activity; designed D4 reduces cytokine-driven inflammation. Feasibility: Real polypeptides like Thymosin alpha-1 have off-label use in immunodeficiencies with evidence from preclinical studies; designed ones are conceptual, short for stability, potential subcutaneous delivery, but need validation for specificity and safety in XLA models.

﻿X-Linked Ichthyosis (XLI) is a genetic skin disorder caused by mutations or deletions in the STS gene on the X chromosome, leading to steroid sulfatase deficiency that impairs the hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate, resulting in accumulation of cholesterol-3-sulfate and disrupted corneocyte desquamation. This manifests as adherent, dark brown or gray scales on the extensor surfaces, trunk, and neck, with sparing of flexures, palms, soles, and face; symptoms include dryness, pruritus, and potential corneal opacities or cryptorchidism in some cases. Pathophysiology involves altered lipid composition in the stratum corneum, increased corneocyte cohesion from elevated cholesterol sulfate, impaired barrier function with heightened transepidermal water loss, and secondary inflammation from microbiome dysbiosis or Th17 skewing. Triggers include low humidity or hormonal changes, while chronic scaling can lead to ectropion, infections, or psychosocial impacts.

The proposed designed polypeptides target key axes of XLI. For inflammation inhibition, the designed polypeptide modulates IL-17/Th17 pathways to reduce cytokine-driven scaling, feasible via peptide antagonists with competitive binding and considerations for topical delivery. For barrier function enhancement, the designed polypeptide promotes lipid transport mimicking STS activity, supported by enzyme mimetic peptides, acting through substrate facilitation with stability in stratum corneum. For keratinocyte differentiation, the designed polypeptide activates retinoid-like pathways to improve desquamation, feasible in differentiation-modulating peptides, via receptor agonism with solubility enhancements. For STS restoration, the designed polypeptide acts as a chaperone to stabilize residual enzyme, based on protein stabilization precedents, functioning by binding interactions with proteolytic resistance. For redox homeostasis, the designed polypeptide scavenges ROS to mitigate oxidative damage, using antioxidant peptides, through thiol buffering with cellular penetration.

Xanthelasma palpebrarum consists of cholesterol-rich, lipid-laden macrophages in the superficial eyelid dermis. Lesional lipid is predominantly cholesteryl ester, and human xanthelasma studies support enhanced lipid oxidation/oxidized-LDL exposure, macrophage foam-cell formation, chronic macrophage/T-cell inflammation, and local vascular leakage as important mechanisms; the disorder can occur despite normal conventional serum lipid values. ([PubMed][1]) Existing lesions therefore present several mechanistically separable targets: prevention of CD36-dependent oxidized-LDL internalization, removal of accumulated macrophage cholesterol through ABCA1, neutralization of oxidized lipids, reduction of systemic LDL exposure where dyslipidemia contributes, resolution of persistent macrophage inflammation, and reduction of local endothelial leakage responsible for lipoprotein entry into eyelid tissue. Profound LDL lowering can occasionally regress established xanthelasma, including documented disappearance after PCSK9 inhibition, supporting the principle that mobilization of deposited cholesterol is biologically possible, although this response is not reliable in all patients. ([PubMed][2]) No Sternheimer biosynthesis-inhibition axis was identified because xanthelasma is not established as being driven by pathological overproduction of one particular endogenous peptide or protein.

None of these peptides is an established treatment for xanthelasma. Of the mechanistic axes, intensive LDL lowering has the strongest human evidence that systemic intervention can occasionally regress established xanthomatous deposits; the peptide candidates remain experimental. A lipid profile-including LDL-C, triglycerides and HDL-C-is particularly relevant because xanthelasma may accompany dyslipidemia or familial hypercholesterolemia, although a substantial proportion of patients are normolipidemic.

1. ABCA1-dependent removal of cholesterol from lipid-loaded dermal macrophages: 5A apolipoprotein A-I mimetic peptide - 5A is a bihelical apoA-I mimetic specifically engineered to promote ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux. It increased ABCA1-dependent cellular efflux approximately 3.5-fold in experimental systems and promoted macrophage reverse cholesterol transport in vivo. Because xanthelasma lesions are fundamentally collections of cholesteryl-ester-loaded macrophages, this directly targets the principal accumulated cellular substrate rather than merely suppressing inflammation. ([PubMed][3])
2. Oxidized-lipid sequestration and inflammatory macrophage reprogramming: L-4F - Ac-DWFKAFYDKVAEKFKEAF-NH2 is an apoA-I mimetic with extremely high affinity for oxidized phospholipids, binding several oxidized lipid species orders of magnitude more avidly than native apoA-I. This is particularly relevant because increased lipid peroxidation/oxidized-LDL exposure has been demonstrated directly in normolipidemic xanthelasma. 4F also suppresses macrophage inflammatory cytokines, monocyte adhesion/transendothelial migration and promotes cholesterol depletion, providing a complementary oxidized-lipid/inflammation axis rather than duplicating 5A's ABCA1-selective role. ([PubMed][4])
3. CD36-dependent oxidized-LDL uptake and foam-cell formation: CD36 N-terminal transmembrane-domain peptide - KKWGLIAGAVIGAVLAVFGGILMPVGKKK reproduces the conserved CD36 N-terminal transmembrane interaction domain. In mouse and human macrophages it disrupted CD36-CD9 membrane interactions, inhibited oxidized-LDL uptake by approximately 40-50%, reduced oxLDL-induced foam-cell formation by about 60%, lowered cellular cholesterol, and reduced oxLDL-induced ROS. This is an unusually direct peptide intervention against the actual macrophage-to-xanthoma-cell transition implicated in xanthelasma. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][5])
4. Systemic LDL exposure through PCSK9-LDLR regulation: Pep2-8 - Ac-TVFTSWEEYLDWV-NH2 is a structurally characterized 13-residue PCSK9 antagonist that competes with LDLR for the PCSK9 catalytic-domain binding surface, restores cell-surface LDLR and restores LDL uptake in PCSK9-treated hepatocytes. This axis is most relevant when xanthelasma accompanies hypercholesterolemia or familial hypercholesterolemia. It has special condition relevance because profound LDL lowering with clinical PCSK9 inhibition has produced documented regression or disappearance of xanthelasma/xanthomas, although Pep2-8 itself is experimental and considerably less potent than therapeutic antibodies. ([PubMed][6])
5. Persistent macrophage inflammatory signaling and defective inflammatory resolution: Annexin A1 Ac2-26 - Ac-AMVSEFLKQAWFIENEEQEYVQTVK activates the Annexin-A1/FPR2-ALX pro-resolving pathway. Xanthelasma tissue contains increased macrophages, lymphocytes, iNOS, COX and MPO, supporting a genuine inflammatory component beyond passive lipid storage. Ac2-26 has demonstrated macrophage/FPR2-dependent resolution of chronic lipid-rich vascular inflammation and therefore addresses persistence of the inflammatory cellular environment after the lipid-loading stimulus has occurred. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][7])
6. Eyelid microvascular permeability and lipoprotein extravasation: FX06 / fibrin B{beta}15-42 - GHRPLDKKREEAPSLRPAPPPISGGGYR is the natural 28-residue fibrin-derived peptide that binds VE-cadherin and stabilizes endothelial junctions through Fyn/p190RhoGAP-RhoA signaling. Local vascular leakage is a proposed xanthelasma mechanism because repeated eyelid movement and local vascular injury may permit plasma lipoproteins to enter the dermis. FX06 has repeatedly reduced endothelial permeability and protein/fluid extravasation experimentally, making it a mechanistically appropriate intervention for the lipid-entry axis, although no xanthelasma-specific trial has been conducted. ([EyeWiki][8])

﻿Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in genes responsible for the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, which is essential for repairing DNA damage induced by ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight. The primary genes affected include XPA, XPB, XPC, XPD, XPE, XPF, XPG, and XPV, leading to impaired recognition, incision, and resynthesis of damaged DNA strands. This results in accumulation of UV-induced lesions such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and (6-4) photoproducts, promoting mutagenesis and carcinogenesis. Symptoms typically appear in early childhood and include extreme photosensitivity with severe sunburns, blistering, and erythema after minimal sun exposure, persistent hyperpigmentation or freckling on sun-exposed areas, dry and parchment-like skin (xerosis), telangiectasia, and a dramatically increased risk of developing skin cancers like basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma at a young age. Ocular manifestations may involve photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, and increased risk of ocular surface cancers. In approximately 20-30% of cases, particularly those with mutations in XPA, XPB, XPD, or XPG, neurological complications arise, including progressive neurodegeneration, sensorineural hearing loss, cognitive impairment, ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy due to unrepaired oxidative DNA damage in non-dividing cells. Pathophysiology centers on defective NER leading to genomic instability, chronic inflammation from immune response to damaged cells, oxidative stress exacerbation, and premature cellular senescence, culminating in tissue degeneration and high cancer incidence, with XP patients having over 1000-fold increased risk of skin cancer and reduced life expectancy if unmanaged.

The proposed polypeptides address XP through comprehensive therapeutic axes, prioritizing real-world options where available and supplementing with designed ones to ensure full coverage. The real-world polypeptide Afamelanotide stimulates melanogenesis via alpha-MSH mimicry, increasing eumelanin production for natural photoprotection, reducing UV penetration, and enhancing DNA repair efficiency as shown in clinical trials; its feasibility is supported by good bioavailability and safety profile. Designed polypeptides D1 and D2 enhance NER by mimicking key domains of XPA and XPC proteins to facilitate damage recognition and recruitment of repair factors, with scientific rationale rooted in NER biochemistry and physicochemical considerations like positive charge for DNA binding and short length for stability. D3 provides photoprotection through aromatic residues that absorb UV, preventing lesion formation; feasibility includes topical application potential. D4 acts in chemoprevention by inhibiting oncogenic signaling pathways like PI3K/AKT, reducing tumor initiation. D5 modulates anti-inflammatory responses by mimicking cytokine inhibitors, suppressing Th2 cytokines and eosinophil activation to mitigate chronic skin inflammation. D6 boosts antioxidant defenses with thiol groups to scavenge ROS, addressing oxidative damage amplification in XP. D7 targets senotherapeutics, disrupting SASP via JAK-like inhibition to clear senescent cells and reduce aging-like phenotypes. D8 offers neurological protection by promoting BDNF-like signaling to support neuronal DNA repair and survival. D9 provides ocular protection by inhibiting VEGF pathways to prevent corneal and retinal damage. D10 and D11 supplement immune modulation and tissue regeneration axes, respectively, with modes of action involving receptor binding to balance immune responses and activate fibroblast growth factors for skin healing; all designed polypeptides are conceptualized with amphipathic structures for cell penetration, low immunogenicity, and enzymatic stability, though requiring further preclinical validation.

﻿Yaws is a neglected tropical disease caused by the spirochete *Treponema pallidum pertenue*, characterized by disfiguring skin ulcers, bone inflammation (osteoperiostitis), and potential tertiary deformities if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct skin contact in endemic, resource-limited regions. Current first-line therapy relies on azithromycin or benzathine penicillin, but emerging azithromycin resistance threatens eradication efforts. The pathophysiology involves bacterial evasion of host immunity via antigenic variation (e.g., TprK protein), chronic inflammation, impaired wound healing, and iron-dependent bacterial metabolism. The proposed polypeptide set addresses seven therapeutic axes: (1) direct antimicrobial activity using endogenous host defense peptides (LL-37, HBD-3, Bac7); (2) disruption of bacterial iron acquisition via lactoferricin B; (3) enhancement of adaptive immunity through thymic regulators (Epitalon, Thymosin {alpha}1); (4) acceleration of tissue repair for chronic ulcers (BPC-157, GHK); (5) suppression of destructive inflammation (D1-cyclic); (6) inhibition of spirochete motility and biofilm-like persistence (D2-linear); and (7) circumvention of antibiotic resistance using gallium-mimetic (D3-helical) and TprK-blocking (D4-stapled) designed peptides. Real-world polypeptides are prioritized for clinical translatability, while designed peptides ensure comprehensive mechanistic coverage where natural options are insufficient.

﻿Yellow fever is an acute mosquito-borne viral illness caused by the yellow fever virus (YFV), a single-stranded RNA flavivirus. Clinical presentation ranges from mild flu-like symptoms to severe disease with jaundice, hemorrhagic manifestations, liver failure, and mortality rates of 20-50% in severe cases.

Primary pathophysiological axes include viral entry and membrane fusion (envelope protein-mediated), replication complex activity (NS3 protease and NS5 polymerase), direct cytopathic effects on hepatocytes, and dysregulated immune response leading to cytokine storm in severe cases. No approved specific antiviral therapy exists; management is supportive, with a highly effective live-attenuated vaccine for prevention. Comprehensive tool-assisted searches (PubMed, web sources) identified in vitro research on peptide-based inhibitors (e.g., NS3 substrate-derived peptidic inhibitors, claudin-derived fusion blockers active against YFV, frog skin AMPs with anti-YFV activity) but no clinical therapeutic polypeptides, no established mature sequences for treatment, and no trials for acute infection (shortfall from min_real_polypeptides=14 documented; research limited to preclinical/single studies without verifiable therapeutic application). 0 real-world polypeptides used; supplemented with 18 designed conceptual short scaffolds (flagged as designed) incorporating >=2 non-standard residues for stability/specificity, strict diversity (>50% difference, <=20% similarity), low hydrophobicity/aromatics, no excessive repeats, and >=30% cyclic (disulfide-constrained) for conformational rigidity. Full coverage across antiviral axes achieved.

﻿Zellweger syndrome (ZS), the most severe form of Zellweger spectrum disorders (ZSD), is a rare autosomal recessive peroxisomal biogenesis disorder caused by pathogenic variants in one of at least 13 PEX genes essential for peroxisome assembly and import of peroxisomal matrix enzymes. Defective peroxisome biogenesis results in absent or severely reduced functional peroxisomes, leading to profound metabolic disruptions including toxic accumulation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA), branched-chain fatty acids (phytanic/pristanic acids), and bile acid intermediates; deficiency of ether phospholipids (plasmalogens); elevated pipecolic acid; and secondary oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Clinically, ZS presents neonatally with characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism (high forehead, large fontanelles, flat face), profound hypotonia, seizures, feeding difficulties, liver dysfunction with cholestasis, renal cysts, sensorineural hearing loss, retinal degeneration, calcific stippling of patellae/epiphyses, and neuronal migration defects causing polymicrogyria/pachygyria and hypomyelination; most affected infants do not achieve developmental milestones and succumb within the first year of life due to progressive neurological deterioration, respiratory complications, or liver failure.

The proposed polypeptides are entirely conceptually designed short sequences, as comprehensive searches across PubMed, clinicaltrials.gov, patents, and related sources identified no real-world polypeptide, peptide, or protein therapeutics (established, investigational, preclinical, or patented) specifically for Zellweger syndrome or peroxisomal biogenesis disorders; current management is supportive (e.g., gastrostomy feeding, seizure control, bile acid supplementation) with emerging experimental approaches limited to gene therapy (AAV-PEX1), pharmacological chaperones for select misfolded PEX proteins, and antioxidants, none involving short polypeptides. These designed polypeptides target five core mechanistic axes derived from established pathophysiology: (1) defective peroxisome biogenesis and assembly, addressed by the first designed polypeptide to conceptually enhance PEX protein stability or import; (2) VLCFA accumulation and membrane toxicity, targeted by the second designed polypeptide to mitigate lipid perturbation; (3) plasmalogen deficiency impairing myelin and cellular integrity, modulated by the third designed polypeptide to support ether lipid homeostasis; (4) excessive oxidative stress from impaired ROS detoxification, countered by the fourth designed polypeptide with antioxidant properties; (5) secondary neuroinflammation and neuronal damage, ameliorated by the fifth designed polypeptide to dampen inflammatory cascades. Collectively, these provide multi-axis conceptual coverage aiming to alleviate metabolic toxicity, protect neural tissue, and potentially extend survival, with feasibility informed by pathway validation in ZSD models and parallels in related metabolic disorders.
